cia-0000103318:
Iraq: Reducing Foreign Labor Force is declassified CIA document 0000103318, dated August 5, 1989 in the catalog. The sample text is dated September 29, 1989, weeks later than the catalog entry. It reports Baghdad preparing to demobilize five divisions by mid-October while cutting the number of foreign workers in Iraq.

The stated aims were to free jobs for returning soldiers and to conserve hard currency for development and imports. New limits would sharply cut what foreign workers could convert and send home, halving yearly remittances to about one billion dollars. About one thousand more Egyptians were leaving than entering each day, the embassy reported.
cia-0000104918:
Mocada Barracks Anniversary Ceremony Described is declassified CIA document 0000104918, dated August 3, 1992 in the catalog. The sample is an FBIS daily report dated September 3, 1992, from Havana radio and television networks. It carries a speech by Fidel Castro at a ceremony in Cienfuegos, given live.

The ceremony marked the thirty-ninth anniversary of the attack on the Moncada Barracks. It also marked the thirty-fifth anniversary of the Cienfuegos uprising, the report header says. Castro addressed relatives of the combatants of July 26 and of September 5, in the text's opening. The item is a full speech text, not a short summary.
cia-0000107418: Dated February 3, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000107418 promises new information on South Africa's nuclear program. Its heading misspells information as Infromation and Africa as Afirca. A South African-Israeli nuclear link is named next, before the heading breaks off at Nuc. The update is presented as new in its own first word. The brief record preserves both misspellings and the broken ending as released.
cia-0000112818: Propaganda in Shanghai - Subversive Activities is the heading, with its date marked as an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112818, dated January 1, 1945. The title pairs propaganda and subversive activities in one wartime city, Shanghai. No person or group is named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note with the subject as released.
cia-0000119718: From September 1956, a CIA briefing paper for the National Security Council on Soviet policy toward the satellite states. It lays out how Moscow managed its East European allies as unrest spread among them that autumn. Briefings of this rank show how the Kremlin's handling of its allies looked from Washington at a tense moment in the bloc's history.
cia-0000132418: The Caribbean through 1960 is forecast in a CIA report dated November 2, 1959. Its subject line runs the first two words together as Thesituation, a typing slip kept from the original. Written as 1959 closed, the report looks a full year ahead. The coming year would bring invasion planning against Cuba into full swing, and the report sets out the region's expected course.
cia-0000135818: From 5 March 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on a reported plot against President Somoza of Nicaragua, sent as a warning to the Lincoln station. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000135918: The declassified CIA cable dated 2 May 1954 takes up why the field failed to act on a task. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136118: 6 April 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about an answer to a reference about a sabotage operation, the scare turning into a plan. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136318: A trip by the figure called REELFOOT is the business of this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. The station wants to learn his thinking, plant ideas with him, and keep his timing sensible on announcing a provisional government, which should clear through LINCOLN first if possible. A side trip is ruled out without further specific authority because the situation is unclear. The cable shows headquarters stage-managing the political face of the PBSUCCESS operation.
cia-0000137318: The Diaz Lanz case has aroused Castro, this CIA briefing reports. It served the 411th National Security Council meeting on 16 July 1959. Asylum and public attention for this traitor anger most Cuban officials. The case dramatizes the communist danger for the Cuban public, the briefing argues. Castro called the defection a cruel blow to the revolution. He is irritable and jumpy. But he stays determined to use any means, including force. Cuban arms missions are in Europe. President Urrutia publicly attacked communism on 13 July.
un-ga-res-a-69-18:
Afghanistan's long war and slow rebuild fill Resolution A/69/18, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before, and the Security Council's texts on the land, among them votes of October 2013 and March 2014. It states firm fealty to Afghanistan's freedom, unity, and whole land. The land's rich mix of peoples and its deep past are honored in the text.

The world pledge to Afghanistan runs long, the text holds, and it must grow ever more Afghan-led. The Bonn meeting of December 2011 frames the path: from a time of handover to a decade of deep change. States back the Kabul path, by which Afghan hands take the lead in rule, safety, and growth.
un-sc-res-418: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 418, entered in this catalog under the year 1978. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-718: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 718, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1991. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1918:
Somali piracy reached into the courtroom in Resolution 1918, adopted in April 2010. Pirate attacks off the Horn of Africa were capturing ships and crews for ransom at record rates. Navies could seize pirates, but states struggled to prosecute and jail them.

The text asks the Secretary-General to report within three months on options for trying pirates, including special courts in the region. It urges all states to make piracy a crime in their own laws. Readers get the legal half of the piracy crisis, the part that continued after the warships left.
cia-0000136618: The 2506 Brigade papers include this Spanish-language item under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, the estimate flagged in the catalog. The brigade was then training in secret for Cuba. No subject is stated in the record for this document. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, grouped with similar estimated-date records from the turn of the year in the exile force's files.
plos-pone-0000018:
Virginia Zaleskas, Daniela Krause, Katherine Lazarides, and co-authors modeled a human blood disease in mice in 2006. A single mutation, JAK2 V617F, drives polycythemia vera, a condition where the body makes far too many red blood cells. The team gave mice the mutation and studied both how the disease develops and how it might be treated.

Their work traces the molecular pathogenesis, the chain from one faulty gene to thickened blood and its risks. They also tested therapy against the mutant pathway in the same animals. A mouse that faithfully mirrors the human illness lets researchers screen treatments before any patient is exposed, and this study built and used that mirror.
cia-0000132618:
Item ten in a CIA Latin America series, dated 1960, reports anti-communist sentiment mounting on the Havana waterfront. The waterfront meant the docks, where port workers loaded and unloaded the ships Cuba lived by. A year into Fidel Castro's rule, the agency was watching for signs of working-class discontent inside Cuba, and this report says it found some among the men on the piers.

Short reports of this kind fed Washington's picture of how firm Castro's grip really was. Sentiment on the docks mattered because ports were union strongholds and pressure points in Cuba's economy. Read now, the piece is a small, dated gauge of mood in Havana at a moment when the United States was deciding how hard to push against the new government.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d18: Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on July 4, 1943, answering the president's letter of four days before. The exchange is Document 18 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. China's leader rarely let a week pass without reminding Washington of his front's needs. The catalog gives the date and the correspondents and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the run-up to Chiang's Cairo appearance.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d118: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 12, 1943, the day he sailed for the Mediterranean. The letter is Document 118 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter sent on sailing day was among the last the president could dispatch before radio silence at sea. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names. It is preserved in the Foreign Relations series, in the voyage sequence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d218:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington from Ankara on 14 November 1943 with a detailed account of Turkish foreign minister Numan Menemencioğlu's talks with Anthony Eden in Cairo. Marked most secret, it relays Numan's own summary, given the night before, plus his later talk with the British ambassador.

Numan's points run to eight. Turkey would rather discuss joining the war than mere air bases, since bases mean war anyway. Her army cannot attack, and without firm Allied air cover Istanbul and Izmir face ruin, railways would be wrecked, and hunger would follow. Eden named no Allied help and set a deadline of 3 December, far too soon. Yet Numan adds that Turkish hesitation would vanish if Anglo-American forces landed in the Balkans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d318:
General John Hilldring, head of the War Department's Civil Affairs Division, sent a secret priority cable from Washington on 25 November 1943 to John McCloy at Cairo. Marked eyes only and signed Marshall, it reports the State Department's views after a conference with Secretary Hull and James Dunn.

On the Rankin C plan for a sudden German collapse, State has no preference between northern and southern zones for the United States. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d418:

Molotov explained two things. Reuters, from Lisbon, had predicted the meeting, and Senator Connally had announced it was going on. Tass could not ignore those reports, so it stated the truth to end rumors that were harming the allies' mutual interests. Harriman gives his own opinion plainly: the British and the Americans have more to explain to the Soviet government than the Soviets have to them. He therefore recommends that Washington not pursue the matter further with Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d518:
Clarence E. Gauss, the American ambassador in China, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 14, 1943. Gauss served in Chungking, China's wartime capital. Weeks earlier, the Cairo Declaration had promised that lands taken by Japan would be returned to China. The State Department printed his report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Gauss was a blunt reporter of China's troubles: inflation, military weakness, and friction between Chungking and Washington. His cables give the view from inside an ally whose strength the declarations praised but whose condition worried its friends. For readers, this report tests the fine words of Cairo against the facts as the man on the spot saw them.
frus-1944-quebec-d18:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on August 4, 1944, as the Allied breakout from Normandy gathered speed. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

August opened with the German front in France collapsing, Paris a month from liberation, and the Warsaw uprising beginning far to the east. Churchill's letters that month reached for the political meaning of the military triumph. For readers, this message belongs to the heady, dangerous weeks when the war's end came into sight and the leaders' correspondence turned increasingly to the Europe that victory would create.
frus-1944-quebec-d118:
From Caserta, Italy, on September 4, 1944, acting political adviser Carmel Offie telegraphed Washington a report from Polish commander General Sosnkowski. Sosnkowski had heard from General Bór, who led the Home Army inside Warsaw. The message reached the Allies through General Wilson, the Mediterranean commander, and it was grim.

Bór reported the Old Town lost and a serious breach in Warsaw's defenses. Food would last to September 7, bread only to September 5, and ammunition was running out. Sosnkowski appealed for large-scale air operations from Italian bases, with British crews taking part. Without material help fast, he warned, Polish endurance alone could not save the city.
frus-1944-quebec-d218:
C.C.S. 320/27, approved by the Combined Chiefs at Quebec on September 16, 1944, states the allocation of occupation zones in Germany in operational terms. British forces under a British commander would occupy Germany west of the Rhine. East of the river, they would hold the land north of a line from Koblenz. That line followed the northern border of Hessen-Nassau to the Soviet area.

American forces would occupy the land east of the Rhine south of that line. Control of Bremen and Bremerhaven, with their staging areas, was vested in the American zone commander, although both ports lay inside the British area. American forces also received access through the western and northwestern seaports and passage through British-controlled territory. Exact boundaries could be drawn later.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d18: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on 5 November 1944, the day before Americans voted in the presidential election. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d118:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d218:

The Soviet government says it can place large orders on long-term credit, up to six billion dollars. The money would buy manufactured goods: oil pipes, rails, railroad cars, locomotives, and industrial equipment. It would also cover Lend-Lease orders not delivered before the war's end. The credit would run thirty years. Repayment would begin only on the last day of the ninth year, and end on the last day of the thirtieth. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d318:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d418:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d18:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d118:

Edwin Arnold titled his Victorian rendering of the Bhagavad Gita The Song Celestial. Arnold gave the battlefield dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna in flowing English verse rather than prose. The same scripture that other entries present in plainer dress sings here in nineteenth-century poetry.

Arjuna's doubt about fighting his kin opens the poem, and Krishna answers with teaching on duty, devotion, and the deathless self. Arnold's version was beloved in its day and introduced many English readers to the Gita. Readers comparing translations will notice how verse changes the pace: argument becomes song, and Krishna's counsel arrives with a hymn-like lift.
tob-10818:
Lewis Spence wrote An Introduction to Mythology for the curious beginner, ranging across Greek, Norse, Egyptian, and Celtic traditions and the mythologies of the Americas. Before retelling tales, Spence asks basic questions: what myths are, why societies make them, and how scholars read them. The survey ranges widely without drowning in detail.

Gods, creation stories, heroes, and flood tales are compared across cultures, with attention to ritual and nature explanations current in Spence's day. Some of his theories have aged, as introductory theories do. Still, as a friendly first expedition into comparative mythology, the book gives newcomers a map before they enter any single tradition deeply.
tob-0118:
John Robison taught science at Edinburgh. In Proofs of a Conspiracy, from 1797, he held that the Illuminati of Bavaria had lived on past their ban. Through lodges and clubs, he said, their agents worked to bring down the faiths and thrones of Europe. In his view, they had helped spark the French revolt.

Robison wrote as an insider of the world he charged, which gave the book force. George Washington got a copy and wrote back on it. Sound or not, the book is a founding text of plot lore. In it one can watch two hundred years of distrust of secret groups take shape.
tob-4118:
Plotinus, the last great philosopher of the ancient world, taught in Rome in the third century. His pupil Porphyry arranged his essays as the Six Enneads, fifty-four tractates in six groups of nine. Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page translated them into English of rare beauty.

All things flow from the One, says Plotinus, through Intellect and Soul, and the soul's task is the flight back to unity. His prose rises from strict argument to sudden rapture. MacKenna spent years polishing each page. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The translation's fame rests on making a hard thinker readable.
govdocs-archive_org-Russian-Active-Measu:
On March 22, 2018, the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence released its report on Russian active measures. The report closed the committee's look into Russian interference operations aimed at the United States, an inquiry that drew heavy public attention and sharp partisan argument.

Inside, the committee lays out its findings on what Russian actors did, and it adds recommendations meant to guard future elections. The document is written as an official record, with the committee's conclusions stated plainly. It stands as one of the main congressional accounts of the interference campaign and of the political fight that surrounded the inquiry itself.
govdocs-archive_org-TheEarthJournalFlatE:
The Earth was a journal of the zetetic movement, the Victorian campaigners who argued that the world is flat and that readers should trust only what they can test themselves. The scan holds an issue of the journal, filed with material dated to 1895.

The surviving pages open with the journal's advertising rates and subscription terms, before its articles begin. Even those business pages are telling: they show a movement organized enough to sell ads, take subscriptions, and publish on a schedule. For historians of fringe science, such journals are the primary record of how flat-earth belief organized and spread in the 1890s.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-18:
Michael L. Rodkinson's eighteenth volume pairs Tract Aboda Zara with Tract Horioth. Aboda Zara, 'strange worship,' sets the rules for Jewish life among pagan neighbors. Horioth, 'decisions,' treats what happens when courts or rulers themselves err in law.

Aboda Zara asks how close one may come to idols, their feasts, and their wine without joining their worship. Its rulings shaped daily trade between Jews and gentiles for centuries. Horioth then weighs the sacrifices owed when a court misleads the people, and when a king or high priest sins. The pairing puts private purity and public error in one frame.
doyle-new-revelation-1918:
Arthur Conan Doyle steps out for the faith in The New Revelation, his book of 1918. Doyle had made Holmes, the great sleuth of cold proof. War grief and long tests turned him to the dark room. Here he tells that path in plain words and claims the dead speak, with proof that passed his own strict checks through the years.

Crowds gasped that Holmes's sire could hold such faith. His fame made the book a world event at once. It took the faith from back rooms to the front page. Doyle gave his last years to its cause.
maier-atalanta-fugiens-1618:
Michael Maier, a German doctor at the court of Rudolf II, made this strange art book in Latin in 1618. Its title means Atalanta Fleeing, from a Greek myth of a swift maid and three gold apples. Maier was deep in the lore of alchemy and the Rosicrucian wave of his age.

The book holds fifty plates, each with a motto, a verse, a speech, and a piece of music. The songs are fugues, meant to be sung as the plates are viewed. It stands as the most famed work of art to come from the alchemist world.
symmes-circular-no-1-1818:
John Cleves Symmes, a former army captain in Ohio, sent this short circular round the world in 1818. In it he made a bold claim about the shape of the earth. He asked learned men and the public to hear him out.

Symmes held that the earth is hollow, with wide holes at both poles. Through those holes, he said, ships could sail to warm seas and lands inside the globe. The one page claim is the birth writ of the American hollow earth craze that ran for a hundred years.
cuvier-theory-of-earth-1818:
Georges Cuvier, the great French master of the bones of dead beasts, set out his scheme of the earth's past in this work. Robert Kerr turned it into English, and this text is from 1818. Cuvier could rebuild a whole beast from a few bones, and men took his word as law.

He held that the earth had seen a string of vast floods and new sets of life. He also held, flat, that no fossil man exists, and none would be found. The men who claimed deep age for man spent the next fifty years in work to break that word.
frankenstein-1818:
Mary Shelley wrote this novel at the age of twenty, and it came out with no name on it in 1818. The first print ran in three parts, the form books took in that age. Its full title adds the words 'The Modern Prometheus' to the name Frankenstein.

Victor Frankenstein, a young man of science, builds a man from dead parts and gives it life. The being, left alone and spurned, turns to rage and grief and asks why it was made at all. The book is the first true work of science fiction, and its theme still haunts us.
heindel-message-of-stars-1918:
Max Heindel and Augusta Foss Heindel wrote The Message of the Stars in 1918. The book is a full text of star lore from the Rosicrucian school. It teaches how to cast and read a birth chart. The Heindels ran the Rosicrucian Fellowship in California.

Signs, houses, and planets each get rules for their force on health and fate. Health takes a large place, with charts of the sick read in full. The pair hold that stars show trends, not fixed doom. The book is a base text of the new esoteric star lore.
taylor-life-of-pythagoras-1818:
Iamblichus wrote the Life of Pythagoras in the late Roman age. Thomas Taylor gave the work English dress in 1818. Pythagoras was the Greek sage at the root of math, music, and soul lore. Few lives from the old world are so wrapped in myth.

The life tells of the sage's trips to Egypt and the East for lore. It tells too of his school in Italy, its rules, and its strange bans. Short wise rules of the sage close the book. The text is the base life of the man who shaped the West's hid line.
plotinus-enneads-guthrie-1918:
Plotinus wrote the tracts that his pupil Porphyry set as the Enneads. Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie gave the full set English dress in 1918. Plotinus was a Greek sage in Rome in the third century. His thought is the root of Neoplatonism and of much of the West's hid line.

Six sets of nine tracts make up the whole work. The One stands at the top, past thought and past name. Mind and Soul flow from it, and the world of sense comes last. Guthrie's full dress let English readers take the whole climb at last.
rodkinson-talmud-vol-5-1918:
Michael L. Rodkinson gave the Babylonian Talmud English dress in a vast set. Book Five of that set came out in 1918. The Talmud is the great store of Jewish law and lore. It grew from talks of rabbis over scores of years in Babylon.

Rodkinson's set was the first bid to give the whole Talmud to English readers. Book Five is one step in a set of twenty in his full plan. Law, tales, and keen debate on the Torah fill its pages. The work is rough in parts, but it broke new ground in its day.
dostoevsky-notes-from-underground-garnet:
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote Notes from the Underground in Russian, and Constance Garnett made this English version in 1918. Many call the short book the founding text of existentialist fiction in the West. Its speaker has no name and writes from a cellar of spite in Petersburg.

The Underground Man rails at reason, progress, and the dream of a crystal palace. He claims man will choose pain and chaos just to prove he is free. In the tale half, he humiliates himself before old school friends at dinner. He then crushes Liza, a girl who shows him love he cannot accept or return. The book's bitter voice still shocks readers with its raw, modern sting.
sandburg-cornhuskers-1918:
Carl Sandburg published Cornhuskers in 1918, his sweeping second collection of Midwest harvests, wars, and workers in verse. The book confirmed Sandburg as the prairie poet of the American heartland in 1918. Harvest fields and troop trains share its pages, for America was feeding armies and sending its sons abroad.

Prairie, the long opening poem, rolls through grass, corn, railroads, and the peoples who layered the Midwest over centuries. War poems mourn and honor the young men leaving farms for France in the great conflict overseas then raging. Work songs, folk figures, and love lyrics keep the collection varied in mood and music from piece to piece. Sandburg's free verse stays plainspoken, built for the ear and the platform as much as the page in print. The volume deepens Chicago Poems' promise into a whole region's epic of labor.
rilke-poems-1918:
Rainer Maria Rilke was a German-language poet born in Prague. Jessie Lemont translated a selection of his early poems in 1918, the first book of Rilke in English. The poems come from his work before the famous later collections. They already show his eye for objects, angels, and inner life.

Many pieces are quiet prayers, portraits, or scenes from nature and art. Rilke turns simple things into signs of a deeper world. Lemont's versions are free at times, yet they carried his voice to new readers. This early selection lets readers watch a major poet taking shape. It is a gentle entry into his work.
cather-my-antonia-1918:
Willa Cather published My Antonia in 1918, a novel told by Jim Burden, a lawyer looking back. Jim recalls his boyhood in Nebraska and his friend Antonia Shimerda. Antonia came from Bohemia as a girl and worked hard on her family's rough farm. Her warmth and strength mark everyone who knows her.

Jim leaves for school and a career while Antonia stays close to the land. Her life includes hardship and betrayal, yet she builds a full family and farm. Cather drew on her own Nebraska childhood and a real immigrant friend. The book is a tender hymn to pioneer women. Many readers count it her finest novel.
russell-mysticism-logic-1918:
Bertrand Russell published Mysticism and Logic in 1918, a set of essays for general readers. The title essay contrasts mystical insight with logical clarity in philosophy. Russell respects the mystic's vision but defends reason as the safer guide. Other essays treat mathematics, causation, knowledge, and free will.

The book includes work from the era of his essay On Denoting, a classic of analysis. Russell writes with wit and unusual plainness for a technical thinker. The collection sold analytic philosophy to the public as no book had before. It remains a fine first Russell. Its defense of reason still reads as bracing and humane.
russell-roads-freedom-1918:
Bertrand Russell published Roads to Freedom in 1918, a work of political philosophy written during the First World War. Russell weighs three rival paths: socialism, anarchism, and syndicalism. He finds merit and danger in each. His own hope is a form of guild socialism with wide personal freedom.

He attacks the wage system, the power of the state, and war as linked evils. Education, leisure, and free thought receive strong defense. Russell wrote as a pacifist facing prison for his views. The book is a classic of libertarian socialism in English. It shows his moral passion alongside his logic.
freud-totem-taboo-brill-1918:
Sigmund Freud published Totem and Taboo in German in 1913. The English text here is A. A. Brill's translation of 1918. Freud brings psychoanalysis to anthropology, the study of early peoples. He compares taboos and totem rites with the fears of his neurotic patients.

His boldest claim tells of a primal horde whose sons killed and ate their father. Guilt from that deed, he argues, founded morality, religion, and social rules. Scholars of anthropology have largely rejected the story as history. As a myth of origins, it shaped much debate on culture. The book remains a daring, disputed classic of its field.
browne-materials-babi-religion-1918:
Edward Granville Browne, the Cambridge orientalist, gathered Materials for the Study of the Babi Religion in 1918. The Babis were the followers of the Bab, the Persian prophet whose movement gave birth to the Baha'i faith. Browne had traveled in Persia and met believers when few Westerners had.

The volume prints Babi scriptures, histories, letters, and Browne's own notes in translation, with the Persian background explained. It preserves texts that were hard to find outside the community itself. Scholars still use Browne's source-book as a doorway into the movement's first, persecuted years. Browne's sympathy for the persecuted Babis colors every page he wrote on them.
warfield-counterfeit-miracles-1918:
Benjamin Warfield taught at Princeton and defended the full trustworthiness of the Bible all his life. His Counterfeit Miracles, published in 1918, argues that true miracles belonged to the age of the apostles and then ceased. It is the classic Princeton case against later miracle claims.

Warfield tests the wonders claimed in his own day: faith healing, cures at Catholic shrines such as Lourdes, and the gifts claimed by new Pentecostal churches. He finds each claim weak where the miracles of the New Testament are strong. Churches that share his view still use the book to judge fresh reports of wonders.
mylius-opus-medico-chymicum-1618:
Johann Daniel Mylius was a Lutheran doctor whose Opus Medico-Chymicum came out in 1618. The work joins medicine and the furnace arts in three treatises. It served as his guide to the chemical remedies of the Paracelsian school.

Mylius tells the working doctor how to prepare remedies from metals and minerals, with furnaces, vessels, and doses spelled out step by step. Pictures and verses on the great work stand beside the practical recipes, in the manner of his age. The book shows how the new chemical medicine reached daily practice in the German lands. Doctors of his church and region read it as a trusted storehouse of cures.
town-system-of-speculative-masonry-1818:
Salem Town, an American Masonic educator, published A System of Speculative Masonry in 1818. Town set out the history and moral teaching of the craft in a clear, ordered form. He wrote for Masons who wanted a defense of their order and for readers outside it.

Town explained the degrees, symbols, and duties of speculative Masonry, which uses building tools as lessons for conduct. He argued that the lodge taught virtue, charity, and faith in God, not a threat to church or state. His system became a standard early American statement of what Masonry claimed to be and why its members valued it.
boethius-tractates-consolation-stewart-r:
The Loeb edition of Boethius appeared in 1918, with H F Stewart and E K Rand translating the Theological Tractates. Boethius, a Roman senator executed in 524, wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison. The Loeb volume pairs that famous work with his five shorter tracts on theology.

In the Consolation, Lady Philosophy visits Boethius in his cell and argues him out of despair over fortune, fame, and evil. The Stewart revision used the 1609 translation by I T for that text. The tractates treat the Trinity and related questions with strict logic. Together the works made Boethius the bridge between Roman and medieval thought for a thousand years.
kautsky-dictatorship-proletariat-1918:
Karl Kautsky published The Dictatorship of the Proletariat in 1918, and H J Stenning's English translation followed in 1919. Kautsky wrote in the first shock of the Russian Revolution. The old pope of Marxism, as some called him, now attacked Lenin's new regime in print.

Kautsky argued that the Bolsheviks had built a dictatorship over the workers, not of them, and that socialism without democracy must fail. Lenin answered with a furious pamphlet calling Kautsky a renegade. Their quarrel split world Marxism over a single question: can socialism come by votes and rights, or only by force? The book remains the classic democratic Marxist critique of Bolshevik rule.
kepler-epitome-astronomiae-copernicanae-:
Johannes Kepler published Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae between 1618 and 1621. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in Latin, its 1618 opening date in the record. The Epitome was the first textbook of heliocentric astronomy, written to teach the Copernican system plainly.

In question-and-answer form, Kepler set out the Sun-centered system and extended his laws to all the planets. The third law, linking each planet's period to its distance from the Sun, first appeared in this work's line of books. Church authorities placed the Epitome on the Index of banned books. Even so, it trained the generation that made heliocentric astronomy the common view of educated Europe.
byron-childe-harold-1818:
Lord Byron traveled through Portugal, Spain, Greece, and Albania after leaving England, and turned the trip into verse. The first cantos of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage appeared in 1812 and made him famous overnight. This text holds all four cantos, complete through the fourth, published in 1818.

Harold is a weary young nobleman drifting through lands marked by war and fallen empires. Byron mixes travel scenes with fierce reflections on freedom, tyranny, and loss. The later cantos pass through Belgium after Waterloo and down through Italy. The poem created the brooding Byronic hero and shaped Romantic poetry across Europe.
keats-endymion-1818:
John Keats wrote Endymion when he was twenty-one, testing whether he could sustain a long poem. It appeared in 1818, and hostile reviewers mocked it so fiercely that legend later blamed them for his early death. The poem retells a Greek myth in four books.

Endymion, a shepherd prince, dreams of the moon goddess and leaves his home to find her. His search crosses earth, sea, and underworld, meeting sorrowful lovers from other myths along the way. Keats fills the journey with lush description and youthful energy. The poem is uneven, as Keats admitted, but it shows his gift growing at full speed.
chekhov-wife-1918:
Garnett's 1918 Chekhov volume is named for The Wife, a tale told by an engineer named Asorin. Asorin's young wife runs famine relief in their district while their marriage cools into dislike. Watching her work among hungry peasants slowly changes his view of her and of himself.

Difficult People shows a family quarrel over a son's request for money, small in cause and deep in hurt. The Grasshopper follows a doctor's wife who worships artists and misses the worth of the quiet man at home. Each story turns on blindness inside a household. Chekhov judges no one outright, yet the verdicts land. The volume catches married life with rare honesty.
chekhov-witch-1918:
The Witch, and Other Stories came to English readers in 1918, in Constance Garnett's translation. The title tale traps a sexton and his wife in a snowbound church hut. When a lost mail driver shelters there, the wife is accused of witchcraft by her own bitter husband.

Peasants, a long story of village poverty, follows a Moscow waiter who returns sick to his home village. In the Ravine traces a peasant family torn by greed, forgery, and a shocking crime. These are among Chekhov's darkest pages on rural Russia. He writes of hunger, ignorance, and cruelty without softening them. The volume shows why his peasant tales shook Russian readers.
hammer-purgstall-mysterium-baphometis-18:
Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, the Viennese orientalist, published his Mysterium Baphometis Revelatum in 1818, in the Fundgruben des Orients. He argued, from trial records and carved stones, that the Knights Templar had secretly worshipped a Gnostic idol he called Baphomet. The memoir, in Latin with German notes, founded the modern Templar myth.

Hammer read the Templar trials as proof of an Ophite cult hidden in the order, and he saw its signs in fonts, seals, and statues across Europe. His learning was vast and his leaps were wild, and both fed the legend. Every later tale of Templar idolatry drinks from this spring. The text is the single most consequential work of Templar myth-making.
menapius-ad-responsum-1618:
F G Menapius published this short German answer, his Duplic, in 1618. The full German title calls it a brief reply to the response of Florentinus de Valentia. Valentia had defended the Rosicrucian brotherhood in a work called Rosa florescens, and Menapius refused to let the matter rest.

The pamphlet fires back point by point in the heated print war over the Rosicrucian manifestos. Each side claimed truth, and each side printed fast to hold the public ear. Menapius gives the critic's voice at full pitch in the fight of 1617 and 1618. Read beside Valentia's defense, it shows a debate held in pamphlets, not in person.
menapius-antikrisis-1618:
The Antikrisis of 1618 is F G Menapius's Latin counter to Florentinus de Valentia. Valentia had defended the Rosicrucian brotherhood in print, and Menapius answered in kind. The short title marks the work as a formal reply within a fast, sharp pamphlet exchange.

Menapius argues the critic's side of the 1618 fight over the Rosicrucian manifestos. He treats the brotherhood's claims as charges to be met, not wonders to be praised. Latin gave his answer reach among learned readers across Europe. The piece survives as one side of a two-sided quarrel, and it makes most sense read against the defense it attacks.
menapius-cento-virgilianus-1618:
F G Menapius took a strange path in 1618 with his Cento Virgilianus de Fratribus Roseae Crucis. A cento is a poem stitched from lines of an older poet, here Virgil, the great Latin epic voice. Menapius built his verses about the Brothers of the Rose Cross out of Virgil's own words.

The result carries the Rosicrucian manifesto fight into Latin verse, a form no plain pamphlet could match. Learned readers could enjoy the craft while they weighed the charge inside it. The poem stands as a rare literary fruit of the furor over the manifestos. It shows how deep that quarrel reached into the culture of its day.
valentia-rosa-florescens-1618:
Florentinus de Valentia, a Benedictine monk, published Rosa florescens in Latin in 1618. The title means the blooming rose, and the work answers slanders by F G Menapius from 1617. Menapius had attacked the Rosicrucian society in print, and Valentia rose to defend it.

Valentia rebuts the charges one by one, in the manner of a formal defense brief. His side of the exchange speaks for those who took the manifestos in earnest. The pamphlet war of those years was fought by such short, hot replies. Rosa florescens is the defense at its fullest, and it pairs with Menapius's attacks across the record.
grick-clypeum-veritatis-1618:
Friedrich Grick called his 1618 German work Clypeum veritatis, the Shield of Truth. The German subtitle calls it a short but thorough answer, and the claim fits the book. Grick wrote in the heat of the pamphlet war over the Rosicrucian manifestos, taking up the charges of F G Menapius.

Grick answers those charges at length, point by point, on behalf of the manifestos' claims. His defense ranks among the fullest printed in those years of furor. The tone is earnest: truth, he holds, needs a shield when slander strikes in print. For readers tracing the fight, Grick supplies the defense in its most complete early form.
cieza-war-of-chupas-markham-1918:
Pedro Cieza de León's War of Chupas, in Markham's translation of 1918, tells how the Almagrist revolt in Peru was broken. The battle of Chupas in 1542 pitted the royal forces against the followers of Almagro the younger. Cieza, the conquest's own annalist, narrates the campaign that led to that field.

He follows the rival armies through the Andes with his usual care for ground, weather, and men. The clash at Chupas ended the first great civil war of Spanish Peru. Cieza writes as the greatest chronicler the conquistadors produced, clear-eyed about their courage and their greed. This late volume of his wars completes a matched set in Markham's translations.
ward-psychological-principles-1918:
Late in his career, James Ward set down Psychological Principles in 1918 as his full system of psychology. Ward was a Cambridge philosopher who also helped shape British psychology as a field. His book treats the mind as active from the start. That stance set him apart from schools that built mind from passive sense data.

He covers attention, feeling, memory, and will as acts of a living subject. Each topic ties back to his wider view of a world of active agents. Teachers of his day treated the work as a standard statement. It sums up decades of his lectures. Modern readers meet here a rich, older psychology.
veblen-higher-learning-1918:
American universities fall under Veblen's knife in The Higher Learning in America, from 1918. Business principles, he charges, have captured the schools meant for disinterested learning. Boards of businessmen govern, and presidents act as executives chasing funds and growth. Scholarship bends toward show, numbers, and vocational training.

Veblen contrasts that order with the higher learning itself: inquiry pursued for its own sake. His subtitle, in effect, is a plea for scholars freed from captains of erudition. The attack became the classic institutionalist critique of education. Faculty still quote its charges a century later. Its satire stings because readers keep finding it true.
spr-proceedings-vol29-1916-1918:
Parts seventy two through seventy four and an appendix fill volume twenty nine, for 1916 to 1918. The war years weigh on every page of the SPR record. Sittings multiply as the bereaved seek word of the dead. The Society for Psychical Research tests those sittings with its old rigor.

Telepathy trials proceed in the background of the grief driven work. Apparition reports from the front and from home enter the files. The appendix gathers society business from three hard years. Volume twenty nine shows the archive under maximum strain. Its standards bend far less than its subject matter grows. Historians of the war's inner life use it.
lust-universal-naturopathic-encyclopedia:
Benedict Lust, the organizer of American naturopathy, packed his whole field into one fat volume in 1918. The Universal Naturopathic Encyclopedia, Directory and Buyers' Guide served as a year-book of drugless therapy. Lust gathered schools, healers, methods, and sellers of health goods between two covers.

Water cure, diet, massage, light, and air treatments all appear, along with lists of practitioners across the country. The directory pages show how wide the drugless movement had grown by the end of the First World War. For anyone tracing naturopathy's roots, the encyclopedia is a snapshot of the field at full stretch.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol18:
Liverpool issued Volume XVIII of the Journal of Discourses in 1877, the year Brigham Young died. Sermons by Young fill much of the volume, preached near the end of his thirty years of leadership. His counsellors, the Twelve, and others speak beside him, all preserved in shorthand reports.

No reader in 1877 could know the era was closing, which gives these pages their poignancy now. The teaching voice sounds as firm as ever, guiding a church about to pass to new hands. Volume XVIII thus holds a special place in the set: the founder-generation's near-final word.
waley-170-chinese-poems-1918:
Arthur Waley opened classical Chinese poetry to English readers with A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems in 1918. The anthology runs from the ancient Book of Songs to the Tang masters, above all Po Chü-i, Waley's favorite. His introduction explains Chinese verse with a clarity that taught a generation how to read it.

Farmers, exiles, courtiers, and old friends drinking wine speak in these short, luminous pieces. Waley's free renderings favor sense and feeling over rhyme, a method that reshaped translation itself. The book remains a landmark: the door through which English poetry first entered China's long tradition.
luzumiyat-rihani-1918:
Ameen Rihani selected and translated The Luzumiyat of Abu'l-Ala in 1918, introducing the blind Syrian poet to English readers. Abu'l-Ala al-Ma'arri, who lived from 973 to 1057, lost his sight as a child and spent his life in skeptical thought. His Luzumiyat, poems he called unnecessarily required, question fate, faith, and human pride.

Rihani, himself a bridge between Arabic and English letters, chose verses that show the poet's bite and pity. Death, vanity, and the cruelty of custom take the lash, while honest folk get tenderness. The selection remains a sharp door into one of Arabic poetry's most freethinking voices.
joyce-exiles-1918:
Exiles, published in 1918, is the only play Joyce completed. He wrote it in the Ibsen manner he admired: a quiet surface, a few rooms, and a moral trap closing slowly on everyone inside.

Richard Rowan, a Dublin writer, returns home from exile with his wife Bertha and their son. His friend Robert presses his love on Bertha, and Richard, instead of forbidding it, seems to push them together in a test of freedom and trust. Nobody escapes the test unhurt. The play asks whether love can survive total honesty, and it leaves the answer painfully open.
eliot-ezra-pound-metric-poetry-1918:
Eliot published this short study of Ezra Pound in 1918, without his name on it. It examines the verse of his friend and champion, the American poet then leading London's modernist charge.

Eliot works through Pound's metrics, his handling of rhythm and line, and his debts to Provençal and Chinese poetry. The tone is technical and admiring at once: one young revolutionary explaining another's craft to a puzzled public. Pound had discovered Eliot and pushed his work into print, and this book partly returns the favor. It is a rare record of modernism's makers theorizing each other mid-revolution.
yeats-per-amica-1918:
Per Amica Silentia Lunae, published in 1918, is Yeats's short book of occult philosophy, written as he began the system that became A Vision. Its Latin title means 'through the friendly silences of the moon'.

The book holds two essays, 'Anima Hominis' and 'Anima Mundi', and the dialogue poem 'Ego Dominus Tuus'. Yeats argues that each soul seeks its opposite, its anti-self, and that a great soul of the world stores the images poets draw on. The ideas are strange, but the prose is among his finest. It is the seedbed of his later work and thought.
wlewis-tarr-1918:
Tarr, published in 1918, is Wyndham Lewis's novel of Parisian art life before the First World War. Frederick Tarr, an English artist, tries to free himself from his German fiancee Bertha and from the bohemian swirl of studios, duels, and dances.

Around him, the painter Kreisler careens toward violence and absurdity. Lewis writes in a hard, glittering style meant to match his vorticist painting: people as machines of appetite and pose. The comedy is savage and the energy enormous. Tarr is modernism's most aggressive novel, a blast against sentiment from the movement's wildest talent. It still divides readers sharply.
russell-logical-atomism-1918:
The Philosophy of Logical Atomism prints the lectures Russell gave in London in 1918. They are his clearest public statement of the system he built with the young Wittgenstein in mind. The world, he argues, is made of facts, not things.

Lecture by lecture he analyzes statements, names, and descriptions. He shows how language can be rebuilt to mirror the structure of fact. Particulars and universals, the atoms of logic, replace the grand systems of older thought. Russell speaks with unusual openness about a philosophy still in motion. These lectures are the best spoken introduction to the founding program of analytic philosophy.
solovyov-justification-good-1918:
The Justification of the Good, published in English in 1918 in Nathalie A. Duddington's translation, is Vladimir Solovyov's moral philosophy. Solovyov, Russia's greatest religious thinker, set out to ground ethics in an absolute good rather than in custom or command.

He builds morals from three natural roots, shame, pity, and reverence, and develops them into a full account of personal and social duty. Against both empty formalism and crude use-ethics, he argues the good must be justified as a whole way of life. The book is the centerpiece of his system. It introduced many English readers to Russian religious thought.
plos-pone-0003418:
Ruth Bollongino, Julia Elsner, and Jean-Denis Vigne read cattle DNA for this 2008 study. Europe's first farm cattle came from the Near East long ago. Earlier DNA work confirmed that origin but could not test male lines. The question was whether wild European bulls, called aurochs, later bred with farm herds.

The team checked Y-chromosome markers, which pass from fathers to sons. They looked at both ancient bones and modern cattle. The markers showed no sign of mixing with wild male aurochs. Farm herds and wild herds seem to have stayed apart.
plos-pone-0003518:
Valérie Kédinger and co-authors followed a shuttle protein at cell borders in this 2008 paper. TRAF4 had plenty of evidence for a key biological role. Yet how it works inside cells stayed unclear. Tight junctions are the seals that join one cell sheet to the next.

Using imaging methods, the team saw TRAF4 move in and out of those junctions. It acts as a dynamic shuttle tied to junction upkeep. That movement supports the balance of the epithelium, the body's lining tissue. One protein thus serves both signaling and structural roles.
plos-pone-0003618:
Catriona S. Bradshaw, Marcus Y. Chen, and Christopher K. Fairley followed a stubborn infection after treatment in this 2008 study. Mycoplasma genitalium causes genital infection in men and women. Patients at a Melbourne sexual health centre received azithromycin therapy. The standard course was a single one-gram dose.

The team determined clinical outcomes and cure rates after that dose. Some infections persisted following therapy, as the title records. Persistence flags a growing treatment problem for this infection. Clinicians may need new drugs or longer courses. This infection is often missed, since tests for it are not routine in clinics.
plos-pone-0003718:
Steven V. Vollmer and David I. Kline published this coral study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Disease outbreaks have done heavy damage to tropical reefs and to the corals that build them. Almost nothing was known about whether corals themselves can resist infection. The authors studied threatened staghorn corals.

They found natural variation in disease resistance among the corals. Some hosts resisted infection where others fell ill. That first evidence of coral resistance matters for reefs in crisis, since resistant stock could seed recovery and guide which corals to protect or breed.
plos-pone-0003818:
Guenter Albrecht-Buehler published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Mammalian genomes hold a strange feature: stretches longer than fifty bases made only of the letters G and A. Chance says such pure GA-sequences should be vanishingly rare. Yet they occur across many species.

The author describes the properties and distribution of these sequences in human, chimpanzee, dog, cat, rat, and mouse genomes. Their chromosomes contain far more of them than random expectation allows. The census of these odd repeats raises the question of what, if anything, they do in the genome.
plos-pone-0003918:
Taisheng Li, Yi Dai, Jiqiu Kuang, and co-authors compared three HIV drug plans in China in 2008. All three plans were built on the drug nevirapine and used generic drugs. The study enrolled adults with HIV-1 who had never taken such drugs. It ran at several centers as a forward-looking cohort.

A total of 198 patients took part across the three treatment arms. The team judged how well each plan controlled the virus and how safe each was. Real-world comparisons help clinics pick plans they can sustain. The results speak to national programs relying on low-cost generic drugs.
plos-pone-0004018:
Alexander S. Klyubin, Daniel Polani, and Chrystopher L. Nehaniv proposed an information rule for robot and animal behavior in 2008. Sensorimotor systems process information as their central resource. The authors define a measure of how well an agent senses and acts. It gauges the options an organism keeps open for its future.

Their PLOS ONE article argues agents should keep their options open. That drive can produce sensible behavior without fixed goals. The principle speaks to robotics, where simple rules must guide machines. It also offers a lens on why animals explore and play. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004118:
Amy Fulton, Sarah T. Peters, Gillian A. Perkins, and co-authors treated a horse herpesvirus with RNA interference in 2009. Equine herpesvirus type 1 spreads through nasal secretions. It causes respiratory disease, nerve disorders, and abortions in horses. Current vaccines protect only partially against it.

Their PLOS ONE article reports RNA interference treated the infection effectively. Small RNAs can be designed to silence viral genes directly. Success in this respiratory infection supports RNA therapy in veterinary medicine. It may also guide similar work on human herpesviruses. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004218:
Lisa Creary and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fetal haemoglobin, or HbF, softens the severity of sickle cell disease, so factors that raise it matter to patients. The team investigated a region on chromosome 6, called a quantitative trait locus, that earlier work had linked to HbF levels.

They tested whether variants in this region are associated with HbF and with F cells, the red cells that carry fetal haemoglobin. Their subjects were healthy people of African descent and sickle cell patients. The study checks a genetic lead that could one day guide treatments raising fetal haemoglobin.
plos-pone-0004318:
Sureshkumar Balasubramanian and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Even when visible differences between plant strains are large, the underlying genetics are often complex. The causal regions must be found by quantitative trait locus mapping. Unfortunately, those mapping methods usually leave large confidence intervals, wide stretches of genome that might hold the gene.

The team present new advanced intercross-recombinant inbred lines of Arabidopsis thaliana for QTL mapping. Repeated crossing shuffles the genome more finely, narrowing the intervals. Better plant lines mean gene hunts end at a gene, not a neighbourhood.
plos-pone-0004418:
Separating many glowing colors inside a living brain is the problem taken up by Mathieu Ducros, Laurent Moreaux, Jonathan Bradley, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. New strains of mice can be bred to make several bright proteins at once in nerve cells. Those proteins help mark which cells are active, but their colors overlap and blur together.

The team tested a method called spectral unmixing, which pulls apart mixed color signals, deep in the smell center of the living mouse brain. They measured how well the method worked under real conditions, not just in theory. The findings guide researchers who use glowing markers to map nerve circuits and watch the brain at work.
plos-pone-0004518:
Removing a cell-cycle brake gene kills mouse embryos very early, report Yong Kim, Jim McBride, Lauren Kimlin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene is Cdk2ap1, also called p12. Its protein restrains CDK2, an engine that pushes cells from the resting phase into copying their DNA.

The team inactivated the gene in mice. Most embryos died between the third and fifth day after conception, before implantation is complete. Timed studies of pregnancies pinpointed that window. A gene whose loss is lethal so early is plainly doing essential work in the first cell divisions. The finding also warns that drugs aimed at this pathway would need great care around early development and fertility.
plos-pone-0004618:
Thinking about yourself switches on a strip of brain called the anterior insula, show Gemma Modinos, Johan Ormel, and Andre Aleman in PLOS ONE in 2009. Functional neuroimaging studies had suggested that midline frontoparietal regions, along the brain's center seam, are at the core of self-related processes. The insula, buried deep in the side of the brain, was reported in some studies but got little attention.

The team examined anterior insula activation during self-reflection. The insula is best known for sensing the body's inner state: heartbeat, gut feelings, and pain. If self-reflection engages it, then thinking about oneself is partly a bodily act, not a purely abstract one. That matters for disorders where self-awareness goes wrong, from depression to schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0004718:
Jelle van Zweden and colleagues tested if ant queen egg marks found in the lab hold true in nature, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Lab tests can give crisp proof for a claim, but only if they match complex real life. That match is seldom checked in a direct way, the authors note.

Queen ants mark their eggs with a scent that workers can read. The team compared neat lab setups with the mess of real nests. Their check shows where simple tests mislead and where they hold. The lesson reaches past ants to all lab based claims about animal behavior.
mayakovsky-chelovek-man-1918:
Vladimir Mayakovsky's long poem Man, printed in Russian in 1918, lifts one man's life to a cosmic scale. The poet-hero loves, despairs, and dies, then rises again in triumph. Around him swirls the revolt that promised to remake Russia and the world.

Mayakovsky uses his bold stepped lines and loud, urgent voice throughout. Love turns to pain, pain to revolt, and revolt to a strange new faith. The poem mixes private grief with public hope. It stands as the great inner life story of Russian Futurism, one soul stretched to the size of an age.
j-p-jacobsen-marie-grubbe-a-lady-of-the-:
Marie Grubbe was a real Danish noblewoman of the seventeenth century, and Jacobsen's novel, here in the 1918 English version, tells her fall. Born to rank and wealth, she throws both away for love. She ends her days as a ferryman's wife, far below her birth.

Jacobsen treats her not as a scandal but as a fierce, sensual soul. Each marriage and each loss strips away pride and safety. Her will to live on her own terms never breaks. The novel stands as a bold tale of a woman who would not be tamed by rank, church, or shame.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-18:
Fear closes in through Volume 18, from 1898, on the Hurons of 1640 and 1641. Raids strike from many sides as the Iroquois wars draw tight. Thwaites prints letters that carry the first clear notes of doom.

Priests describe burned fields, blocked rivers, and friends lost to ambush. Still the chapels fill, and still the work of teaching goes on. Courage under a growing shadow gives these reports their force. The drama of the whole series sharpens from this point on. Readers can feel the walls closing in around Huronia with each new report. Peace feels farther off with every season that passes.
journal-of-discourses-vol-18:
Volume Eighteen, from 1877, records the passing of the prophet himself. Young dies in August, and the apostles take up the kingdom's lead. The first transfer of power in Mormon history unfolds in these pages.

Sermons of grief give way to calm claims of unbroken authority. The apostles preach unity and prove the work can outlive its founder. No crack shows in the kingdom's frame as the reins change hands. Readers watch a new faith pass its first great test of survival. The founder rests, the mission rolls on, and the record shows both in full.
commons-history-of-labour-us-vol1-1918:
John Commons and his students published the first volume of the History of Labour in the United States in 1918. The Wisconsin team worked from newspapers, union records, and government reports to build a documentary history. Nothing on this scale had been tried for American workers before.

Volume 1 runs from the colonial era to the Civil War. It covers the first workingmen's parties, the fight for the ten-hour day, and the early growth of trade unions in the young republic. The editors let the records speak, with narrative tying the evidence together. The set became the foundation work of American labor history, and later scholars have built on its archive ever since, even when they argue with its judgments.
commons-history-of-labour-us-vol2-1918:
The second volume of Commons's History of Labour in the United States appeared in 1918 alongside the first. Commons led a team of researchers at Wisconsin who treated labor's past as a subject for documents, not legend. Their history aimed to show how American workers organized, struck, and bargained their way into national life.

Volume 2 carries the story from the Civil War to the end of the nineteenth century. It covers the Knights of Labor, the Haymarket affair of 1886, and the rise of the American Federation of Labor under Samuel Gompers. The narrative shows unions turning from broad reform crusades toward practical bargaining over wages and hours. With the first volume, it remains a standard starting point for the history of American labor.
simmel-konflikt-modernen-kultur-1918:
Simmel's Conflict of Modern Culture appeared in German in 1918, the year of his death and of Germany's defeat. The short book grew from a wartime lecture on the spiritual crisis of the age. Simmel, Berlin's most brilliant essayist on modern life, turned his method on the war-torn present itself.

His theme is the clash between life and form. Life forever creates forms, works of art, institutions, and creeds, then chafes against them and breaks them to live again. Modern culture, he argues, has sharpened that old conflict until form itself seems the enemy. The lecture reads as a farewell to a breaking world by a man who had taught Europe how to see it. Short as it is, the book distills Simmel's philosophy of culture into a single, somber argument.
soviet-constitution-1918:
The Russian Soviet Republic adopted its first constitution in 1918, months after the Bolsheviks seized power. The All-Russian Congress of Soviets approved the text in July, in the middle of a civil war. It was Lenin's October Revolution given the form of law, the first constitution of a self-declared socialist state.

The charter declares all power to lie with the soviets, the councils of workers, soldiers, and peasants. It strips former exploiters, landlords, capitalists, and priests, of the vote, and weights city votes above country ones. Private ownership of land is abolished in its opening declaration of rights. The founding document of the Soviet order was bold in promise and brief in life, replaced as the Union took shape. Its model, class rule written as law, influenced communist states for the rest of the century.
cia-0000008918:
An American F-105 pilot's death in Bac Thai province is recorded in a CIA report dated January 1974. Bac Thai, north of Hanoi, lay under the routes Thunderchief crews flew against the north. The report came a full year after American combat flights ended.

Deaths confirmed this late closed cases that had stayed open since wartime losses. Officials had to be sure before a missing man was declared dead. The file's care with province and aircraft type reflects that duty. It belongs to the slow postwar work of turning uncertainty into record, one airman at a time.
cia-0000009018:
An American seen working for the Viet Cong is the strange subject of a February 1972 CIA report. The file traveled with a cover memo addressed to a Bennett, a trace of its path through offices. Sightings of this kind raised hard questions: defector, prisoner under pressure, or mistaken identity?

Analysts could not ignore such reports, yet each demanded strict checking. A false claim could smear a captive; a true one changed a case entirely. The report preserves the allegation as received, with its official routing intact. It shows wartime intelligence handling its most puzzling category of sighting.
cia-0000009818:
An American pilot was captured near Stung Treng, an August 1970 report states, with enemy order of battle notes for the Stung Treng area attached. Stung Treng, in northern Cambodia, sat astride routes the Ho Chi Minh Trail used to enter South Vietnam. Pilots downed there fell into borderland captivity.

Pairing the capture with local enemy strength gave readers the setting: which units could hold or move him. Order of battle notes turned an incident into a usable file. The report shows incident reporting done whole, man and military landscape together. It belongs to the months when Cambodia's war was newly open.
cia-0000009918:
Four American pilots were captured near Ban Hang Long, in Houa Phan province, in January, an October 1967 report states. The village name matches the cave site in a companion report from the same month. Four pilots taken near one place suggests a hard season for aircraft over Sam Neua.

A capture report filed nine months after the event shows the delay built into Laos news. By October, the men's trail could already be cold or well documented elsewhere. Either way, the January date anchored their files' first chapter. The two Hang Long reports together give the cave prison a human count.
cia-0000012418:
Meeting number thirty-eight falls on October 5, 1961, deep in the final productive weeks. The colonel's autumn sittings in Paris were gathering the last full harvest. Within a year he would be arrested, tried, and shot in Moscow. None of that shadow lies on the record itself, which keeps the flat, numbered order of the sessions as they happened.

The thirty-eighth session's record continues the October run. Handlers asked, the source answered, and clerks numbered the pages. For readers, the page glows with hindsight: a great case in its final season, working at full strength.
cia-0000013618:
Brazil's prospects after its 1964 coup are weighed in a CIA paper from April 1965. The generals had taken the giant country a year before, ending a civilian government Washington had feared was drifting left. Their new regime was settling in: congress tamed, opponents jailed or exiled, and an economic team installed to remake the country's finances under military guard.

The paper assesses the coup's aftermath in the regime's first year. It reads the new order with the optimism Washington preferred at the time. For readers, it shows the dictatorship being graded early, by the ally that had welcomed its birth.
cia-0000013918: Four American soldiers of the First Air Cavalry Division were captured in Binh Dinh Province, in a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. The division fought hard in that coastal province. Losing four men from one unit in one area marked a sharp local blow. The note records their capture for the division's own grim ledger.
cia-0000015318: A letter to Sam Goudsmit from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated July 2, 1958. Strong thanks Goudsmit for his letter of August 14, the title's dates again askew. The Goudsmit thread ran through the whole Davidson affair. Even the slips show how much paper one man's claims could stir up. The Goudsmit letter is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015418: Anyone who photographed a strange object could be handed a CIA information sheet dated January 5, 1960. The form asks for the camera and lens, the date and time, the direction faced, and the place. It also asks how the object looked and moved. Standard questions turned wild claims into reports that photo experts could compare, check, and file in a common shape.
cia-0000022318: Words about Rudolf and Helen Abel, built around a letter of thanks from Helen, fill a CIA record dated in 1962. Rudolf Abel was the Soviet spy swapped for Gary Powers that year. A thank you letter from his wife adds a family note to a state bargain. The entry shows the swap's paper trail reaching into the Abel home.
cia-0000022618: Photo comparison case number 12,770 has its results kept in a CIA record dated in 1971. No man is named in the title, so the case stays a number here. Thousands of such cases built up as pictures came out of Southeast Asia. Each result either opened a lead or closed one, and both kinds of answer mattered to the search.
cia-0000045918:
Arab nationalism stood at high tide when CIA analysts wrote about it in July 1958. Egypt and Syria had just merged into one republic under Gamal Abdel Nasser, the movement's loudest champion. The paper treats that surge of feeling as a force shaping the whole Middle East.

It weighs how pride in Arab unity pressed on kings, parties, and armies across the region. It also asks what the movement meant for Western influence and for Israel's safety. Its judgments fed the debate over how far Nasser's appeal would spread. Read now, the paper catches the moment when Washington saw Arab nationalism as a central force to reckon with.
cia-0000049018: A CIA item from 1981 lays responsibility on the Treasury Police for the killings of six members of one family in El Salvador. The Treasury Police were among the security forces most feared for death-squad work. Naming a state force as the killer, in an official file, was the kind of charge the Truth Commission later weighed.
cia-0000049118: General Jose Guillermo Garcia Merino is the named subject of a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. Garcia had served as El Salvador's minister of defense in the war's bloodiest years. A file on such a man, kept this late, shows the system's long memory for its wartime commanders.
cia-0000049218: Francisco A. Moran is the named subject of a CIA item from 1992, kept with the Truth Commission records. His name echoes an earlier trace in this series, on a Francisco Antonio Moran, filed two years before. Single-name files like this one hold whatever the system gathered on a man across the war's end.
arxiv-2606-07718: This research write-up reached arXiv in 2026 with new results to share. It takes up the subject named in its title: A case study of evaluating AI agents on a neuroscience data-to-discovery pipeline. The subject area is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. Comparison is the point: the paper tests methods side by side.

plos-pone-0004818:
Alexandre Valin and colleagues showed that skin fibroblasts from Gorlin syndrome patients exhibit features of carcinoma linked fibroblasts, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gorlin syndrome, or nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, causes predisposition to basal cell carcinoma, the commonest cancer in adult humans. Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene PTCH1 are responsible for this autosomal dominant syndrome with multiple developmental abnormalities and tumors.

Even healthy skin fibroblasts carried tumor like traits. Stroma may prime cancer growth in carriers. That shifts focus beyond lining cells alone. Prevention strategies might target the microenvironment. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0005418:
Elena Rusconi and her co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how people know their own bodies. Knowing the shape and layout of one's body is often seen as a basic part of self-awareness. Yet little was known about how the brain holds a built-in map of that structure.

The team made a new two-hand version of a classic finger test. People had to judge which finger had been touched, without looking at their hands. Their answers gave proof that the brain keeps a clear structural map of the body. The work helps explain how touch and body sense fit together.
plos-pone-0005518:
Laura Dugan and co-authors studied inflammation and the aging brain in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A signal called IL-6 rises in the blood in many poor health states of later life, from heart disease to frailty. The team asked what raised IL-6 does inside the aging brain itself.

In aged mice, IL-6 harmed a class of calming brain cells in the front of the brain. It acted through an enzyme that makes harsh oxygen chemicals. Thinking scores suffered along with the cell loss. The chain points to new ways to protect the aging mind.
plos-pone-0005618:
Igor Ruvinsky and co-authors studied mice whose ribosomal protein cannot be tagged, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Ribosomes build all proteins in cells, and one of their parts, S6, is often tagged to adjust that building. Mice engineered so S6 cannot be tagged are born and breed normally at first glance.

Closer study found growth faults, low energy, and weak muscles in these mice and their cells. The faults show that a single tag on the protein machine matters for muscle strength. That insight bears on diseases of growth and metabolism.
plos-pone-0005718:
Basirudeen Kabeer and co-authors tested in 2009 how well a blood test for tuberculosis works in people who also have HIV. Finding TB fast in HIV patients is hard, and a quick, sure test is badly needed. The test they checked measures interferon gamma released by immune cells.

The team measured how often the test catches true TB cases in this group. HIV weakens the very cells the test depends on, so its accuracy was in doubt. Clear numbers on that accuracy help clinics decide when to trust the test and when to use others. In co-infected patients, a wrong call can cost lives.
plos-pone-0005818:
Lisa Kinch, Melanie Yarbrough, and Kim Orth defined a new protein domain family in 2009. A bacterial toxin called VopS attaches AMP tags to host proteins, jamming their signals. Its working piece, the fic domain, shares a sequence motif with other proteins.

The team showed that motif marks a wider family, which they named Fido, spanning Fic, Doc, and AvrB proteins. AMPylation, once thought rare, may be a broad bacterial strategy. Recognizing the family lets scientists spot the trick in new pathogens quickly. It also adds a tool bacteria use that drug design might block.
plos-pone-0006418:
Repeated DNA stretches that expand cause many nerve and muscle diseases. Joao Paulo Tavanez and colleagues studied inclusions formed by polyalanine expansions in the protein PABPN1 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Expansions in coding regions are translated into long runs of a single amino acid.

The nuclear inclusions sequester Hsp70 chaperones and type I PRMT enzymes, per the title. Trapped helper proteins cannot do their normal jobs elsewhere. Sequestration may be a shared damage mechanism across repeat diseases. The detailed guest list of the inclusions guides that idea. The guest list gives drug work a set of clear parts to aim at.
plos-pone-0006518:
Arkan Abadi, Elisa Glover, Robert Isfort, and colleagues measured what happens when a limb is immobilized, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animal models and cell culture have been invaluable for explaining muscle atrophy. However, few studies had examined immobilization effects in men directly. The team studied human volunteers whose limbs were immobilized.

Their title reports a coordinate down-regulation of mitochondrial and other metabolic pathways. In other words, the resting muscle turns down its energy machinery as a set. That coordinated response helps explain why casted limbs weaken so fast. It also gives targets for keeping muscle alive during injury recovery or spaceflight.
plos-pone-0006618:
Susana Oliveira, Jorge Pinto, Gonçalo Picarote, and colleagues studied iron regulation under cell stress in PLOS ONE in 2009. Endoplasmic reticulum stress induces a complex network of pathways collectively termed the unfolded protein response. Clarification of these pathways has linked them to many diseases. The team examined how the stress-inducible factor CHOP affects expression of hepcidin, the master iron hormone.

Their title reports CHOP affects hepcidin expression by modulating C/EBP alpha activity. A stress pathway thus reaches into iron control. That link may explain anemia seen in chronic disease and inflammation. It connects two fields that rarely meet.
plos-pone-0009418:
Lyssia Gruaz and co-authors published this inflammation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When T cells touch monocytes directly, the monocytes pour out inflammatory signals. That contact trigger likely fuels long-running sterile inflammation in many diseases. HDL, the so-called good cholesterol, was known to block that production.

The team used HDL to block the contact activation in human monocytes. Blocking it revealed a fresh pattern of cytokine and inflammatory genes. Patterns revealed by a blocker show which genes the contact truly controls. The result also adds an anti-inflammatory talent to HDL's known list.
plos-pone-0009518:
Elizabeth Sweeney and colleagues confirmed a link between cartilage and blood in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Collagen X is a protein in growing cartilage near bone ends. Earlier mice with faulty collagen X had both skeletal flaws and blood flaws. That hinted the two systems are linked. The team used congenic mice, bred to share one genetic background, to test the claim cleanly.

Even with background held constant, faulty collagen X disrupted blood formation. So the effect is real, not a side effect of other genes. The skeleton's scaffold thus helps cradle blood development in the marrow. The finding may inform care for marrow diseases.
plos-pone-0009618:
Jantina Manning and co-authors studied how cells fetch a key building part in PLOS ONE in 2010. Before a cell divides, it builds a structure called the centrosome. That structure organizes the fibers that pull chromosomes apart. A protein named gamma tubulin is a core part of it. The team showed that another protein, NEDD1, binds gamma tubulin directly.

That direct binding is how gamma tubulin is recruited to the centrosome. Without the hand off, the structure cannot form properly. Every cell division depends on this small delivery step. The work details a piece of machinery that cancer drugs already try to jam, since dividing cells need it most.
plos-pone-0010418:
Courtney Karner and colleagues showed that a protein called Lrp4 is crucial for building kidneys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kidney formation starts when a small bud grows from a duct into nearby tissue.
