That meeting triggers the branching tubes that become the kidney. Many signals must align for the bud to start at all. The team studied mice lacking Lrp4 to see its part.

Without Lrp4, the bud's start went wrong and kidneys failed to form properly. The mouse mirrors a human syndrome with similar defects, Cenani-Lenz syndrome. Animal models that match human conditions help trace their causes. This one pins early kidney growth to a single protein's signal. It may also explain limb and bone signs seen in the syndrome.
plos-pone-0010518:
Catherine Pfister, Folker Meyer and Dionysios Antonopoulos profiled microbes living on California mussels in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mussels crowd rocky shores and filter huge amounts of water. Their feeding and waste move nitrogen through coastal food webs. A rich microbial community coats their shells. The team used shotgun metagenomics, reading all DNA in a sample at once, to catalog that community.

The catalog shows which microbes ride on mussels and what jobs they may do. Some likely help cycle carbon and nitrogen in the shore zone. A mussel bed thus acts as a hub in coastal nutrient networks. Knowing its microbes refines models of shore ecology. It also gives a baseline as oceans warm and acidify.
plos-pone-0010618:
Yuyan Zhang and colleagues studied a cancer drug target in zebrafish embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme thymidylate synthase helps cells build DNA. Chemotherapy drugs like 5-FU attack it, which is why it matters in cancer care.

In the embryos, the enzyme's own message RNA appeared to bind and restrain the enzyme. Two cancer drugs changed that self-control in measurable ways. Watching the loop in a living embryo shows regulation that dish studies can miss. The finding may help explain why some tumors resist drugs aimed at this enzyme.
plos-pone-0010718:
Yun-Shiang Chang and colleagues modeled the surface armor of a shrimp virus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. White spot syndrome virus has killed farmed shrimp on a huge scale worldwide. The virus particle is large for a virus, wrapped in a membrane studded with structural proteins.

The team combined data on those proteins into a three-dimensional model of their complex. The model shows how the proteins fit together on the membrane. Knowing the armor's layout points to weak seams that vaccines or treatments could target. Shrimp farming loses billions to this virus, so even basic maps carry real economic weight.
plos-pone-0010818:
Behazine Combadière and colleagues ran an early human trial of a needle-free flu vaccine, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Standard flu shots train antibodies well but raise weak killer T cell responses. Killer CD8 cells matter most against new flu strains that antibodies miss. The skin is rich in immune sentinels, and hair follicles offer a route in.

Volunteers received inactivated flu vaccine through the skin in a randomized phase I trial. The skin route preferentially amplified CD8 effector T cells. That bias is exactly what flu vaccinology has been missing. A safe, needle-free patch that trains killer cells could change both yearly flu shots and pandemic response.
plos-pone-0010918:
Belinda Cornes, Clara Tang, Thomas Leon and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hirschsprung's disease is a birth defect in which nerve cells are missing from parts of the gut, blocking digestion. One change in the RET gene, called R114H, shows up in roughly six or seven of every hundred Chinese patients but had never been seen in European patients.

Such clustering hints at a founder effect, where today's carriers descend from one ancestor who first carried the change. The team analyzed gene patterns in hundreds of Chinese patients, including those carrying R114H, and estimated the mutation's age with statistical methods. Cornes and colleagues test whether a single mutational event seeded this risk across a population. Founder mutations simplify screening and reveal how disease genes travel through history.
plos-pone-0011018:
Brooke Fridley, Gregory Jenkins, Matthew Deyo-Svendsen and co-authors published this genetics methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genome-wide association studies had flagged well over a thousand DNA sites linked to diseases, but the flagged markers are rarely the causal variants themselves. Sequencing every flagged region in thousands of people was still too expensive, so the team proposed a shortcut.

Genotype imputation, which fills in unmeasured variants from reference patterns, can also augment real sequence data, letting a study sequence fewer people deeply and extend the information statistically to the rest. Fridley and colleagues lay out how to combine partial sequencing with imputation to catalogue the rare variants hiding in disease-linked regions. Their strategy aims to move association studies from signposts to the actual functional spelling changes behind disease.
plos-pone-0011118:
Huang, Su, Li and colleagues compared three Chinese groups in PLOS ONE in 2010. All three groups share an unusually high rate of cancer of the food pipe. The team read the Y chromosome, passed from father to son, to test whether the groups share paternal roots.

The evidence supported common ancestry among the three high risk groups. Shared roots raise the chance that shared genes help explain the shared cancer risk. That does not rule out food, drink or local habits, which also matter. Still, the genetic link gives cancer researchers a sharper place to look for risk factors.
plos-pone-0011218:
Shin, Pierce, Gillenwater and colleagues built a low cost microscope in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their device uses optical fibers and a consumer grade digital camera to capture glowing images of living cells inside the body. Such imaging normally demands costly specialist equipment.

The budget microscope still delivered useful cellular images in living tissue. Affordable imaging could bring cancer screening to clinics with few resources. Early cancer found by direct cell viewing can be treated far more successfully. The study demonstrates frugal innovation: smart assembly of cheap parts can match the job of pricey tools.
plos-pone-0011318:
Singhal, Ren and Kern improved a DNA lab method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gels that sort DNA by size are a daily tool, but long fragments can bunch together and blur. The team developed gel conditions using borate compounds and related chemistry that spread those long fragments more clearly.

Sharper separation means DNA pieces can be sized and read more accurately. Labs gain the improvement without buying new equipment, since only buffer conditions change. Clearer gels aid everything from gene cloning to forensic checks. The study is a reminder that basic technique advances quietly lift a whole field.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1218:
Ambassador Harriman in Moscow wrote to the Secretary of State on 28 July 1945. Harriman was the American voice the Kremlin knew best. His cables from the Soviet capital carried weight on every question where Moscow's word mattered.

This dispatch reached the secretary in the summit's final days. Harriman watched Soviet conduct from inside while the leaders bargained in person. His reports tested the table talk against the facts of the capital. A cable from his hand is part of the record's Soviet thread. It shows the Moscow post feeding the endgame from its own vantage point.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1318:
A second Pauley message to the President bears the date 19 July 1945. The reparations envoy reported twice in a day because his file sat at the center of the summit's money fight. His mission's findings bore on every figure the leaders traded.

Pauley had seen Germany's ruins himself. His judgment on what could be taken without starving the land carried weight no paper claim could match. This message is the day's companion piece. Together the pair shows the reparations expert pressing his evidence on the president at the very hour the bargaining over Germany's bill began in earnest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1418:
Charles Bohlen, a special assistant to the secretary of state and the department's leading Russian hand, wrote a memorandum dated 28 March 1960. The volume prints it with the Yalta papers, fifteen years after that conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Bohlen had served as Roosevelt's interpreter at Yalta, so his later word on the meeting carries a witness's weight. A memorandum written in 1960 shows the conference still being argued over long after its makers were gone. Readers get hindsight in primary form: a man who was in the room, setting down what he believed the record showed. It is an unusual, late voice in a volume of wartime papers.
frus-1945-50-intel-d18:
G. E. Ramsey of the Budget Bureau staff wrote to Martin, the assistant director for estimates, on 24 September 1945. The paper came four days after the OSS was dissolved. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

With the order signed, the questions turned to money: what the leftover units would cost, and which budgets would carry them. Ramsey's memorandum to the estimates chief fits that turn exactly. Readers following the Budget Bureau thread can watch it shift from judging plans to pricing them. The shift is easy to miss and worth catching, because the prices set in these weeks bounded what the new intelligence system could actually do.
frus-1945-50-intel-d118:
Minutes of the fifth meeting of the National Intelligence Authority are dated 7 August 1946. Five meetings in six months show the board settling into its role as the system's court. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The August meeting sat in the middle of the FBI and CIG dispute, and its minutes record the board at work on live business. Readers can set the minutes beside the letters of Hoover and Vandenberg from the same weeks. The letters argue; the minutes decide, or defer. That pairing is the volume's method at its best. It lets a reader follow a bureaucratic battle from first shot to ruling without leaving the printed record.
frus-1945-50-intel-d218: "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 19 June 1947. It is document 218 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. A new law was about to remap the whole field: the armed services, the National Security Council, and the CIA all hung on it. Such a note often marks the end of a chain: the talk is over, the choice is made, and this page says so.
frus-1945-50-intel-d318:
Formal minutes cover the 13th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 15 May 1947. It stands as document 318 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. Later fights over who agreed to what often end with a page like this one. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d418:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to Charles Cabell, the Air Force director of intelligence, on 6 March 1950. The letter is document 418 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Air Force was the youngest service, and air intelligence grew fast with it. Cabell later served as deputy director of the CIA itself. A letter between the two men in 1950 shows service intelligence and central intelligence learning to work side by side. Cabell's later years at the CIA make this early link between the two men read with added point.
frus-1861-d18:
On 10 October 1861, Norman Judd sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 18 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Autumn brought no end to the war, and Europe began to plan for a long divide. Judd's October report kept Washington aware of Prussian views at that turn. Such steady reporting, dull as it may seem, was the means by which the Union held its ground abroad. Prussian goodwill, though quiet, denied the South a friend in the north of Europe. Quiet goodwill in the north kept one more door shut in the face of the South.
frus-1861-d118:
On 20 September 1861, William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley at his Austrian post. The letter is document 118 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Vienna took a strict view of rebellion and a cool view of the Union. Motley had to argue the Union's case in that chill air. Seward's September letter kept his historian envoy armed with the line from home. His envoy's pen was as fine as his historian's, and his letters were prized at home. Prized letters were read aloud in the cabinet more than once that year.
frus-1861-d218:
Seward wrote again on 30 July 1861, this time to Mr. Marsh. It was printed as Document 218 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d18:
Seward wrote again on 13 February 1862, this time to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 18 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d118:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 2 August 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 118 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d218:
On 23 June 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart, the acting head of the British legation in Washington. In a letter printed as Document 218 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Stuart, a legation secretary standing in for Lord Lyons, had to manage protests and questions his chief would normally carry. Seward wrote to him in the same brisk style he used with Lyons. Letters from late June belong to the opening of the Seven Days battles near Richmond, which soon tested foreign faith in a Union victory. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d318:
Filed late in the sequence, Document 318 is a Dayton report dated 4 August 1862, sent from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printers grouped it with later papers in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton wrote this report the same day as two others in the file, so August's Paris business arrived in Washington in a thick packet. The report belongs to the summer of French pressure for joint action on the war. Its late placement is a filing artifact; its content week is early August. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d418:
On 15 April 1862 Horace J. Perry dispatched a report from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It appears as Document 418 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Perry served as secretary of the Madrid legation and often as its acting head, so his reports carried real weight in Washington. That spring he wrote while Spain weighed its next step in Mexico and while Shiloh's heavy cost was still news in Europe. His account of Spanish thinking helped Seward decide where to press and where to wait. That judgment served the broad effort to keep foreign powers out of the American war.
frus-1862-d518:
On 15 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 518 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Two days before Antietam, Seward was writing to nearly every post in Europe, The Hague included, to set the line his ministers should hold. The Dutch questions remained the practical ones of ports, trade, and neutrality, but the week's real subject was resolve. A government that expected to win said so in advance, in writing, to all its agents. The instruction is a good example of Seward's preventive diplomacy: settle the story before events can be twisted by the other side.
frus-1862-d618:
On 25 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Bradford R. Wood in Copenhagen. The instruction is Document 618 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Danish file's autumn paper.

Seward wrote eight days after Antietam and three days after the emancipation order, in the week he was informing every post in Europe of both. Denmark heard the news from Wood in due course, with Washington's reading of it. A five-month gap in the printed Danish file before this letter shows the post's quiet. The autumn order shows it being gathered back into the general effort. After September, no European court, however small, was left outside the emancipation story.
frus-1862-d718:
On 13 October 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Luis Molina, Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The letter is document 718 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the two men's exchange in the volume.

A closing letter in a run like this one often sums up where the business stands. Seward's note ends a month of brisk letters between Washington and the Costa Rican legation. The file is a neat case of how foreign ties were kept. They were kept not by grand acts, but by short letters, sent on time, by men who knew each other's names. That is the record this volume keeps.
frus-1863p1-d18:
On 21 December 1862, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 18 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Two letters to Adams in two days close Seward's year in the printed file.

Back-to-back sheets let the secretary add a point the last mail had missed. Seward used them to keep Adams stocked with the government's views as the war and the talks in Europe both moved. This letter is the second of the pair. With its mate, it shows the close hand Washington kept on its most key post at the turn of the year.
frus-1863p1-d118:
Washington's answer to the mid-March mail came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 14 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 118 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, answering the Adams mail of mid-March.

Seward's answers did the steering in this exchange. They told Adams which of his reports had hit home and what line to take next with the British. This letter is a lone sheet between clusters, the kind that kept the loop tight. It shows the secretary at his steady work, one steamer behind the news and one ahead of the talks.
frus-1863p1-d218:
A dispatch dated 18 June 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 218 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d318:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 11 November 1862. The note is document 318 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For readers, the Stuart letters fill in the working level of the famous Lyons and Seward exchange. They show the legation's routine grind behind the headline crises. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d418:
Writing in Washington on 19 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 418 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. It dates from the spring when British debate over aiding the South was still live, and every note counted. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d518:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington sent an official note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 18 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d618:
Document 618, dated 12 September 1863, records a letter from Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020218:
Anoop Kumar, Cristiana P. Velloso, Yutaka Imokawa, and their team studied limb regrowth in PLOS Biology in 2004. Urodeles, the salamander group, can regrow whole limbs. The team isolated muscle fibers from these animals and watched the cells change back into a flexible, stem-like state.

That reversal, called dedifferentiation, is a key step in forming the growth bud that rebuilds a limb. The study ties the process to a gene called Msx1. When Msx1 is active, muscle fibers can loosen their mature form. Mammals cannot do this, so the salamander system shows what would need to change. The work frames regrowth as a controlled return to youth by adult cells.
plos-pbio-0020418:
Stephanie M. Brandt, Marc S. Dionne, Ranjiv S. Khush, and their team studied Salmonella in fruit flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Salmonella bacteria inject effector proteins into host cells to take control. In the fly, those effectors, plus a host signal called Eiger, which matches our TNF, drive infected cells to die.

Cell death can defend the host by removing the germ's home, or help the germ by clearing its path. This study shows both sides pushing toward death in the infected fly gut. The fly model lets researchers separate bacterial tricks from host responses with clean genetics. Lessons from it feed into the wider fight against Salmonella food poisoning.
plos-pone-0000118:
Seth W. Coleman and Gil G. Rosenthal published this animal behavior study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their subjects are swordtail fry, baby fish only days into life. The study asks how these tiny fish spot danger and find their own kind, testing whether they use chemical cues, visual cues, or both.

Young fish that fail to detect predators rarely survive long. The authors present the fry with scent and sight signals from predators and from fellow swordtails and record the responses. The work shows how early in life these senses come online, and it adds to what is known about how fish read their watery surroundings.
plos-pone-0000218:
Kirsi H. Pietiläinen, Marko Sysi-Aho, Aila Rissanen, and colleagues published this twin study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines identical twins where one twin had become obese and the other had not. The authors found that acquired obesity is tied to changes in the serum lipidomic profile. That profile is the pattern of fats in the blood, and the tie holds independent of genetic effects.

Because identical twins share their genes, differences between them point to lifestyle and environment. The lipid changes therefore track the obesity itself, not inherited risk. Such profiles may flag the metabolic harm of weight gain early, before diseases like diabetes take hold.
plos-pone-0000318:
Laura A. Díaz-Martínez, Juan F. Giménez-Abián, and Duncan J. Clarke published this chromosome study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cohesin is the protein ring that holds sister chromosomes together until division. Working in human cells, the authors reach a striking conclusion, stated in the title. Cohesin is dispensable for cohesion at the centromere, the chromosomes' central pinch point.

That result surprised a field that treated cohesin as the glue itself. Something else must help hold centromeres together in human cells. The paper reopened a basic question in cell division and pushed researchers to look for the missing mechanism.
plos-pone-0000418:
Patricia L.R. Brennan and colleagues compared the genitals of male and female waterfowl, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Ducks and their relatives are famous among biologists for elaborate, fast-changing genital shapes. The team tested whether male and female structures have evolved together, each shaping the other over time.

Such coevolution can arise when the sexes' interests conflict over mating and fertilization. If female structures evolve to keep control over which males succeed, male structures evolve in response. Waterfowl make the pattern visible because the anatomy is so extreme. The study is a widely noted example of how sexual conflict can drive rapid evolutionary change.
plos-pone-0000518:
Stéphanie Schrambach and colleagues mapped where two immune alarm proteins appear in the body, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The proteins, MICA and MICB, appear on stressed or infected cells and flag them for immune attack. The team described their in vivo expression pattern and its relevance to auto-immunity and cancer.

Where a flag is normally raised decides where mistaken attacks can happen. If healthy tissues display MICA or MICB, the immune system may target them, feeding autoimmune disease; tumors may raise or shed them to escape. An expression map is the reference that such disease studies need before they can claim anything is abnormal.
plos-pone-0000618:
Yinyi Huang, P. T. Tran, Snezhana Oliferenko and their team found a new genetic way to strip cells of major parts, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. They removed both the nucleus and the spindle pole bodies, the yeast version of centrosomes. Both parts were thought to be key organizers of the cell's inner framework.

Even without them, the cells still assembled microtubules, the framework's rods, and actomyosin rings, the bands that pinch a cell in two. That result tests long-held beliefs about who runs cell organization. Cell biologists get a fresh method here, plus evidence that the framework can organize itself more than expected.
plos-pone-0000718:
Debbie Winter, Ben Vinegar, Hardeep Nahal and colleagues built a visual browser for huge biological data sets, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Exploring microarray data and other high-throughput results had become vital for generating hypotheses in post-genomic research. For specialists outside bioinformatics, though, many tools present overwhelming amounts of data in forbidding forms.

Their answer is an electronic fluorescent pictograph browser, presenting data as pictures rather than tables. Pictographs let a researcher spot patterns across thousands of genes at a glance. Tools like this decide who gets to use big data. Bench biologists gain entry too, even without programming training. Results become readable pictures instead of raw numbers.
plos-pone-0000818:
Sa'ar Mizrahi, Gal Markel, Angel Porgador and colleagues found a surface protein that sharpens natural killer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. NK cells kill tumor and virus-infected cells without needing prior antigen stimulation. Their killing is regulated by inhibitory, lysis, and co-stimulatory receptors on the cell surface. CD100, also called Semaphorin 4D, is a 150-kilodalton transmembrane protein found on such cells.

The title reports that CD100 on NK cells enhances secretion of interferon-gamma and killing of target cells expressing CD72. A receptor pairing that boosts both alarm signals and killing could be exploited in cancer immunotherapy. It also redraws CD100's job description beyond nerve guidance, where semaphorins were first known.
plos-pone-0000918:
Lisa Denning, Jennifer Anderson, Ryan Davis and co-authors tested resequencing microarrays for a group of muscle nerve disorders, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Congenital myasthenic syndromes are inherited faults where nerves fail to drive muscles properly. Many genes can cause them, so testing one gene at a time is slow.

Resequencing arrays screen many candidate sites at once, offering an alternative to classic capillary sequencing. The team describe how their custom array performed on real cases. A faster screen means families get answers sooner, and doctors can match care to the exact fault. The paper is a practical check on whether the shortcut can be trusted.
plos-pone-0001018:
Blaise Genton, Gerd Pluschke, Lukas Degen and colleagues ran an early malaria vaccine trial using virus like carriers, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial used influenza virosomes, hollow virus shells that can carry other material safely. Virosomes had already proved fit for subunit vaccines, designs that use only pieces of a germ.

Two synthetic peptides, short malaria protein pieces, were mounted on the virosomes. Healthy adult volunteers received them in a randomized, placebo controlled phase one trial. The aim was proof of concept: can this carrier raise strong antibodies against malaria pieces. Early trials like this decide whether a vaccine idea earns larger tests.
plos-pone-0001118:
Annexin A2 is a protein that binds cell membranes and helps organize traffic inside the cell. Etienne Morel and Jean Gruenberg explain its workings in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The protein usually works as a four-part complex that includes a small partner chain called p11, or S100A10.

Morel and Gruenberg asked whether annexin A2 needs that partner to reach endosomes, the sorting stations that move cargo through the cell. Their title states the answer. The p11 chain is not required for annexin A2 to reach endosomes, or to do its work in endosomal transport. The result narrows down which parts of the complex truly matter.
plos-pone-0001218:
Changing the dose of a single gene often shifts the levels of hundreds of other proteins, a puzzle seen in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease. Lei Mao and colleagues investigated that ripple effect in embryonic stem cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They carried out a proteomic investigation, measuring many proteins at once.

The proteomic shifts they observed suggest the presence of balancer proteins in protein regulatory networks, proteins that absorb or compensate for changes. The idea would explain why cells stay stable despite genetic perturbations. Their work reframes gene dose effects as a network property, not just a single gene's fault.
plos-pone-0001318:
Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death worldwide from a single infectious agent. Decades of data suggest that human susceptibility to it has a genetic component. Xin Ma and colleagues resequenced all the coding regions of Toll-like receptor genes to test their contribution, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Toll-like receptors play a critical role in initiating the innate immune response to TB.

Full-exon resequencing reads every protein-coding segment, catching rare variants that chip studies miss. The authors report that Toll-like receptor variants contribute to human susceptibility to tuberculosis disease. Their results support targeted genetics for a disease usually fought at the public health level.
plos-pone-0001418:
Anne Tisserant and Harald König wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how gene messages are cut and rejoined. Cells can splice a message in more than one way, and signals from outside the cell can steer the choice. A core splicing factor must first sit on the message. The pair asked how signals change that seating.

They show that cell signals shift where and how firmly the factor binds before splicing starts. That early step helps decide which version of a protein the cell will make. The finding adds a control point to a key gene process. It may help explain how cells adapt fast when their state changes.
plos-pone-0001518:
Sarah Brosnan and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on trade in chimpanzees. Economists hold that barter lies at the root of social wealth and much of human culture. Yet how barter arose in evolution was little known. The team tested when chimps will trade goods with each other or with people.

Chimps did trade in some setups but held back in others. Their choices hinged on trust and on what each side gained. The pattern hints at what must be in place for barter to thrive. It gives a base for tests on how human trade grew from primate roots.
plos-pone-0001618:
Timothy J. Page, William F. Humphreys, and Jane M. Hughes studied a small shrimp that lives only in underground waters in Western Australia. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article looks at Stygiocaris, a genus of cave shrimp, and asks how its species are related to each other. The shrimp belong to a rare group of animals found in coastal limestone caves where fresh water and sea water mix.

Page and his co-authors used nuclear and mitochondrial genes to trace both the large-scale and small-scale family links among these shrimp. Work of this kind helps show how cave species split apart and adapt to life in the dark. The full text gives the gene data and the family tree the team built from it. It also gives their account of what the tree says about the history of these hidden animals.
plos-pone-0001718:
Helga Schneider, Hongyan Wang, Monika Raab, and their co-authors studied a signaling adaptor in T cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The adaptor is SKAP-55, known for helping T cells stick to other cells through LFA-1 adhesion. Whether it also shapes other signaling was unknown. Adaptors act as nodes that can coordinate several jobs at once.

The team reports that SKAP-55 binds RasGRP1, an exchange factor that switches on the p21 ras protein. That binding negatively regulates the p21 ras to ERK pathway. The full text gives the binding tests and the pathway measurements. One adaptor that both aids adhesion and brakes a growth pathway shows how T cells keep activation strong but bounded.
plos-pone-0001818:
Chaoyang Lin, Jun Fang, Xiaoli Xu, and their co-authors engineered rice that can be selectively terminated in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gene transfer improves crops and yields valuable proteins such as drugs. The unplanned spread of commercial transgenic crops by pollen and seed is a major public concern.

Their built-in containment strategy creates rice plants that farmers can kill off on demand while nearby ordinary rice is unharmed. The full text gives the genetic design and the field tests. A built-in kill switch answers a long-standing public worry about gene-altered crops grown outdoors.
plos-pone-0001918:
Meltem Muftuoglu and co-authors studied a chemical tag that tunes a DNA repair protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, WRN, fails in Werner syndrome, an illness that ages the body far too fast. WRN takes part in many tasks that keep DNA sound, among them base excision repair, which fixes small daily lesions in the code.

The team asked whether acetylation, a small chemical tag placed on proteins, changes what WRN can do. They report that the tag regulates WRN's work as a catalyst and shifts how well repair proceeds. Tags like this may be dials that cells use to aim repair where it is needed.
plos-pone-0002018:
Joseph Gillespie and co-authors charted the family tree of a group of bacteria that live only inside cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Rickettsia species cause human ills from epidemic typhus to Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Their genomes were being read at a fast pace, giving a rich set for comparison.

To build a sound tree, the team first sorted genes into orthologous groups, sets of genes that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. Only then can branch order be trusted. A clean tree of these parasites helps trace how an inside-cell life evolves and trims a genome down.
plos-pone-0002118:
LaReesa Wolfenbarger and co-authors pooled field studies on how Bt crops affect other insects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE meta-analysis. Bt crops are engineered to make the insect-killing Cry proteins of the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. Uncertainty persists over their effects on arthropods they are not meant to target, from predators to pollinators.

The team performed meta-analyses on a modified public database, grouping non-target arthropods by functional guild, the job each group does in the field. Bt cotton anchors the analysis. Pooling many field studies gives a firmer answer on bystander harm than any single field season can.
plos-pone-0002218:
Chiara Marchesi and co-authors measured stem cell levels in the blood of patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Duchenne is a severe muscle-wasting disease of boys. Blood and cell markers can predict the course of many diseases, and the team asked whether certain stem cells might do the same here.

They counted subclasses of circulating progenitor cells marked by CD133. Levels of some groups matched a milder course of the disease. A blood test that hints at how fast Duchenne will progress would help families plan and help trials judge whether a treatment truly works.
plos-pone-0002318:
Tohru Nakagawa and co-authors built a tissue test to predict which prostate cancers will spread after treatment, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many men see their PSA level rise again after initial therapy for prostate cancer. Some will develop local or distant recurrence needing more treatment, while others show no progression at all.

The team hypothesized that a panel of expression biomarkers in the tumor could separate those paths. Their panel predicts systemic progression after PSA recurrence. A test like this could spare low-risk men harsh extra therapy while catching high-risk cases early enough to act.
plos-pone-0002418:
In 2008, Kucherenko and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Mariya M. Kucherenko, Mario Pantoja, Andriy S. Yatsenko, and others. Its subject is genetic Modifier Screens Reveal New Components that Interact with the Drosophila Dystroglycan-Dystrophin Complex. The Dystroglycan-Dystrophin (Dg-Dys) complex has a capacity to transmit information from the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton inside the cell.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002518:
A research team led by Destouches reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Damien Destouches, Diala El Khoury, Yamina Hamma-Kourbali, and others. Its subject is suppression of Tumor Growth and Angiogenesis by a Specific Antagonist of the Cell-Surface Expressed Nucleolin. Emerging evidences suggest that nucleolin expressed on the cell surface is implicated in growth of tumor cells and angiogenesis.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002618:
Work from Sande and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Marianne van der Sande, Peter Teunis, Rob Sabel, and others. Its subject is professional and Home-Made Face Masks Reduce Exposure to Respiratory Infections among the General Population. Governments are preparing for a potential influenza pandemic.

Therefore they need data to assess the possible impact of interventions. Face-masks worn by the general population could be an accessible and affordable intervention, if effective when worn under routine circumstances. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002718:
Sara Sanz-Blasco led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was mitochondrial ca 2+ overload underlies aβ oligomers neurotoxicity providing an unexpected mechanism of neuroprotection by NSAIDs. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Sara Sanz-Blasco, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Dysregulation of intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis may underlie amyloid β peptide (Aβ) toxicity in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) but the mechanism is unknown. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002818:
Carolina Ibáñez-Ventoso led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequence relationships among C. elegans , D. melanogaster and human microRNAs highlight the extensive conservation of microRNAs in biology. The catalog record names Carolina Ibáñez-Ventoso first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. MicroRNAs act in a prevalent and conserved post-transcriptional gene regulatory mechanism that impacts development, homeostasis and disease. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002918:
Patrick Reynolds, Jeffrey Simms and Robert Duronio used domain swapping in fruit flies in 2008 to study protein destruction. Cullin-based ligases tag proteins for removal and help run many cell processes. Their Roc subunit holds a RING domain that grips the charged partner needed for tagging.

Drosophila has three Roc proteins with different jobs. By swapping domains between them, the team identified what decides which cullin each Roc binds. Published in PLOS ONE, the results clarify how cells assemble distinct destruction machines from similar parts, a basic question in cell control. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003018:
Armand Paauw, Martien Caspers, Frank Schuren and co-authors charted genomic diversity in the Enterobacter cloacae complex in 2008. These bacteria are increasingly found as hospital-acquired pathogens. Yet identifying them by appearance and chemistry is unreliable and hard to reproduce between labs.

Even genotyping tools of the time were being superseded for telling species apart. The PLOS ONE study uses genome-level diversity to sort the complex more soundly. Better identification matters in hospitals, where the species behind an outbreak guides infection control and antibiotic choice. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003118:
Shrimati Datta and Nora Sarvetnick studied how IL-21 limits lymphocyte numbers in 2008. IL-21 is a cytokine in the common gamma-chain family that participates in immune and inflammatory processes. The cytokine has also been linked to autoimmunity in humans and rodents, which made its normal role worth pinning down.

To investigate the mechanism, the team examined how IL-21 affects the immune system through T cell homeostatic mechanisms, the balancing systems that hold cell counts steady. IL-21 limits peripheral lymphocyte numbers that way, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a brake on cell numbers matters for both deficiency and excess.
plos-pone-0003218:
Rune W. Berg, Susanne Ditlevsen and Jørn Hounsgaard study spike timing in spinal neurons in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In neurons, spike timing is set by integration of synaptic potentials together with intrinsic properties. Although integration time is functionally crucial, it remains elusive during network activity. Mechanisms of rapid processing are well documented in some systems but harder to capture here.

The title reports that intense synaptic activity enhances temporal resolution in spinal motoneurons. Readers see busy input sharpen, rather than blur, timing in these cells. That finding matters for motor control, where precise timing of muscle commands is essential.
plos-pone-0003318:
Damon H. Meyer and Adam M. Bailis study lost chromosome ends in yeast in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Telomerase is the complex that copies and guards telomeres, the DNA caps at chromosome ends. Cells with no telomerase lose a bit of cap DNA at each division. In time they lose viability and their genomes grow unstable.

The title reports that lack of telomerase changes how often chromosomes swap arms by homologous recombination in baker's yeast. Readers see worn ends lead to large-scale genome shuffles. Such translocations mark many cancers, so yeast work helps show how they start.
plos-pone-0007418:
Hendrik P. N. Scholl, Monika Fleckenstein, Lars G. Fritsche, and colleagues tested eye disease genes for progression effects in 2009. Age-related macular degeneration is a prevalent cause of blindness in Western societies. Variants in genes CFH, C3, and ARMS2 had repeatedly been shown to confer significant risk for the disease in earlier genetic studies.

The authors ask whether those loci also drive progression. They focus on geographic atrophy, the advanced dry form of the disease. They report the loci are significant for susceptibility but not for disease progression. That distinction matters for trials that aim to slow atrophy.
plos-pone-0007518:
Paul Davies and David Brown published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on prion diseases and the soils where their agent may linger. Prion diseases, such as scrapie in sheep, spread through an infectious protein. Sporadic cases imply an environmental source for that agent. Soil is a suspected reservoir. The team tested how the metal manganese affects prion survival in model soils, and what happens to infectivity.

Manganese helped the prion protein survive longer in the soil models. It also increased how infectious the prions were to cells. That combination makes manganese-rich environments a greater concern for disease spread. Soil chemistry, usually ignored in outbreak thinking, may shape where prions persist. The result argues for including the environment's metal content in risk assessments. It also helps explain the patchy geography of prion diseases.
plos-pone-0007618:
Anita Pepper and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the gene behind fragile X syndrome. That condition, a leading inherited cause of intellectual disability, comes from silencing the FMR1 gene. Yet too much of the gene's product is also harmful; dosage must be kept in range. How normal expression levels are maintained was unclear. The team studied a protein called Argonaute2 in fruit flies and its effect on the fly version of the gene.

Argonaute2 suppresses fragile X expression in the fly. That suppression prevents defects in nerve development and egg formation. So a small-RNA pathway protein acts as a dosage guard for this sensitive gene. Dosage guards matter where both shortage and excess cause disease. The fly work gives human fragile X research a new regulatory thread to pull. It also shows Argonaute proteins doing more than silencing targets outright.
plos-pone-0007718:
Amaresh Ranjan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tackles a weak point of artificial blood vessels. Small synthetic grafts often fail when clots form or the wall thickens. Lining a graft with the patient's own vessel cells could prevent both problems.

The team grew endothelial progenitor cells taken from human blood vessels. Such cells can coat the inside of a small-diameter prosthesis. A living lining makes the graft act more like a natural vessel. The work is an early step toward safer bypass grafts for people with blocked heart arteries.
plos-pone-0007818:
Hilbert de Vries and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a gene variant tied to a fungal sensor in bowel disease. The sensor, dectin-1, sits on immune cells and detects fungal cell walls. When triggered, it signals through the adaptor CARD9, much like the Crohn's-linked gene NOD2.

The authors ran a genetic association analysis on one functional variant. They also measured dectin-1 levels in gut lining from patients. Their question was whether this variant tracks with inflammatory bowel disease. The study adds one more piece to the genetics of gut inflammation.
plos-pone-0007918:
Jean-Michel Garcia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks which flu protein draws the antibodies that can stop H5N1 bird flu. Being sick with one flu strain can leave a person with some guard against other strains. Those shared defenses might blunt a new flu that jumps from birds.

Two proteins on the virus coat were the main suspects. The team built fake viruses to test each one on its own. The guard came from antibodies aimed at haemagglutinin, the coat protein the virus uses to enter cells. That answer tells vaccine makers where to aim. A shot that raises such antibodies could soften a future outbreak.
plos-pone-0008018:
Heidi Blank and colleagues found that sulfur handling can push yeast to divide, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Yeast cells were known to need sulfur work before a new round of division can start. The open question was whether that work merely allows division or truly drives it.

Cells rich in extra DNA copies ran a longer reducing phase in their cycle and pushed more sulfur through their pathways. That push came before, and seemed to spur, the start of division. The result gives sulfur a command role in the cell cycle, not just a support job.
plos-pone-0008118:
Yongjin Park and colleagues modeled protein networks as changing over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. A network drawn once, with all links merged, hides the truth that links come and go as proteins are made and destroyed. Tissue and time both redraw the map.

Their method groups the network afresh at each stage using a layered Bayesian model, a statistics frame that weighs doubt honestly. The moving map caught shifts that a fixed map missed. Drug and disease studies that ignore the timing of links may be aiming at partners that are rarely in the room together.
plos-pone-0008218:
Frank H. Guenther and colleagues reported a wireless brain-machine interface in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such devices use electrodes placed in the cerebral cortex. They aim to restore function to people with profound paralysis. Earlier systems for communication mostly let users type slowly. This work targeted real-time speech synthesis instead.

Signals from the speech areas of the brain were sent wirelessly to a synthesizer. The system turned intended speech sounds into audible output as they occurred. Real-time voice could give paralyzed people a far more natural way to communicate. The study shows an early working step toward that goal.
plos-pone-0008318:
Laetitia Horzinski and colleagues studied a diagnostic test for brain disorders in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in eIF2B genes cause a family of leukodystrophies. These disorders destroy white matter in the brain. The classic form brings childhood ataxia and vanishing white matter. The observed clinical spectrum has grown much wider in recent years.

The team evaluated eIF2B activity as a diagnostic tool. Measuring the factor's GEF activity could confirm unclear cases. A functional test helps when gene results are ambiguous. It could speed diagnosis for families facing these rare disorders.
plos-pone-0008418:
Daisuke Kawabata and colleagues studied lupus treatment effects in mice in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. A major goal in treating systemic lupus erythematosus is long-term remission. Cytotoxic therapies such as cyclophosphamide are used toward that goal. Little information existed on how they affect the rebuilding B cell repertoire. That repertoire decides which antibodies the body can make afterward.

After cyclophosphamide treatment, selection of high affinity DNA-reactive B cells was enhanced. DNA-reactive cells are exactly the kind that drive lupus. A treatment that favors their return could explain relapses. The finding guides safer use of cytotoxic therapy.
plos-pone-0008518:
Anne Wisdom and co-authors study a new cold virus group in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human rhinoviruses are the main cause of the common cold. A species called HRV-C had only recently been described. Its frequency and clinical effects were still unclear. The team screen thousands of respiratory samples from Edinburgh. They use a test targeting the VP4 region of the virus. They also study how HRV-C interacts with other respiratory viruses.

They estimate how often HRV-C causes infection in that sample set. They link it to clinical features and seasonal patterns. Genetic analysis shows recombination shapes its diversity. The work defines HRV-C as a real clinical player, not a curiosity.
plos-pone-0008618:
Jorge Castro and co-authors study how antidepressants work in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Those drugs boost new nerve cell growth in the hippocampus. That growth has been tied to many molecular paths. The role of other brain areas had got far less attention. One such area is the amygdala, which handles emotion and stress. The team test if the amygdala shapes the drug effect.

They measure new cell growth in the hippocampus and depression-like behavior. The amygdala proves needed for both drug effects. Without it, new cells and better behavior do not appear. Drug action is thus a circuit effect across brain areas.
plos-pone-0008718:
Antje Vogelgesang, Verena May, Uwe Grunwald, and colleagues checked immune cells in stroke patients. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ischemic stroke cuts blood to part of the brain and kills tissue. Soon after, patients lose many T cells from their blood. That dip raises the risk of infections like pneumonia. Counts alone do not show how well the remaining cells work.

The team tested the working state of blood T cells after stroke. Their assays measured responses that healthy cells should give. Knowing whether survivors are weak or merely fewer matters for care. It may guide steps to prevent post-stroke infections.
plos-pone-0008818:
Jerry Conway, Laura Sherwood, M. Thelma Collazo, and colleagues raised llama antibodies against botulism toxins. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The toxins that cause botulism come in seven types, all of them dangerous. A good test must tell the types apart fast. Llamas make small, tough antibodies of a special kind. Small size makes them handy for test kits used in the field.

The team raised one antibody for each of the seven toxin types. Used as a set, the seven can spot any type in a sample. Fast, sure tests matter for food safety and defense. Tough llama antibodies may beat normal ones when conditions are rough.
plos-pone-0008918:
Ethan Cerami, Emek Demir, Nikolaus Schultz, and colleagues let computers find the core pathways inside a lethal brain tumor. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain tumor in adults. The Cancer Genome Atlas had just profiled it in depth. Such data floods are hard to read gene by gene. Automated network analysis can surface the pathways that matter most across patients.

The network approach distilled core altered pathways from the genomic noise. Shared pathways suggest shared drug targets for many patients. A core map beats long lists of single-patient mutations. The work shows how to mine atlas-scale cancer data.
plos-pone-0009018:
Samantha Tracht, Sara Del Valle, and James Hyman modelled whether face masks slow a new flu, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The new virus was influenza A H1N1, declared a pandemic in June 2009. Vaccines and antiviral drugs were in short supply early on. Masks were a cheap option countries and families could use at once.

Their mathematical model tested mask use under different assumptions. It varied how many people wore masks and how well the masks filtered. The runs showed how much spread masks could cut in each case. Planners facing the next pandemic gain numbers, not just guesses, for mask advice.
plos-pone-0009118:
Xiaoyang Wan and co-authors found two proteins that put a brake on a growth signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The signal is Wnt4, part of a family steering development and cancer. EAF1 and EAF2 are proteins tied to both embryos and tumours. EAF2 in particular can act as a tumour suppressor in prostate tissue.

Both proteins fed back to dampen Wnt4's signalling. Negative feedback keeps the pathway from running too hot. The brake is built into the pathway's own downstream machinery. Losing it could help explain some cancers and birth defects.
plos-pone-0009218:
Patricia Fauque and co-authors published this reproduction study in PLOS ONE in 2010. More and more babies begin with in vitro fertilization, yet the method's effects are now questioned. Early embryos grow for days in lab dishes rather than in the body. At that stage, the embryo's outer cells touch the culture fluid directly, and those cells later form the placenta.

Using mice, the team compared placentas from embryos made naturally and in dishes. They read the full set of genes switched on in each placenta. Fertilization and culture in vitro strongly changed that gene pattern. The result warns that lab conditions at the very start can echo into the organ that feeds the baby.
plos-pone-0009318:
Hua-Ling Chen, Chiou-Hwa Yuh, and Kenneth Wu published this zebrafish study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nestin is a protein found in the young cells that build the brain. Scientists use it as a marker for those neural progenitor cells. What nestin itself actually does during development was unclear.

Working in zebrafish, where the gene is conserved, the team removed nestin's function. Brain and eye development suffered as a result. The cause was excess death among the progenitor cells that nestin normally protects. So the familiar marker turns out to be a working part of development, keeping young brain cells alive.
plos-pone-0011418:
Ming-Szu Hung and co-authors reported in 2010 that an unusual copy of a growth gene helps drive lung cancer. The gene makes a protein kinase involved in cell growth, and its extra copy is streamlined, lacking the spacer sections most genes carry. Such intronless copies are often dismissed as dead leftovers, but this one is active in lung tumors.

The team found that a common variant of the streamlined gene plays a cancer-promoting role in lung cancer cells. That finding adds a new suspect to the list of lung cancer drivers and a possible marker for risk. It also challenges the habit of ignoring streamlined gene copies in genome scans. If more such copies prove active, cancer genetics may have been overlooking a whole class of contributors hiding in plain sight.
plos-pone-0011518:
Matt Cahill and co-authors explored in 2010 how the length of DNA reads decides whether a bacterial genome can be assembled cleanly. New sequencing machines read DNA in short fragments, and repetitive stretches longer than the reads tangle assembly, since the computer cannot tell which copy a fragment came from. The team tested assembly across prokaryote genomes while varying read length.

They found that read length strongly affects repeat resolution, and that longer reads crack stubborn genomes that more short reads cannot. The practical guidance is that sequencing strategy should fit the genome: sometimes longer reads, not more reads, are the answer. Labs planning a genome project can spend their budget where it counts. As sequencing gets cheaper, this kind of strategy paper keeps the savings from being wasted on the wrong kind of data.
plos-pone-0011618:
Bonnie McGill, Ariana Sutton-Grier and Justin Wright studied how plant variety affects soil nitrogen cleanup, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Through a process called denitrification, soil microbes return excess nitrogen to the air. That service protects streams and lakes from pollution that would otherwise feed harmful algal growth.

The authors asked whether having many kinds of plant traits steadies that cleanup across seasons and soil types. They found that diverse plant traits did buffer swings in the process. For land managers, the result means keeping varied plant communities can keep a vital water-cleaning service reliable year-round.
plos-pone-0011718:
Tsuyoshi Hayashi and co-authors listed the proteins of the Legionnaires' disease germ at each growth stage, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Legionella pneumophila turns harmful in response to growth state, growing most dangerous late in lab culture, after its fast growth phase ends. Which proteins change as it enters that state was the open question.

Their protein survey compared levels between growth phases. The list ties clear protein shifts to the control of the germ's harmful traits. A stage-by-stage record of a germ retooling itself as it grows gives researchers firm leads for blocking infection.
plos-pone-0011818:
Yanmin Hu and co-authors took a fresh path to finding antibiotics, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In a real infection, germs that are splitting and germs that are not live side by side. Standard drugs kill the splitters well but barely touch the quiet ones, so killing is slow or partial and infection can bounce back.

By aiming at non-splitting germs, the team's search yielded a new skin antibiotic for staph infections. A cream that hits the quiet germs strikes the pool that other drugs miss. The tactic could stretch to other stubborn infections where quiet germs ride out standard therapy in tissue.
plos-pone-0011918:
Carole Fakhry and colleagues asked in 2010 how often researchers need to sample the mouth to track HPV infection fairly. Oral HPV matters because some types can lead to throat cancers. The team worked with an HIV-positive cohort, collecting fourteen mouth rinse samples in a row from each person.

They compared what two-week sampling showed against what samples six months apart would have suggested. Wide gaps between tests can make infections look shorter or longer than they are, biasing natural history studies. The comparison gives future studies a concrete basis for picking a sampling schedule instead of copying habit.
plos-pone-0012018:
Aksana Andreyeva and co-workers reported in 2010 that a brain protein called CHL1 organizes the nerve terminal's release machinery. When a nerve ending releases its chemical message, the SNARE protein complex drives membrane fusion, changing shape drastically in the process. Shape-changing proteins risk clumping and damage, yet little was known about the chaperones guarding them.

The team found CHL1 acting as a selective organizer on the presynaptic side, chaperoning the SNARE complex. Selectivity matters: a general helper would blur the careful assembly that fast signaling needs. Knowing who guards the release machinery opens a new angle on synapse failure in brain disease.
plos-pone-0012118:
Florence Kermen, Sébastien Sultan, Joëlle Sacquet, and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about smell, memory, and new brain cells. The smell center of the adult brain keeps gaining newborn neurons, and learning seems to help some of them survive. The puzzle was how the brain picks which new cells to keep for a lasting memory of a scent.

Their work points to a settling step in the smell center itself, where a fresh memory trace must be locked in. Only when that happens do the chosen new neurons survive and the memory last. The finding links a tiny brain region to the long life of a memory, and to the cells that carry it.
plos-pone-0012218:
Manfred Bohn and Dieter Heermann modeled how the genome folds inside the cell nucleus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chromatin, the DNA-and-protein fiber, folds at many scales at once, yet its large-scale arrangement had resisted every tidy explanation. Experiments kept showing tight loops and clustered regions without a unifying cause.

Their model shows that loops formed simply as the fiber drifts and sticks can reproduce those patterns. A single simple mechanism that matches many observations is powerful: it turns a confusing catalog of structures into one process with rules. That gives experimentalists clear predictions to test about how genes find their partners in three dimensions.
plos-pone-0012318:
Michael Allan, Christina Korownyk, Kate LaSalle, and co-authors checked whether clinical trials talk about money, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Randomized controlled trials decide which treatments medicine adopts, yet health care costs, above all drug costs, dominate the budgets of the organizations that must pay for those treatments. A trial can prove a drug works while saying nothing about whether it is worth its price.

The team measured how often trial reports include costs, and what features make a trial more likely to mention them. If cost talk is rare, decision-makers are flying blind on value even when the science is clear. The paper gives medical journals and funders a baseline for demanding better.
plos-pone-0012418:
Stephen Murray, Judith Morgan, Coleen Kane and colleagues asked what sets the length of pregnancy in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Early birth is a huge health problem in people, causing many infant deaths and costing billions. Twin studies hint that genes play a part, and the mouse lets scientists test that idea under controlled conditions.

By comparing mouse strains and crosses, the team showed that gestation length is strongly set by genetics, including genes of both mother and pups. A firm genetic base means mouse strains can be used to find the actual genes. Those genes may point to pathways that time birth in humans as well.
plos-pone-0012518:
Sandhya Buchanan, David Pyatt and John Carpenter freeze-dried human blood stem and progenitor cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Stem cell therapies promise much, but cells usually must ship frozen, a costly chain that many clinics cannot support. Dried cells stored on a shelf would travel anywhere, if they survived the drying alive.

The team lyophilized hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and stored them at room conditions, then checked whether the cells kept their identity and growth potential. Preservation held up surprisingly well in their tests. Shelf-stable cells could widen access to cell therapy far beyond rich hospital centers.
plos-pone-0012618:
Griffin, Cairns, Ghani and co-authors modelled a malaria prevention plan for babies. The plan gives infants a drug called sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine at set visits, even when they are not sick. Health officials support the plan where the drug still works, but parasite resistance can wear it down.

Their 2010 analysis linked how well the plan protects infants to measures of drug resistance in local parasites. That link helps officials decide where the plan still pays off and where it needs replacing. Good models of this kind save money and protect babies from needless doses.
pmc-1382018:
Voight, Kudaravalli, Wen, and co-authors map signs of very recent positive selection in the human genome. Selection leaves marks when a helpful gene variant spreads fast through a population. Finding such marks reveals how modern humans adapted to local foods, climates, and diseases.

The team scanned the whole genome for variants that had risen quickly but had not yet taken over completely. Each strong signal points to a trait that mattered in the recent past. Their map gave other researchers a list of regions to study for links to health, diet, and survival.
pmc-3241518:
Morris, Wooding, and Grant examine time lags in translational research, the path from discovery to patient benefit. Their study reviewed literature that describes and quantifies those lags in developing health interventions. They identified a small set of papers that actually measured the delays.

Few of those papers could be compared directly, they found, despite the famous claim that translation takes about seventeen years. Measuring lags honestly matters because funders promise faster translation to patients. The review shows how thin the evidence behind that promise was, and what better tracking would require.
pmc-4595218:
Benchimol, Smeeth, Guttmann, and their co-authors issued the RECORD statement in 2015. Routinely collected health data, gathered for care and administration rather than research, were being used for studies more and more. Their speed and scale raised issues that older reporting guidelines did not address.

RECORD extends existing guidance for observational studies that use such data. It asks authors to describe data sources, coding, and linkage in enough detail for readers to judge the work. Clear reporting matters because routine data can hide errors in records and coding. The statement helps journals and reviewers hold this fast-growing research type to a sound standard.
pmc-5241818:
Zheng, Terry, Belgrader, and their colleagues described a droplet-based system in 2017 for profiling single cells. Reading the full set of gene messages in single cells is basic to grasping how complex living systems work. Older methods could handle only small numbers of cells at a time.

Their system counts messenger RNA from tens of thousands of cells in a single sample run. Cells are encapsulated in droplets, up to eight samples at a time, and each cell's messages get a unique barcode. That scale reveals rare cell types hidden in bulk averages. The approach powered the wave of single-cell atlases in immunology, cancer, and development.
pmc-5496518:
McKeith, Boeve, Dickson, and their team updated the rules in 2017 for diagnosing dementia with Lewy bodies. A consortium for this disease refined its advice on both clinical and tissue-based diagnosis. The prior report had been in wide use for the last decade.

The new rules draw a clear line between the clinical signs used at the bedside and the lab markers that support the call. This dementia mixes memory loss with vivid visions, swings in alertness, and stiff, slow movement. It is often mistaken for Alzheimer's disease, which can lead to harmful drug choices. Clearer rules help doctors spot it sooner and care for patients in a safer way.
pmc-6821018:
Catherine Kelly, Alan Karthikesalingam, Mustafa Suleyman, and coauthors listed challenges for clinical artificial intelligence in 2019. Health AI research was racing ahead, with demos across many branches of medicine. Yet very few tools had reached real clinical use.

The authors name the gaps: messy real-world data, workflow fit, regulation, and proof of benefit. They warn that models trained in one hospital may fail in another. Fairness and monitoring after launch get equal weight with accuracy. The paper became a sober checklist for teams moving AI from papers to wards. The authors also address who stays accountable when an algorithm's advice is followed or ignored.
pmc-7095418:
Peng Zhou, Xing-Lou Yang, Xian-Guang Wang, and coauthors reported the pneumonia outbreak virus of probable bat origin in 2020. Since SARS emerged, many related coronaviruses had been found in bats. Some were already known to be able to infect human cells.

The team sequenced the new virus and showed it shares most of its genome with a bat coronavirus. Lab tests confirmed it enters cells through the ACE2 receptor, like the SARS virus. The evidence pointed to bats as the likely original host. Their report anchored early scientific agreement on the outbreak's origin.
pmc-7164518:
Linlin Zhang, Daizong Lin, Xinyuanyuan Sun, and coauthors solved the crystal structure of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease in 2020. The main protease cuts viral proteins into working pieces, so the virus cannot mature without it. That makes it a prime drug target.

The structure revealed the enzyme's shape in fine detail. The team also improved an earlier inhibitor design against the related SARS enzyme and showed strong blocking in tests. A shared structural blueprint let chemists worldwide start designing drugs at once. Protease inhibitors later became a real class of COVID-19 medicines.
pmc-7285218:
Fabien Magne and co-authors asked a pointed question in 2020: can a simple ratio of two gut bacteria groups serve as a sign of an unhealthy gut in people with obesity? The two groups, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, dominate the human gut. Researchers had proposed that when their balance shifts, it marks a disturbed microbial community linked to inflammation and metabolic trouble.

The authors review what studies actually show about this ratio in patients with obesity, and how consistent the pattern really is. They weigh its promise against its limits, since diet, medicines, and lab methods can all sway the numbers. Their cautious account is a useful check on a popular shortcut that is sometimes read as more certain than the evidence allows.
plos-pone-0360418:
Shiwei Wu and colleagues examined in 2026 whether simple blood based scores measured before surgery can flag patients likely to develop a pancreatic fistula after distal pancreatectomy. In that operation, part of the pancreas is removed, and a fistula, a leak of pancreatic fluid, is among its most feared complications. The scores under study combine signs of inflammation and nutrition from routine preoperative tests.

The team analyzed how strongly those indices correlated with fistula risk in their patients. A cheap warning drawn from blood tests already ordered would let surgeons watch high risk patients more closely and act at the first sign of a leak. Studies of this kind aim to turn ordinary lab results into early, practical protection.
plos-pone-0356818:
Daniel Martel and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It characterizes the dual functions of CK1.2, a protein from Leishmania, the parasite that causes leishmaniasis. Dual means the protein works in two arenas: inside the parasite itself and inside the macrophage, the human immune cell the parasite invades and lives within.

A protein that serves the parasite in both places is an attractive drug target, since blocking it could strike twice. Characterizing both functions carefully is the groundwork for that hope. Parasitologists and drug developers working on a neglected tropical disease are the readers for this two-sided portrait.
plos-pone-0351518: Garcia Castillo, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on leaf-cutter ants in the tropics of the Americas. The study asks a plain question: do ant species with broad tastes cope with farm and town land use better than picky ones? Comparing wide-ranging and narrow-ranging species can show which ants survive when people reshape the land. That matters for farms and forests that depend on ants to move soil and seeds.
plos-pone-0359618: Sun and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a desktop virtual reality game for design students. The game teaches color composition, how hues are matched and balanced in basic design work. The team built the game and then tested how well it teaches. A playful, low-cost tool could help beginners grasp color rules that lectures alone make abstract.
plos-pone-0359418: Pacheco and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on nursing students in Saudi Arabia. They asked whether gender changes the link between belief in one's own study skills and actual grades. That belief, called academic self-efficacy, often predicts effort. If the link differs by gender, teachers can tailor support instead of giving every student the same advice.

plaw-115-191-2018: Congress passed this federal law, the John Muir National Historic Site Expansion Act, in 2018. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-115-188-2018: Congress passed this federal law, the Department of Veterans Affairs Senior Executive Accountability Act, in 2018. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. It is kept here as part of the lasting public-law record.

Much progress has been made toward deciphering RHO gtpase functions, and many studies have convincingly demonstrated that altered signal transduction.
