europmc-pmc7029418: India and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on the burden of mental illnesses across the states of India: the global burden of disease study 1990-2017. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
plaw-115-177-2018: This 2018 federal law amends title 38, United States Code, to authorize the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to furnish assistance for adaptations of residences of veterans in. Amendments like this fine-tune existing programs without rewriting the whole law. It stands as Public Law 115-177 of the 115th Congress.
europmc-pmc7221918: Published in 2020, this review paper takes on a review on recent advances (new steps forward) in nitrogen-containing molecules and their biological (from living things) uses. It walks through what the field currently knows, study by study. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc8155318: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on apolipoprotein e binding drives structural (about shapes) and compositional rearrangement of mrna-containing lipid nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
plaw-115-206-2018: In 2018, Congress passed a federal law to extend a project of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission involving the Cannonsville Dam. The full text carries the binding legal details. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.

europmc-pmc7289118: This 2020 research paper covers double-membrane vesicles (tiny sacs) as platforms for viral replication. Viruses, as obligate intracellular parasites, exploit of cells pathways and resources in a variety of fascinating ways. europmc-pmc8080618: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at advanced glycation end products and other adducts in aging-related diseases and alcohol-driven tissue injury. europmc-pmc9935618: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on aimed at epigenetic (gene-switching) regulators to overcome drug resistance in cancers. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
plaw-115-104-2018: Congress passed this federal law, the African American Civil Rights Network Act, in 2018. The short title states its purpose; the enrolled text holds the binding details. europmc-pmc8369118: A 2021 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at patient-reported (from patients themselves) outcome (result) measures: a review of generic and condition-specific measures and a discussion of trends and issues. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
king-henry-iv-part-2-pg1518: The autumnal sequel in this edition: Falstaff aging and ailing, Hal growing into his crown, and the famous, painful rejection. Funnier and sadder than Part 1, it is Shakespeare's great play about time. The end of an era, onstage and off.
in-the-shadow-of-the-glen-pg1618: J. M. Synge's 1903 one-act play about a young wife, an old husband thought dead, and a tramp who offers escape. Poetic, earthy, and quietly rebellious, it announced a major new voice. Irish drama's beautiful beginning.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume eighteen of Carlyle's Frederick: Rossbach and Leuthen, the miraculous victories against overwhelming odds. The king's genius shines brightest in these desperate campaigns. Military history written as epic poetry, in Carlyle's most exalted strain. Carlyle's battle-pieces have never been surpassed in English prose.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-18: Volume eighteen collects more of Montaigne's late essays. He ponders reputation, rest, and the slow approach of age. The thinker grows gentler with the years but no less sharp. A calm and golden evening of the mind.
plos-pone-0356518:
Sai-Leung Ng, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, asks what actually drives Hong Kong shoppers to buy secondhand clothing. Surveys everywhere say people love the idea; the author wanted the mechanics. An online survey of five hundred forty-five respondents fed a structural model. It extended the classic knowledge, attitude, practice chain with two situational factors: price consciousness and perceived risk. Hong Kong's cheap new clothing might erase the usual thrift motive, so both belonged in the test.

The results partly overturned the textbook chain. Environmental knowledge pushed purchases directly, and perceived risk did too, while attitude mattered only indirectly, by shaping how risky secondhand clothes felt. Price consciousness did nothing at all, neither driving nor mediating purchases. Ng credits the city's fiercely competitive, duty free retail market, where new clothes are already cheap enough to mute thrift. Green retail strategy there should sell knowledge and trust, not discounts.
plos-pone-0358218:
Kun He and three colleagues combine data mining with a rat model to find the genes that drive uveitis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Uveitis, inflammation inside the eye, can blind, and its autoimmune machinery is partly mapped. The team mined a dataset of immune cells from patients and healthy donors, and crossed it with six disease gene databases. From the one hundred thirty-nine genes that surfaced, they built an interaction network. Hub genes were picked by their connections.

The gene set clustered in inflammation, immune response, and viral defense pathways. The hubs were then checked in rats with induced autoimmune eye inflammation, measuring their activity in eye, liver, and spleen tissue. The animal results supported the computational nominations, tying the database exercise to disease. The authors offer the hub genes as candidate markers and drug targets, in a field where diagnosis still leans on a clinician's eye and experience.
plos-pone-0357918:
Naveed Shahid led a team of six authors modeling a poultry disease in PLOS ONE in 2026. Newcastle disease can devastate flocks, and planners use epidemic models to foresee its course. Shahid's team added delayed, chance-based terms to capture how outbreaks unfold with lags and random variation.

The authors checked the model's stability and worked out approximations that make it usable. A model that reflects delay matters because control steps, like vaccination or culling, also act with lags. Veterinarians and farm officials gain sharper forecasts of when an outbreak will peak and fade. Better forecasts support faster, better-sized responses that can save flocks and limit spread between farms.
plos-pone-0357018:
Yun Zhang led a team of seven authors who used language models to track public opinion in China, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their market was portable energy gear, a fast-moving sector where social media chatter can signal demand shifts early. The team analyzed large sets of social media comments with large language models.

Zhang's group turned that chatter into a data-driven read on what buyers think, want, and complain about. Companies in fast markets can use such monitoring to spot problems and trends sooner than sales figures reveal them. The study also tests how well current language models handle opinion at scale. For market researchers, it is a worked example of AI listening posts done with care.
plos-pone-0358118:
Cong Liang, Hongyan Niu, and Lina Xue built a scale to measure how much care dialysis patients need, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People on hemodialysis depend on nurses for many tasks, but no existing scale captured that dependency well. The team developed the HD-CDS scale and ran a first evaluation of how it performs.

Liang's tool lets clinics measure real dependency and staff their units to match what patients actually need. Understaffing a unit of highly dependent patients risks safety; overstaffing wastes scarce nurses. A validated scale turns staffing arguments into measurements. The preliminary testing reported here is the first step; wider use will show whether the scale holds up across different units and patient mixes.
plos-pone-0347018:
Heeseung Choi and a team including patient and clinician reviewers check whether a Korean translation of a shared-decision rating tool works as intended. The tool scores how well doctors and patients make treatment choices together, following a six-step model. Translators moved it into Korean through forward and back translation with checks for meaning, then doctors and several hundred patients used it in real shared decisions.

Statistical checks supported a single overall score for both the patient and doctor versions, and both scored high on internal consistency. The doctor version matched closely with an established doctor questionnaire, while the patient version aligned moderately with its partner tools. Choi and colleagues say Korean clinics can now measure shared decision quality with a tested local instrument.
plos-pone-0354918:
Setegn Muche Fenta and a large team mined health surveys from thirty-three Sub-Saharan African countries. The surveys covered 195,000 toddlers. The team counted how many vaccine doses children actually receive. It also looked at what drives the count up or down. Their 2026 analysis used count regression models. These handle the many children with few or no doses, while allowing communities to differ.

The average child received only about five and a half doses, far short of a full schedule. Doses rose with mothers' schooling and work. They rose with household wealth, holding a health card, and delivering in a facility. Frequent antenatal visits and vitamin A receipt helped too. Doses fell in rural areas. Each contact with the health system, the pattern suggests, is another chance to vaccinate that systems should not waste.
plos-pone-0355218:
Nan Tao and co-authors studied how visitors picture three living historic neighbourhoods in Yunnan, China. These districts mix heritage protection, daily community life, and tourism in the same streets. Their 2026 study proposed a five-part lens covering people, space, setting, place, and felt atmosphere, then tested it on visitor writing.

The team mined visitor posts, measured their feelings with a text model, and weighed what mattered most against how well each site performed. All three districts blended old buildings, street life, and local routine, but they differed in how developed tourism was. Historic remains were a shared strength everywhere. Weak points included basic facilities and some visitor experiences, which the authors flag for improvement.
plos-pone-0355018:
Jackline Akello and colleagues report in 2026 on the strain felt by health workers in Uganda. Their focus is care for women who are pregnant and live with sickle cell illness. Interviews and group talks were held at referral hospitals. Doctors, midwives, and other maternity staff took part.

Workers described gaps in their own knowledge and fear when cases turned grave. Sadness ran deep when outcomes were poor. Myths in the community made the work harder still. Short supplies, missing guidelines, and no joined up specialist care added strain. The authors call for team based care, better training, and system reform.
plos-pone-0354118:
Jeff Vallance and Lynn Corcoran interview in 2026 people who had a stroke linked to a small hole between heart chambers, most of whom later had it closed with a device. Such heart linked stroke may leave special worries about exercise. Talks explored what helped or blocked a return to physical activity after the event and procedure.

Fear, anxiety, and worry about the closure device formed one barrier group. Fitness change varied, with some feeling fitter and others less active than before. Lasting tiredness, leftover symptoms, and odd heart sensations also held people back. The authors call for clearer guidance and support on returning to activity.
plos-pone-0351418:
Cédric Gutfreund led a team of seven authors on this 2026 crystal structure study of an enzyme that copies an artificial genetic material. The material, called HNA, uses a different sugar backbone from DNA and could serve in future sensors and catalysts. Their enzyme, engineered from a heat-loving microbe's copying protein, converts HNA back into DNA.

Frozen mid-action with its template, the enzyme clamps shut much like the natural version does with DNA. One HNA building block also flips its sugar shape as the complex closes. Gutfreund says that flexibility must guide the next round of enzyme design.
plos-pone-0354718:
Yuanmin Zhang led a team of six authors on this 2026 computer science paper about grouping unlabeled text into topics. Clustering short documents is hard because word features are sparse and tangled. Their model learns by contrasting similar and different texts, sharpens the signal with mutual information, invents more negative examples, and uses a newer network type built for complex patterns.

Across eight standard data sets it took top accuracy on seven. Applied to Chinese social media posts about technology, it separated themes like artificial intelligence and consumer gadgets cleanly, showing real-world promise.
plos-pone-0354618:
Dragoș-Vasile Leordean and Eugen-Richard Ardelean published this 2026 benchmark study of artificial intelligence that finds objects in microscope images of tissue. They ran the newest YOLO detector family against several rival architectures on five histology data sets, using shared training rules and measuring accuracy, speed, and computing cost.

One mid-generation model, YOLOv11, performed strongly across most collections. The authors also add a rescoring trick that spreads confident labels to neighboring boxes, lifting results most when the base model's confidence is poorly calibrated. Their comparison aims to guide labs choosing detection software.
plos-pone-0354818:
Fertitta and colleagues, in a 2026 methods paper, build a standard way to measure skin tumors in mice used to study neurofibromatosis type 1. People with this inherited condition often grow many small skin tumors, and no approved drug treatment exists. Testing new drugs in mice first requires measures that different labs can trust and repeat.

Their mouse model marks the tumor-forming cells with a glowing tag, so tumors can be tracked and counted in images. The team defined measures at two scales, from whole-tumor counts and glowing area down to cell makeup in tissue slices. They wrote automated image tools and checked them against careful hand counts. The automated scores matched hand work closely, showed no steady bias, and ran far faster, up to a hundred times quicker. The shared workflow should let drug studies in this model be compared more fairly.
plos-pone-0354518:
Abera and colleagues, in a 2026 review, pool studies on vitamin D shortage in Africans with type 2 diabetes. Africa has plenty of sun, yet shortage is common and may worsen blood sugar control. Genes that shape how the body uses vitamin D could matter too. The team searched major databases for studies up to mid-2025.

Twenty-two studies with thousands of people from eleven countries were combined. About half of the patients lacked enough vitamin D, with the highest share in East Africa. People who were deficient had notably worse long-term blood sugar readings than those with enough. One well-studied gene variant showed no clear link to diabetes risk, though the estimate was very uncertain. Study results varied widely, so the authors call the pooled figures a starting point. They argue that checking vitamin D in African diabetes care deserves more attention and better local studies.
plos-pone-0353118:
Jafari and colleagues, in a 2026 trial, test whether pregnant women fare better when the same midwifery students care for them throughout. Continuous care from a known provider is known to help mothers, and using final-year students could extend that care where staff are scarce. No trial had checked this student-led version before.

Low-risk women in the later months of pregnancy were assigned at random to student continuity care or usual care, with both groups also getting standard services. About ninety women took part, and all were followed after birth. Women with student support reported far better birth experiences on a standard questionnaire. Their ratings of care during pregnancy, labor, and the weeks after birth were also higher, as was overall satisfaction. Cesarean births were somewhat fewer in the student group. The authors present student continuity as a practical way to give more women a known, steady caregiver.
plos-pone-0349318:
van Wijk and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare two exam question types for telling strong medical students from struggling ones. Multiple-choice questions are efficient but invite guessing and cueing. Very short answer questions force students to produce the answer themselves. The team mined six exams from three cohorts of medical students in their first and second years.

Single short-answer items separated students more sharply than single multiple-choice items in every exam. Across exams, short-answer scores also tracked students' overall grade averages more strongly, and were better at flagging both the weakest and the strongest fifth of students. The authors argue the format earns its marking cost: used across a program, short answers can spot students who need help earlier, and confirm excellence more fairly. They place the work within a standard framework for judging whether a test measures what it should.
plos-pone-0354418:
Yang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link three simple body and blood measures to thinking decline and dementia, using the giant UK Biobank. One measure blends blood sugar and fat markers into an insulin resistance index. Another describes body shape, especially a wide waist for one's weight. The team followed more than three hundred seventy thousand people.

All three measures, including the two multiplied together, tracked with poorer scores on thinking tests. People in the highest quarter of each measure carried notably higher dementia risk than those in the lowest quarter, with the body shape index showing the strongest link. The patterns held for Alzheimer's disease and for vascular dementia as well. Because all three measures come from cheap, routine data, the authors suggest they could help flag people for earlier brain checks, while noting such links alone do not prove cause.
plos-pone-0354018:
Yue Chang proposes an automated way to find and measure cracks in concrete, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human inspectors judge small cracks inconsistently and sometimes at personal risk, while computer methods starve for labelled training images. The author's answer pairs an image-generating network, which fabricates extra realistic crack photos, with a segmentation network sharpened by attention modules to outline real cracks in new pictures.

Trained this way, the model outlined cracks with accuracy and F1 scores in the low eighties. A fractal measurement step then quantified each crack's geometry. The pipeline points toward cheaper, safer routine checks of bridges, dams, and towers, where catching a crack early prevents costly failures.
plos-pone-0352318:
Thurayya Eid and three colleagues study what good supervision does for nursing students on hospital placements in Saudi Arabia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE survey. One hundred and forty-five students at three teaching hospitals in Riyadh rated the support they received from supervisors, their own confidence in clinical tasks, and their satisfaction with the placement. The question matters nationally, as health reforms demand many more well-trained nurses.

Support, confidence, and satisfaction all climbed together, and statistical modelling showed supervision boosting satisfaction partly by first building confidence. The authors recommend standardising how supervisors are trained and how feedback is given, so a student's experience stops depending on which ward they land in.
plos-pone-0352018:
Frisch and colleagues reviewed a liver treatment for hormone-linked tumors that had spread from elsewhere in the body in a 2026 study. The treatment sends tiny radioactive beads through blood vessels into liver tumors. Thirty patients treated over seven years at one center were checked with scans before and after care.

Tumors with richer blood flow on early scans tended to shrink more after treatment. The team also weighed scan measures against how long patients lived, which averaged close to three years. Being able to receive a follow-on targeted therapy linked most strongly to longer life. Early blood flow on scans may help doctors pick who benefits most from the bead treatment.
plos-pone-0344618:
Selvi and colleagues compared three kinds of feedback for student writing in Turkey in a 2026 study. Eighty-four university students learning English wrote argument essays over ten weeks. One group used a grammar checker, one used a chat-based AI tool, and one relied only on teacher comments.

All groups grew in planning and thinking strategies over time, but the chat-based AI group gained most in self-managed learning. Its writing also improved in accuracy and content quality beyond the other groups. Gains were strongest for mid-level learners. The authors suggest smart AI feedback can lighten teacher load, though that effect was not measured directly in the trial.
plos-pone-0353018:
Oliver Mendoza-Cano and seven colleagues map this 2026 PLOS One analysis of Mexico's measles resurgence in 2025 and 2026, after more than twenty years without home-grown transmission. Falling vaccination coverage and pandemic disruptions had left pockets of low immunity. Using national case reports at municipal level, the team applied a scanning method that finds clusters of cases beyond what population size would predict.

More than eight thousand confirmed cases appeared across several hundred municipalities. The largest cluster sat in northern Mexico and held nearly half the cases, while a later western cluster and many brief, intense local outbreaks followed. A final faint, wide cluster suggested transmission was spreading diffusely. The authors recommend region-specific surveillance and catch-up vaccination drives to close the immunity gaps.
plos-pone-0350118:
Quang Tuan Rémy Nguyen and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of speech in Huntington's disease. It tests whether speech recordings can reveal psychiatric symptoms. Eighty-nine patients with confirmed disease recorded six storytelling and description tasks at a Paris hospital. Their speech was analyzed for word choice, meaning, and sound traits. Machine learning models were trained to detect symptoms rated by clinicians.

The models detected obsessive-compulsive behavior, depression, and apathy at rates well above chance. Language-based traits were the most steady performers. Sound traits added help for depression. Irritability resisted detection by every trait type. The authors present speech analysis as a promising, low-burden way to flag mental health problems. That matters in a disease where clinic visits are already demanding.
plos-pone-0350918:
Danielle Lamb and seven colleagues follow the mental health of England's health workers through the pandemic's first three years. Their 2026 cohort study, called NHS CHECK, enrolled over twenty-two thousand staff from seventeen hospital trusts. Surveys ran four times between April 2020 and March 2023. They measured common mental disorders, depression, anxiety, alcohol misuse, trauma symptoms, moral injury, and burnout. Non-clinical staff were included alongside doctors and nurses.

The burden barely budged. About half the participants met the threshold for a probable common mental disorder at every single wave. The strongest predictor of later trouble was already being unwell at the start. Clinical and non-clinical staff suffered alike, with no consistent gap. Younger, female, and lower-paid staff fared worse, as did those feeling unsupported by colleagues and managers. Sustained distress on this scale threatens staffing itself, through absence and turnover, long after the emergency wards emptied.
plos-pone-0351318:
HuiYing Jin and five colleagues build a skin lesion classifier designed to learn from very few examples. Their 2026 study addresses a real bottleneck in medical imaging. Rare lesions offer few training pictures, boundaries blur, and sizes vary wildly. Their network carries three cooperating modules. One adjusts its viewing window to each lesion's scale. Another blends information across resolutions, weighting the most useful channels. A third uses image gradients to sharpen attention on borders and texture.

Few-shot experiments ran on two public datasets of skin images. The system beat existing baseline models across several metrics. It also generalised promisingly between the datasets. Visual checks confirmed the model genuinely looks at the lesion, not the surrounding skin. Dermatology AI usually starves on rare conditions. A classifier built for scarcity could extend computer-aided diagnosis to the lesions doctors see least and worry about most.
plos-pone-0352418:
Dandan Xu, Kun Hu, and Linlu Cai generate advertisement images that obey a planned layout. Their 2026 study builds a two-stage framework. Layout decides where the eye lands, and with it whether the product registers. Text-to-image systems handle simple scenes well but garble complex ones. Stage one turns a written brief into a full layout plan. A transformer generator plans background and objects together, learning long-range links between words and regions. Earlier systems planned objects alone.

Stage two paints the image inside that plan. A fine-grained interaction step keeps text, layout, and pixels in constant conversation. Object fidelity, whether the product itself survives generation intact, is the named optimisation target. Advertisers cannot use a beautiful image whose bottle is warped. The framework treats layout as a contract: plan the whole scene first, then render it faithfully enough to sell.
plos-pone-0350218:
Aiju Li and colleagues built a forecasting system for river runoff across China, the numbers that decide flood warnings and reservoir releases. Rivers remember at several speeds at once, quick storm pulses and slow seasonal swells, and water flows downhill through connected basins, so a model must respect both clocks and maps. Their design fuses time scales with a gating step and teaches spatial attention the true upstream-downstream links.

Tested on a national gridded benchmark built from a public global flood dataset, the method beat existing approaches overall and kept its forecasts spatially consistent with the river network. For agencies watching monsoon floods, forecasts that honor basin shape, not just local history, could mean earlier and better-placed warnings. The work is a modeling study, so its proof rests on benchmark data rather than a live season.
plos-pone-0351218:
Gene testing can fine-tune heart drugs, yet cardiologists rarely order it. Maram O Abbas and colleagues interviewed fifteen cardiologists across public and private care in the United Arab Emirates about what blocks adoption, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Doctors voiced strong support in principle, especially for high-risk patients. Barriers sat at every level: test cost and turnaround, unclear rules, patchy lab access, and uneven doctor training. The analysis followed an established framework covering the tool, the setting, and the people involved. The authors say the mixed public and private system needs shared pathways before gene-guided prescribing can become routine heart care.
plos-pone-0348118:
Ahmad Ahadi and colleagues combined two cleaning forces, electric plasma above water and bubble collapse inside water, to strip blue dye from wastewater. Each method alone makes reactive oxygen that attacks pollutants. Together in one rig, they treated dye at several strengths in distilled and tap water, with most colour gone in under five minutes.

Full clearing always arrived within fifteen minutes. Direct coupling, where plasma and bubbles act together, beat a split setup. Energy use per gram removed beat prior reports for the strongest dye mix. Light checks confirmed hydroxyl radicals, the main attackers, were present. A fast, frugal hybrid could scale to factory dye waste if costs hold.
plos-pone-0349118:
Temesgen Yaekob Ergano and Sure Pulla Rao examined finance and growth across sub-Saharan Africa in 2026. Whether deeper banking helps economies grow, or at times harms them, is a live policy question for the region.

Using a method suited to data that track countries over time, they weighed several banking and money measures against growth. Bank reserves, open trade, and broad money links looked positive, while heavy bank lending to private borrowers dragged growth down. The contrast hints that careless lending can undo the gains of a growing financial system, a caution for regulators pushing credit expansion.
plos-pone-0349218:
Naishen Qin and co-authors mined two decades of the United States adverse event database in 2026 for drugs tied to cardiovascular harm. Spontaneous reports cannot prove cause, but patterns across millions of records flag risks worth probing.

More than one and a half million heart related reports were analysed with four signal methods. Three drugs topped the list, all since withdrawn or restricted, which supports the method. Subgroup patterns differed by sex and age, and known cancer drug heart damage also appeared. The authors caution that some signals may reflect the illness treated rather than the drug, a nuance prescribers must keep.
plos-pone-0350818:
Frida Torell, Michael Dimitriou, and co-authors studied how the arm's fastest reflexes change with the task at hand. When a robot tugs the arm, muscles answer in waves, from a near-instant stretch reflex to later, more flexible responses. Their 2026 study used a delayed reaching task, varying load, waiting time, tug direction, and target position while recording activity in seven arm muscles.

Shoulder muscles adjusted their responses to the task from the earliest wave, though a steady background load blunted that tuning. The latest wave showed the strongest task influence, growing when target and tug pulled in opposite ways. The results show reflexes are not fixed wiring. Even the quickest responses carry information about what the person is trying to do.
plos-pone-0349418:
Jia-hao Wang, Yan-ming Hao, and co-authors examined two blood measures in patients hospitalized with fractures caused by fragile bones. One measure, homocysteine, is tied to vessel damage and weak bones, while parathyroid hormone controls how bone is rebuilt. Their 2026 study covered more than two thousand fracture patients at one hospital and compared fasting blood levels taken at admission.

Higher homocysteine came with higher hormone levels, but the pattern was not a straight line. The hormone rose steadily up to a point, then climbed more sharply beyond it. The link looked stronger in patients with high blood pressure, poor kidney function, or low magnesium. The authors caution that the clinical value of homocysteine in judging risk still needs confirmation in further studies.
plos-pone-0348518:
Zakir Hossion and co-authors tested whether a simple ratio from a routine blood count can forecast how pneumonia patients will fare in hospital. Costly inflammation markers are not always available in Bangladesh, where their 2026 study followed one hundred adults admitted with community-acquired pneumonia at Dhaka Medical College Hospital. The ratio compares neutrophils, first-responder cells, to lymphocytes, and a set cutoff marked it as high.

Two thirds of patients had a high ratio, and they were significantly more likely to die, need oxygen or intensive care, and stay longer in hospital. The link with a long stay was especially strong. The ratio's accuracy was moderate for predicting long stays and modest for other outcomes. The authors present it as a cheap, immediate aid for judging risk where advanced tests are scarce.
plos-pone-0349618:
Nicole Freene and co-authors set out to calibrate activity trackers for heart patients, whose bodies respond to exercise differently from healthy adults. Guidelines urge these patients to reach moderate-to-vigorous activity, yet the tracker thresholds in use were built on other populations. Their 2026 study fitted eighty-six patients with hip and wrist devices during rest, daily activities, and a treadmill test with measured breathing gases.

Resting energy use came out about twenty percent below the textbook value trackers assume. Hip-worn counts tracked exercise intensity strongly and gave the best thresholds for identifying moderate-to-vigorous activity, while wrist readings related weakly. A check in a separate international group of patients broadly supported the new cut-points, though individual variation stayed wide. The authors offer heart patients a fairer yardstick for their activity.
plos-pone-0350418:
Ngo Cao Nghia, Phan Khanh Duy, and Bao Quoc Truong-Dinh surveyed hotel guests in Vietnam and Thailand to learn how frontline staff turn satisfied customers into passionate brand advocates. Such evangelism, where guests promote a hotel unprompted, is marketing gold. Their 2026 two-wave survey of more than four hundred guests tested staff digital skill, proactive help, and relationship building, alongside brand image and customer trust.

Both image and trust carried staff behavior into advocacy, but the balance differed by country. In Vietnam, symbolic brand image dominated, while in Thailand, trust built through relationships prevailed. Loyalty programs strengthened the trust route in Thailand, and repeat visits shaped the image route differently in each place. The authors advise hotels to adapt their advocacy strategy to local culture rather than copy one playbook.
plos-pone-0347918:
Grace Chang, Rahul Malhotra, and Benjamin Seligman asked whether money and education change how much physical ability older Americans need to stay independent in daily life. Bathing, dressing, and eating without help is a defining outcome of healthy aging. Using a national retirement study, they linked walking speed and grip strength to daily-living limits, then tested whether education, income, or wealth softened that link.

Thousands of participants were followed both at one point in time and as new limits developed. If wealth buys help, equipment, and home changes, then richer adults might stay independent despite weaker bodies, while poorer adults cannot. The answer guides whether support programs should fund strength itself or fund the workarounds that money usually buys.
plos-pone-0348018:
Oak E. Milam and Gary Marsat study weakly electric fish, which sense nearby fish of their own kind through faint electric fields. Their 2026 paper asks how the fish brain knows where another fish is located. They focus on a brain area that first handles these electric signals and on the different cell types found there.

The team played an artificial signal shaped like a real fish signal and recorded from cells across the body surface map. Some cells, including deep-layer cells of one response type, carried sharp place information. Other cell groups carried much weaker place clues. The split suggests the brain sorts this signal stream into separate paths very early in processing.
plos-pone-0349018:
Xiaosa Wang and co-workers ask whether the amount of fetal DNA floating in a pregnant person's blood early on predicts early birth or small babies. The DNA comes from the placenta and is already measured in common screening tests. Their 2026 study matches hundreds of cases with thousands of controls to balance other risk factors before comparing outcomes.

Higher fetal DNA levels went with lower risk of early birth at every level measured. For low birth weight, the link appeared only at the highest levels, like a threshold. The patterns held across most groups of mothers. If confirmed, a value already in the chart could give doctors an early warning sign at no extra testing cost.
plos-pone-0347118:
Youssef Zougheib and co-workers follow how fast nearsightedness worsened in Lebanese children across the COVID-19 lockdown years. Lockdown pushed children indoors onto screens, and eye doctors feared a surge. Their 2026 study tracks one hundred children seen at a Beirut medical center, joining eye records going back years with family reports of screen and outdoor time.

Worsening ran fastest during the lockdown school years, then slowed to about half that pace afterward. Screen time rose and outdoor time fell sharply during lockdown. Yet within the group, reported hours alone did not predict whose eyes worsened most. Younger children favored tablets and logged fewer screen hours. The era clearly mattered, even if single habits explain less than expected.
plos-pone-0347518:
AshaRani and colleagues catalog Singapore's programs for promoting mental health in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. Searching medical and gray literature from 2000 onward, they gathered one hundred six studies describing programs that aim to build wellbeing rather than only treat illness.

Programs served many groups, with a particular concentration on older adults in hospitals and community settings, and covered people with mental disorders, physical illnesses, and developmental conditions. Each program was documented with a standard checklist so future reviews can replicate or compare them. The map exposes where provision is thick and where it is missing, giving Singapore's planners a base for systematic evaluation.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1318 is a brief UN Security Council decision adopted on 7 September 2000, during the period of the Millennium Summit, when world leaders gathered at the United Nations in unusual numbers. Its entire operative content is a single act of adoption.

By it, the Council adopts an attached declaration on making itself more effective at keeping world peace, with a special focus on Africa. The declaration committed the Council's members, many represented at head-of-state level for the occasion, to strengthen peacekeeping and conflict prevention, with special weight on Africa's wars. The hosted text carries the decision itself; the declaration it incorporates set the tone for peacekeeping reform debates that followed.

Nine days of cover for Balkan rules came from this brief text of 2002. On 21 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1418 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. The text concerns the wars in the former Yugoslavia. It extends a deadline set a year before in Resolution 1357. That text dealt with the arms ban and linked steps for the region.

Two short lines do the whole job. The rules of Resolution 1357 stay in force until 30 June 2002. The Council stays seized of the matter. The bridge kept the legal frame from lapsing. A fuller step on Bosnia's post-war order came next.

After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, loose ends from the sanctions era remained. Resolution 1518, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003, created a fresh committee to handle one of them. The earlier sanctions committee had been shut down in May 2003. Yet lists of Saddam-era officials and entities still needed maintaining.

The new body includes every Council member. Its task is identifying people and groups whose assets states must freeze and transfer. It inherited the old committee's list and its working rules. Members acted under Chapter VII, the Charter's enforcement chapter. The committee kept the financial pressure of Resolution 1483 alive after the old machinery was gone.

Egypt seized the Suez Canal in July 1956, and the world held its breath. Britain and France were furious. Egypt's leader, Nasser, claimed the canal as his own. Talks ran in New York through the fall. Resolution 118 passed with no dissent on 13 October 1956. It set six tests for any deal on the canal.

Ships of all flags must pass freely, with no bias. Egypt's rule over the canal must be honored. The canal's work must sit apart from any state's politics. Tolls would be set by pact between Egypt and canal users. A fair share of fees would fund the canal's growth. Fights with the old canal firm would go to judges, not guns. Two weeks later, war came anyway.

Resolution 318, adopted on 28 July 1972 by fourteen votes to none with one American abstention, works on the machinery of Rhodesia sanctions. The Council had asked its sanctions committee in February to propose ways of making the measures against the illegal regime bite harder, including changes to the committee's own terms of reference. The committee's special report was now in hand.

The Council reaffirmed that sanctions against Southern Rhodesia would remain fully in force until their objectives were completely achieved. It deplored the states still defying the 1968 sanctions resolution in breach of their Charter duties. And it restated the Rhodesian people's right to self-determination and independence, recognizing the legitimacy of their struggle to win it.

Resolution 18, adopted on 13 February 1947 by ten votes to none with the Soviet Union abstaining, takes up the postwar call to cut armaments. The General Assembly had resolved in December 1946 that regulating and reducing weapons and armed forces was a top task for strengthening peace. The Council accepted that assignment and organized itself to act on it.

It created a commission, made up of the Council's own members, to draft practical proposals within three months at most. The proposals were to cover general arms reduction and effective safeguards to police it. The Council also agreed to take up the Atomic Energy Commission's report quickly and decide how to speed its work, an early pairing of conventional and atomic disarmament.

North Korea's first nuclear test brings sweeping sanctions in Resolution 1718, adopted unanimously on 14 October 2006. Pyongyang claimed it had tested a nuclear device on 9 October, defying the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty it had quit and ignoring warnings from the Council days earlier. Members called the test a grave challenge to the non-proliferation regime and a danger to peace in the region and beyond.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned the test and demanded no further nuclear or missile launches. It barred the sale to North Korea of heavy weapons, missile and nuclear-related materials, and luxury goods, and imposed travel bans and asset freezes on people tied to the programs. States were told to inspect suspect cargo within their laws.

Resolution 1618, adopted on 4 August 2005, condemns the bombing campaign then tearing at Iraq's transition. The Council reaffirmed support for Iraqis building representative government under the 2004 framework, and praised their courage in pursuing political and economic change under constant terrorist threat. Iraq's government was commended for steps toward national dialogue and unity.

In the strongest terms, the Council condemned without reservation the terrorist attacks in Iraq, treating every such act as a threat to peace and security. It singled out the shameless and horrific attacks of the previous weeks, which had killed large numbers of civilians. The text ties the condemnations to the Council's wider counter-terrorism resolutions, from 1999 and September 2001 onward.

Portugal's colonial wars are judged a threat to peace in Resolution 218. It passed on 23 November 1965, with seven votes in favor and four members not voting either way. Thirty-two African states had brought the case to the hall. Portugal had spurned the Council's 1963 texts on its colonies. In their place, it stepped up harsh rule and armed sweeps against Africans who sought freedom and self-rule.

The Council held that this course, toward both the colonized and their neighbors, gravely shook world peace. It deplored Lisbon's refusal to act. It pointed back to its 1963 steps, which told states to halt arms sales to Portugal for use in colonial wars. The case fed the long squeeze that ended the empire a decade later.

Cyprus sees a fresh opening in Resolution 1818, adopted on 13 June 2008. The two sides' leaders had agreed in March and May to work toward a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. The Ledra Street crossing had opened, building trust. The Green Line stayed broadly calm, and work on missing persons and mine clearing was moving ahead.

The Council gives full support to the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, UNFICYP, and extends its mandate until 15 December 2008. It urges both sides to build on the momentum and prepare the ground so full talks can start smoothly. It asks them to consult UNFICYP on marking out the buffer zone. It also calls on the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces to restore the earlier military position at Strovilia. A report is due by 1 December 2008.

Resolution 1018, adopted on 7 November 1995, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the death of Judge Andrés Aguilar Mawdsley on 24 October 1995, which left a vacancy on the Court for the rest of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Council fixes the election date. It decides the election will take place on 28 February 1996, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its fiftieth session.

Piracy in the Gulf of Guinea draws a regional response in Resolution 2018, adopted on 31 October 2011. Attacks and armed robbery at sea off West and Central Africa threatened shipping, seafarers, who were sometimes taken hostage, and the region's development. Nigeria and Benin had begun joint patrols off Benin's coast. The Council said a fix was needed, led by the region's states.

The Council condemns all piracy and armed robbery in the Gulf of Guinea. It encourages ECOWAS, the Economic Community of Central African States, and the Gulf of Guinea Commission to build a joint strategy. It covers laws criminalizing piracy, a framework for sharing information and coordinating operations, and bilateral or regional patrols that respect freedom of navigation. It calls for cooperation in prosecuting suspects, including financiers, and asks flag states to issue defensive guidance to ships. A UN assessment mission is welcomed, and international help is encouraged.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 69/18 (2014), titled 'The situation in Afghanistan,' is the Assembly's annual omnibus statement on the country at the moment the international combat mission wound down. It reaffirms Afghanistan's sovereignty and unity and reviews the transition of security responsibility to Afghan forces, due to finish at the end of 2014.

The Assembly pledges continued support for Afghanistan's government and people, condemns violence by the Taliban, Al-Qaida, and other extremist and criminal groups, and deplores the heavy toll on civilians. It backs the Kabul process of Afghan ownership, the Tokyo partnership framework, regional cooperation through the Heart of Asia process, and the coordinating role of the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan. It also presses for refugee returns, human rights, anti-corruption work, and counter-narcotics efforts. The resolution sketches the international community's terms for staying engaged through Afghanistan's transformation decade.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Piracy off the coast of Somalia is the subject of Resolution 1918, adopted on 27 April 2010. Pirates were seizing ships in busy shipping lanes and holding crews for ransom. Yet many suspects caught at sea were released without any trial. Courts in Somalia and nearby countries lacked the laws, staff, and prison space to handle the cases.

The Council said that failing to prosecute pirates weakened the whole effort against piracy. It called on all states to make piracy a crime under their own laws. States were also asked to look favorably on trying and jailing suspects caught off Somalia. The Council ordered a report within three months. The report had to set out options for new courts, including special chambers in national courts, a regional court, or an international court.

Arms sales to South Africa became a binding ban on 4 November 1977. Resolution 418 was adopted unanimously that day. South Africa had built up its armed forces and attacked neighboring states. It also repressed its own people at home. There was concern that it stood close to making nuclear weapons.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ruled that South Africa's drive to acquire arms threatened world peace. All states had to stop supplying South Africa with arms and related material at once. The ban covered weapons, ammunition, military vehicles, and spare parts. States had to review their existing arms contracts and licenses. They also had to refuse all cooperation with South Africa in making nuclear weapons. It was the first time the arms embargo on South Africa became mandatory for everyone.

Peace for Cambodia was signed in Paris on 23 October 1991, after years of war. The Paris agreements set out a complete political settlement of the Cambodian conflict. A transitional United Nations authority would help run the country toward elections. Resolution 718, adopted unanimously in 1991, gives the agreements the Council's full support.

The Council authorized the Secretary-General to name a special representative for Cambodia. It welcomed his plan to send a survey mission there at once. The mission would prepare for the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia. That authority was the body the agreements created. All Cambodian parties were called on to obey the cease-fire in full. They also had to cooperate with the Supreme National Council of Cambodia and with the United Nations. The text opened the door to one of the largest United Nations operations of its time.
un-sc-res-1418:
Nine days of grace for a set of terms on the former Yugoslavia were granted on 21 June 2002. Those terms had been set a year earlier, in Resolution 1357 of 21 June 2001. They concerned the peace force and the arms embargo in the region. Resolution 1418 was adopted unanimously, and it is very short.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the terms of Resolution 1357 would continue in force until 30 June 2002. That nine-day span is the whole extension the text grants. The Council also decided to remain seized of the matter. A bridge of days, rather than months, is unusual in this series. It held the legal position steady while the Council prepared its next, fuller decision on the former Yugoslavia.
un-sc-res-118:
Egypt had seized the Suez Canal in July 1956, and talks were under way that autumn. On 13 October 1956 the Security Council set the terms any settlement had to meet. Foreign ministers of Egypt, France, and Britain had spoken. The Secretary-General had reported on their private talks. The Council distilled the talks into a list of requirements. They became known as the six principles for Suez.

Transit through the canal must be free and open, without hidden bias. Egypt's sovereignty must be respected. The canal's running must be kept apart from any country's politics. Tolls and charges should be set by agreement between Egypt and the users. The principles were agreed days before Britain, France, and Israel attacked Egypt.
un-sc-res-318:
Rhodesia's sanctions machinery was strengthened by the Security Council on 28 July 1972. The sanctions committee had delivered the special report the Council requested in resolution 314 (1972). Some states still traded with the illegal regime against resolution 253 (1968) and their Charter duties. The Council said the sanctions would stay until the aims of that resolution were fully achieved.

The Council reaffirmed the right of Southern Rhodesia's people to self-determination and independence. It recognized the legitimacy of their struggle to win those rights. It approved the committee's recommendations for tighter enforcement. All states still holding economic ties with Rhodesia were told to end them at once. Member states had to carry out resolutions 253 (1968) and 277 (1970) in full, and acts breaking them were condemned. States were asked to give the Council every help needed to make the sanctions bite.
un-sc-res-18:
General disarmament machinery was set in motion by the Security Council on 13 February 1947. The General Assembly had resolved on 14 December 1946 that the regulation and reduction of armaments was a top task for peace. The Council accepted that charge as one of its most urgent duties.

The Council resolved to work out practical measures on arms reduction and on information about United Nations forces. It set up a commission of its own members to draft proposals within three months. The new body would cover general regulation and reduction of arms and the safeguards to enforce them. Atomic matters were kept outside its reach, under the Atomic Energy Commission. The Military Staff Committee was asked for urgent advice on the forces to be put at the Council's call. The body became the Commission for Conventional Armaments.
un-sc-res-1718:
North Korea's claimed nuclear test of 9 October 2006 drew sanctions within five days. The Council voiced the gravest concern at the challenge to the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It noted Pyongyang's refusal to return to the six-party talks. It deplored the North's announced withdrawal from the treaty.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned the test as a flagrant breach of its resolutions. It demanded no further nuclear test or ballistic missile launch. The North had to retract its treaty withdrawal and return to the treaty and to atomic agency safeguards. Its missile work would stop, and it had to abandon all nuclear weapons and programs fully, in ways that could be checked and not undone. The Council then barred the supply of heavy weapons, missile and nuclear goods, and luxury goods to the North, under a new sanctions committee. This text built the core of the North Korea sanctions regime.
un-sc-res-1618:
Iraq's terror campaign drew a blanket condemnation on 4 August 2005. Attacks in recent weeks had killed more than one hundred people. Thirty-two children died in one bombing, and election staff and a member of the constitution-drafting commission were also killed. Attacks on foreign diplomats caused deep concern. The Council praised Iraqis who kept the political transition moving under the threat.

The Council condemned without reserve, in the strongest terms, the terrorist attacks in Iraq. Any act of terrorism counted as a threat to peace and security. Deepest sympathy and condolences went to the victims and their families. The Council affirmed that terrorism must not be allowed to break Iraq's transition to democracy. Member states' duties under resolutions 1373 (2001) and 1267 (1999) were restated. All states were urged to deny terrorists safe haven, bring them to justice, and stop funds and weapons from reaching them.
un-sc-res-218:
Portugal's colonies were judged a threat to the peace on 23 November 1965. Thirty-two African states had brought the question to the Council. Portugal refused to apply resolutions 180 (1963) and 183 (1963). Instead it was stepping up repression and military operations against the African population. Their hopes of self-determination and independence were being crushed by force.

The Council affirmed that Portugal's policies toward its colonies and their neighbors gravely disturbed international peace and security. It deplored Lisbon's failure to recognize the right of the peoples under its rule to self-determination and independence. Portugal was called to give that right immediate effect in its territories. The Council restated its urgent demands: free the political prisoners, stop repression, and let the peoples choose their future. All states were told to give Portugal no help that let it continue the repression. States had to report the steps they took to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1818:
Cyprus, split between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities since 1974, is the subject of Resolution 1818 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 13 June 2008. It belongs to a long series of votes that keep a United Nations peacekeeping force on the island.

The text extends the mandate of that force, called UNFICYP, through 15 December 2008. It welcomes the opening of the Ledra Street crossing in Nicosia. It also welcomes new promises by the two leaders to seek a shared federation. The Council urges both sides to start full talks soon and keep the peace process moving.
un-sc-res-1018: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1018, adopted on 7 November 1995, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. A judge of the court, a Venezuelan jurist who had served since 1991, died on 24 October 1995. His seat stood empty for the rest of a term due to end in February 2000. The Council fixes 28 February 1996 for the election to fill the seat. The Security Council and the General Assembly vote on the same day, each on its own.
un-sc-res-2018:
Adopting Resolution 2018 on 31 October 2011, the Council acted on Piracy in the Gulf of Guinea. Pirates and sea robbers off West Africa threatened shipping, trade, and growth. Crews were seized as hostages, and attacks turned violent. Nigeria and Benin had begun joint patrols off the Benin coast.

The Council condemns all such attacks and urges a full regional answer. States should pass laws that make piracy a crime where none exist yet. West and Central African bodies should build a shared plan with information sharing and joint patrols. Flag states must warn their ships on how to avoid and resist attack. The text also welcomes a United Nations team sent to study the threat and report back.
un-sc-res-1518:
Iraq led to a Council vote: Resolution 1518, adopted unanimously on 24 November 2003. The old sanctions committee from 1990 had been wound up in May. Work remained to trace money taken out of Iraq by the fallen regime. Those funds were meant to pass to a fund for Iraq's recovery.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council creates a new committee of all its members. The committee will keep naming people and bodies whose assets abroad must be frozen. Frozen funds then move to the Development Fund for Iraq. It takes over the old committee's lists and its working rules. Its mandate stays open to later widening.
europmc-pmc10076218:
Zhang and co-workers present a method that profiles gene activity and gene control marks in tissue at the same time and place, in a 2023 study. New spatial tools can map where genes are active inside a tissue slice. Older methods captured only one layer of that information at a time, which limited what scientists could learn.

The team's co-profiling approach captures both layers from the same tissue section. They test it on mouse and human tissues. The method lets researchers link gene control states to cell behavior in place, a step toward fuller maps of organs.
europmc-pmc10427418:
Shah led the GLOW trial in 2023, a global test of a new drug pair for stomach cancer. The drug, zolbetuximab, is an antibody that seeks a protein called CLDN18.2 on cancer cells. Patients had advanced cancer of the stomach or the joint with the food pipe. Their tumours held the target but lacked a second mark, HER2.

In all, 507 patients got the drug or a dummy drug, each with the same two chemo drugs. Shah found that the drug pair slowed growth for longer. Median time before the cancer grew was 8.21 months, versus 6.80 months. Median survival was 14.39 months, versus 12.16 months. Severe side effects were near equal in both arms.
europmc-pmc10786718:
Kim and a large global team pooled gene data on Parkinson disease across many ancestries in this 2024 study. Parkinson disease is a brain illness that affects movement and worsens over time. Past gene hunts found over 90 risk variants, meaning small DNA changes tied to higher risk. Most of those hunts, though, drew on one ancestry group at a time.

The pooled analysis covered about 49,000 cases and 2.4 million controls from four ancestry groups. It found 78 DNA regions tied to the disease, 12 of them possibly new. The team also flagged 25 genes whose activity levels track with risk. The authors say the broader mix lays groundwork for finding risk regions missed in single-group studies. That matters because drug targets found in one group may not tell the full story.
europmc-pmc11836418:
Xiong and colleagues surveyed breast cancer science in a 2025 review. Breast cancer is a lead cause of cancer death in women. Tumors differ a lot from one person to the next. Sorting them into molecular subtypes has sharpened care.

New work covers tumor stem cells, microbes inside tumors, and daily body clocks. Smart software now aids scans and diagnosis with better accuracy. Fresh drugs support care tailored to each patient and subtype. Xiong argues the best plan matches risk and tumor type. That match defines modern precision care for breast cancer.
europmc-pmc1310918:
Geiser and co-authors tracked ultrafine particles crossing lung cell membranes in 2005. Within hours of breathing them, such particles appear in liver, heart, and nervous tissue. How they cross membrane boundaries was largely unknown. Rats inhaled titanium dioxide particles of 22 nanometers median size.

Particle locations were mapped one hour and 24 hours after exposure. Electron microscopy with elemental analysis pinpointed single particles. Cultured lung cells were exposed in parallel tests. Particles entered cells without being eaten by the usual engulfing route. Geiser shows a non-eating entry path for ultrafine particles. Lung cells in dishes took up the same small bits. The bits were seen in the lung one hour and one day after the rats breathed them in.
europmc-pmc1382018:
Voight, Kudaravalli, Wen, and Pritchard mapped recent natural selection in the human genome in 2006. New genetic variants favored by selection reveal local adaptation. The scan used HapMap data across three continental groups. A new method hunted variants rising in frequency but not yet fixed.

Widespread selection signals appeared in all three groups. Most signals were specific to one region. A significant excess was shared across groups, though. The strongest signals by some measures came from the Yoruba population. That counters claims of little recent selection in sub-Saharan Africans. Selected loci should hold trait variation worth mapping.
europmc-pmc1414018:
Pearse and co-authors ran a trial in 2005 on care right after major surgery. They tested goal-directed therapy, where staff tune fluids and drugs to hit a set oxygen delivery target. Half of 122 high-risk patients got the tuned care. The rest got standard care on the ward.

The tuned group got more fluid and far more of a heart drug. Fewer of them had problems after surgery, 44 percent against 68 percent. Their hospital stay was also shorter, a median of 11 days against 14. Death rates did not differ much. Pearse argues that early tuned care can cut harm after big operations.
europmc-pmc1762318:
A working tooth grew from stem cells in a pig's jaw. Sonoyama and co-authors reported that regeneration in 2006. They isolated a new stem cell population from the root tip of human teeth, called SCAP, alongside known ligament stem cells.

Transplanted into minipigs, the two cell types built a root and ligament complex. The structure was strong enough to support a porcelain crown and serve in normal chewing. The approach blended stem cells, engineered materials, and standard dental crown methods. Sonoyama presents it as a route to biological tooth replacement rather than metal implants.
europmc-pmc1794418: The face-specific N170 component is modulated by emotional facial expression. — a 2005 science paper on face-reading brain waves. It finds emotion modulates N170. The paper is the face-wave study: the findings on facial ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc1810318: ARACNE: an algorithm for the reconstruction of gene regulatory networks in a mammalian cellular context. — a 2005 science paper on the ARACNE network tool. It reconstructs the gene networks. The paper is the ARACNE guide: the findings on the network tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1853118: Novel Crohn disease locus identified by genome-wide association maps to a gene desert on 5p13.1 and modulates expression of PTGER4. — a 2005 science paper on a Crohn gene desert. It maps the 5p13.1 locus. The paper is the Crohn study: the findings on PTGER4, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1876818: A two-locus global DNA barcode for land plants: the coding rbcL gene complements the non-coding trnH-psbA spacer region. — a 2005 science paper on a plant DNA barcode. It builds the two-locus barcode. The paper is the barcode study: the findings on land plants, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2186318: p38 MAPK, microglial signaling, and neuropathic pain. — a 2005 science paper on microglial signaling and pain. It maps the p38 MAPK signaling. The paper is the pain study: the findings on neuropathic ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2291018: Sunscreens cause coral bleaching by promoting viral infections. — a 2005 science paper on sunscreens and coral bleaching. It finds the viral promotion. The paper is the bleaching study: the findings on coral ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2323218: FlyMine: an integrated database for Drosophila and Anopheles genomics. — a 2008 science paper on the FlyMine database. It guides the fly database. The paper is the FlyMine guide: the findings on the database tool, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2397418: A short review on SSF - an interesting process option for ethanol production from lignocellulos — a 2008 science paper on SSF ethanol making. It reviews the SSF process. The paper is the SSF review: the findings on ethanol, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2570418: Inflammatory and coagulation biomarkers and mortality in patients with HIV infection. — a 2008 science paper on blood flags in HIV. It links the blood flags for labs. The paper is the flag study: the notes on HIV ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2634718: Deficient mismatch repair system in patients with sporadic advanced colorectal cancer. — a 2008 science paper on deficient mismatch repair. It finds the deficient repair. The paper is the repair study: the findings on colorectal ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2661018: Statistical methods for detecting differentially abundant features in clinical metagenomic samp — a 2008 science paper on germ-count stat tricks. It runs the stat tricks for labs. The paper is the trick study: the notes on germ ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2689218: Calcium signaling in neurodegeneration. — a 2008 science paper on calcium's brain-rot role. It studies the calcium signals for labs. The paper is the calcium study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2706318: Folding versus aggregation: polypeptide conformations on competing pathways. — a 2008 science paper on folding vs aggregation. It studies the polypeptide conformations. The paper is the folding study: the findings on folding ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2721818: A distinct macrophage population mediates metastatic breast cancer cell extravasation, establis — a 2008 science paper on guard-cell cancer escapes. It tracks the cancer escapes for labs. The paper is the escape study: the notes on breast ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2759918: Anti-proliferative activity of silver nanoparticles. — a 2008 science paper on silver nanoparticles. It tests the anti-proliferative activity. The paper is the silver study: the findings on nano ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily still.
europmc-pmc2776018: Validation of reference genes for quantitative expression analysis by real-time RT-PCR in Sacch — a 2008 science paper on reference-gene validation. It validates the quantitative genes. The paper is the validation study: the findings on Sacch ills, filed here in session.
dalton-countrey-justice-english-1618:
Michael Dalton, a lawyer, published The Countrey Justice in 1618 as a working manual for England's local magistrates. Justices of the peace handled most crime in their counties, and Dalton's book told them how. Among its chapters stands the witchcraft section that shaped English trials for a century.

Dalton sets out the law on witches, the signs to weigh, and the procedure to follow. Generations of justices reached for his guidance when a village accused a neighbor. The chapter codified witch procedure in practical form. This handbook was the legal backbone of the English witch trials. Its calm pages show persecution running on paperwork as much as on fear.
hutchinson-historical-essay-witchcraft-e:
Francis Hutchinson, an Irish clergyman living in England, published his Historical Essay Concerning Witchcraft in 1718. It is the first history of English witchcraft, a new kind of book on the subject. Hutchinson looks back at the trials as a scholar of the Enlightenment, with the Salem cases across the Atlantic among his evidence.

He treats famous cases one by one and finds fraud, fear, and bad courts behind them. His manner is cool and his verdicts are plain. With this essay, history itself turns its eye on the persecution. The sober reckoning with the witch trials begins here. Hutchinson helped make disbelief in witchcraft respectable among educated readers.
plos-pone-0004918:

HP1 proteins do not drive pericentromeric cohesin enrichment. The classical picture fails in human cells. A negative result like this forces a rethink. plos-pone-0005218:

plos-pone-0005318:
