arxiv-2606-16118: Can large language models do legal reasoning — and can we trust their answers? This paper tests LLMs both as legal problem-solvers and as "autoformalizers" that translate legal text into precise logic, checking whether their outputs are faithful to the law. The authors map the models' limits, a cautionary study for anyone deploying AI in legal work.
arxiv-2606-16218: In nearby dwarf galaxies, older stars and metal-poor stars are arranged in a striking pattern — a strong age–metallicity gradient. This astronomy paper argues the pattern is driven by stars migrating outward over time plus "environmental quenching" that shut off star formation. The authors test the idea against observations of real dwarf galaxies.
arxiv-2606-16318: A pure math paper on blend-spread math — near tugs wed to far tugs — at a knife-edge pitch. The authors prove rock-bottom rest shapes live there. For hard-math pros who weigh spread with near and far hands. Knife-edge proofs are the prize catch.
arxiv-2606-16518: Sky-storm clerks watch the AE gauge — a storm roar score that dogs sats and grids. This paper scorns flat-wind means and bakes the wind's wild churn into the call. For storm-call crews who crave truer red alerts. Churn-wise calls beat calm-mean calls.
arxiv-2606-16918: Quirk gauges can meter past plain limits — quirk metering. This paper steers such metering with lopsided spin webs (Heisenberg) through built-in hiss. It is for quirk-gauge pros. Lopsided webs, keen meters. Hiss can't hide the signal. Steered meters beat stray ones.
20906-the-journal-of-negro-history-volum:
No truth rings stronger, says volume three of The Journal of Negro History, than Bremer's line on America. The fate of the Negro, she said, is the romance of your history. The 1918 volume opens its work under that bold banner.

Hero sketches show lives once used and scorned by Christian men, the editors note. Studies here trace how a distinct American culture grew from that pain. Woodson's journal kept building Black history on records, not myth. Volume three shows the field in its third year, already rich, rigorous, and set on reshaping how America told its own past.
21833-experiences-of-a-dug-out-1914-1918:
A senior staff officer tells what the Great War looked like from headquarters in Experiences of a Dug-Out, by Major-General Sir C. E. Callwell, published in 1920. Callwell had written lives of generals and studies of the Dardanelles before this memoir. Here he looks back on 1914 to 1918 from inside the machine that ran the British war effort. Some pieces first ran in Blackwood's Magazine.

He defends the soldiers' view against critics who, he says, had it all their own way during the fight. Grievances could be aired freely while serving men stayed silent, he notes. The frontispiece shows him at the Crow's Nest with Russian allies. It is a frank, professional memoir of the war behind the lines.
21880-the-medallic-history-of-the-united:
America's first century is told in medals in J. F. Loubat's Medallic History of the United States, covering 1776 to 1876. One hundred seventy etchings by Jules Jacquemart picture the coins and medals of honor struck for the nation's deeds. Loubat, a member of the New York Historical Society and a knight of several orders, dedicated the work to Elihu B. Washburne, late minister to France.

A hundred years of history, he argues, already holds deeds and names enough to make the medals a valuable record. Battles, treaties, and great citizens appear in bronze and gold. The book is at once a catalog for collectors and a patriotic history. Each medal fixes a moment the young republic chose to remember in metal.
arxiv-2601-07418:
Research by Valentin Leeb and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with collinear p p -wave magnetism and hidden orbital ferrimagnetism. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. In the absence of spin-orbit coupling, collinear magnets are classified as even-wave magnets, i.e., either ferro-, antiferro-, or altermagnets. It is based on the belief that collinear magnets always feature an inversion-symmetric band structure, which forbids odd-wave magnetism.

Here, the authors show that collinear magnets, which break time reversal symmetry in the non-magnetic sector. Can have an inversion symmetry broken band structure and lead to unconventional types of collinear magnets. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-08118: Large language models now act as stand-in users in tests of chat systems and in training data creation. A 2026 arXiv study warns that simple act-as-a-user prompting yields wordy, unrealistic speech. That gap creates a need for principled checks on these user proxy agents. The paper introduces a pairwise indistinguishability metric, judged with a dedicated prompt shown in its tenth figure. The goal is to test whether proxy users sound like real users side by side. Better proxies could make system evaluation cheaper and more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-07718:
Shaoting Zhu and colleagues build a framework that lets humanoid robots hike through rough, unstructured terrain. Robust hiking needs a shift from reacting by feel to seeing ahead and planning. Adding outside sensing is hard, they note. Mapping methods suffer drift in state estimation. LiDAR methods, for example, handle torso jitter poorly while the robot walks. Their 2026 preprint presents a scalable perceptive parkour framework.

The framework aims to keep perception useful despite the shaking and slipping of real hiking. Robots that can cross wild ground could help in search, inspection, and disaster response. Perception that fails whenever the body jolts is not enough for those jobs. The authors target that gap directly. Humanoid robotics scholars are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07818:
A large Cosmoglobe team maps how dust in our galaxy glows, and what that glow tracks. They fit five tracers of thermal dust emission to ten frequency maps from Planck and COBE-DIRBE. The maps span 353 gigahertz to 25 terahertz. Their goal is mapping each host environment's importance by frequency and sky position. One tracer is emission from ionized carbon. Their 2026 preprint is part five of the Cosmoglobe DR2 series.

Thermal dust emission is a foreground that cosmologists must remove to see the early universe. It is also a signal in its own right for studying the interstellar medium. Correlating dust with ionized carbon shows where dust lives relative to ionized gas. Cleaner foreground models improve cosmic microwave background analysis. The paper speaks to cosmologists and interstellar medium scholars alike.
arxiv-2601-07918:
Dhruv K. Desai and colleagues model jets launched by newborn millisecond magnetars. These are rapidly rotating, strongly magnetized neutron stars. They form in stellar core collapse, neutron star mergers, and white dwarf collapse events. Such objects have long been proposed as engines of gamma-ray bursts. Accompanying supernovae and kilonovae may share the same engine. Their 2026 preprint studies the relativistic jets these magnetars produce.

Relativistic jets are narrow streams of matter moving near light speed. Whether a magnetar can launch and sustain one decides several burst models. Simulations must handle extreme magnetism and rotation together. The results inform how gamma-ray burst light and afterglow should look. The paper serves high-energy astrophysicists. It connects an engine candidate to the explosions observers actually record.
arxiv-2601-08518: Alexandre Sanfelici Bazanella and Mateus Gaspary de Freitas wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on gas metal arc welding, called GMAW. The authors set out a way to steer the electric current in the weld as it runs. The steer works in closed loop, so it reads the current and acts on what it reads. It was designed by formal methods, from a math model of the process as a switched circuit whose values come from data. The code runs in C on a small chip controller.
arxiv-2601-09018:
Samuel Myren, Nidhi Parikh, and Natalie Klein tackle a flaw in deep learn tools for time data: they fail when the world shifts. A tool trained on one plant or one year may score well in tests. Put it on a new plant, and scores fall. Train and test data no long share the same form. That shift is the norm in field work, not a rare case.

The team uses meta learn, where a tool learns how to adapt fast. It trains on many shifts, so a new shift takes few steps to fit. A reader who sorts time data gets a plan built for drift. It aims to keep scores up when the source of data moves.
arxiv-2601-09118:
Jackie Alex and Guoqiang Huan build a lean net to find flaws on rail tracks from color plus depth shots. Rail flaws must be caught fast, before a crack grows to a crash risk. Past sight tools are heavy, slow, and still miss flaws. A field tool must run on small gear at the track side, not on a vast host.

Their net is called LPCANet. It uses a light pyramid that reads the shot at more than one size. A cross focus step joins color facts with depth facts at each size. A reader in rail safety gets a tool built for the field: lean, fast, and set to catch small flaws.
arxiv-2601-09418:
Alexandros Groutides writes a short note on toric periods in a family of representations of p-adic groups. His 2026 arXiv paper fixes the correct normalization for the toric period on a parabolically induced unramified family. The family lives over a two-variable Laurent polynomial algebra and its quotient field.

The point is to choose the normalization so the period behaves well under restriction to the smaller family. Period formulas of this kind feed relative Langlands questions, where integrals over subgroups detect deep arithmetic data. A clean normalization keeps later formulas from picking up stray factors. The note is brief but aimed at a precise technical gap.
arxiv-2601-09618:
Alex Huang links a famous academic metric to central bank policy. The 2026 arXiv paper studies the Journal Impact Factor, a core index used to judge journals, over five decades. Despite its weight in academic life, the factor's history has rarely been tied to the wider economy.

Using time series from 1975 to 2026, the author runs period-based regressions against Federal Reserve policy. The real interest rate serves as the proxy for policy stance. The question is whether cheap or dear money tracks the rise and fall of impact factors. Any such link would say something new about how finance shapes science.
arxiv-2601-09818:
Tarus Pande, V M S K Minnikanti, and Shyamprasad Karagadde solve moving-boundary heat problems with a shallow neural network. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, which needs far fewer units than a classic perceptron. Spline-based curves keep its power high for its size.

The framework approximates both the temperature field and the moving interface directly. It enforces the core equations, phase balance, and the Stefan condition through built-in physics checks. Moving boundaries appear in melting, freezing, and casting. A small, accurate solver could make such simulations cheaper to run and easier to embed.
arxiv-2601-10018:
Hasti Sharifi, Homaira Huda Shomee, Sourav Medya, and Debaleena Chattopadhyay study how older adults get help with tech. Good help can ease the use of apps and devices. But many older users find it hard to state their snag. Tech words may be new to them.

Age linked shifts in thought can add to the load. A vague ask can lead to the wrong help. The team looks at these talk gaps in depth. They test AI based aids that can bridge the gaps. Such aids could restate a snag in clear terms. That would let the user get the right fix with less stress.
arxiv-2601-10718:
Junyu Liu and co-authors design a Japanese AI agent system about HPV vaccination. Japan paused its active push for the HPV vaccine from 2013 to 2021. That pause left a wide gap between clinics and hesitant people. False claims on social media made the gap worse. Standard public health messages cannot answer each person and watch public talk at once.

The system aims to do both jobs together. It can field individual queries about the vaccine while tracking wider discourse. That pairing matters in a country rebuilding trust in a vaccine that prevents cancer. The design paper shows how AI agents might support health outreach where trust is thin and questions are personal.
arxiv-2601-11718:
Andrea Gnarini, Swati Ravi, Philip Kaaret, and a large team report new X-ray data on Cyg X-2. Cyg X-2 is a bright pair made of a neutron star and a low mass star that feeds it gas. The team watched it while it sat in the state known as the horizontal branch.

They used two space tools at the same time, IXPE and NuSTAR. IXPE checks how X-rays are aligned, while NuSTAR maps their energy spread. The title reports a high level of alignment found in this state. Such data help test how gas flows and glows close to a neutron star.
arxiv-2601-12118:
Christos Liaskos, Evangelos Papapetrou, Kostas Katsalis, and a broad team wrote a tutorial on control of metasurfaces from a network view. Metasurfaces are thin structures that can steer waves in real time. They could lift data rates, privacy, and energy use, and could even sense the space round them.

The tutorial treats each surface as one node in a larger net. That view helps plan how many surfaces act as one system. It links wave control to network control in plain terms. New teams gain a shared map of the field.
arxiv-2601-12218:
De-Ji-Xiang-Mao, Ai Huang, and Yifu Wang study stability in a nutrient taxis system with two degeneracies. In such a system, cells move toward food, and both cell spread and food use can vanish at set points. That double degeneracy makes the maths hard.

They show that arbitrary structures in the three-dimensional case can stabilize. Taxis models help explain how bacteria and cells form patterns round food sources. Firm stability results tell which patterns can last. The work treats a hard, singular system in full 3D.  The result holds for a range of start shapes.
arxiv-2601-11418:
Mostafa Atallah and five coauthors build circuits for quantum walks with less waste. Their 2026 preprint skips Pauli decomposition in the build. A continuous-time quantum walk spreads a walker on a graph. Its Hamiltonian sets how the walk flows over time.

Pauli decomposition is the usual but costly route to circuits. The new algorithm is called matching decomposition in the work. It splits the walk Hamiltonian into exactly doable parts. Each part matches a matching in the graph below. A graph compression step then merges edges to shrink the count. The method serves arbitrary simple sparse graphs, a broad class. Fewer parts mean shorter circuits on real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2601-11618:
Luis Rosario Freytes defines attention in geometric, regime-explicit terms. The 2026 preprint names the frame Geometric Attention, or GA. Transformer attention is usually given as one fixed formula. GA instead specifies a layer by four independent inputs.

The first input is a finite carrier of addressable indices. The second is an evidence-kernel rule for weights. Masked proto-scores and a link induce nonnegative weights there. The third input is a probe family of admissible observables. The fourth is an anchor and update rule for kernels. It selects which representative kernel applies and how. The split makes hidden choices in attention explicit. Designers can then vary one choice at a time.
arxiv-2601-13118:
Alessandro Midolo and co-authors ask what makes a good prompt when a language model must write code. Such models are now used a lot for code tasks. Past work showed that apt prompt craft can lift the code a model gives back.

Yet staff who write prompts had no clear guide set for code tasks. The team fills that gap with a study of real prompt use. They sort what prompt parts help, what parts do not, and how staff phrase them. From that sort they draw guide lines for code prompts. For dev teams, the value is plain. Better prompts mean fewer bad drafts and less time spent on fix ups.
arxiv-2601-13318:
Leonardo de Lima, Renata Del-Vecchio, Hermie Monterde, and Heber Teixeira use a shared basis to move quantum states on special graphs. A threshold graph is a graph built by add of lone or fully linked nodes, step by step. Past work showed a star and any threshold graph on the same node count share the same eigenbasis for the Laplacian matrix.

The team builds on that fact to prove two results. One marks which threshold graphs are simply structured in their terms. The shared basis then helps treat pair state transfer, the move of a state from one node to a next. Such moves are a base act for quantum nets on graphs.
arxiv-2601-13518:
Jiayi Yuan and co-authors let a pipeline design its own red team tools for AI models. Red team work hunts flaws in a model by attack in a set way. Most auto red team tools rest on flows a human set in advance. Human flows hold human bias and cost a lot to roam wide.

Their pipeline is called AgenticRed. It uses a language model's in context learn to draft and hone red team systems on its own. Each round's finds feed the next draft. No human hand steers the loop. For safety teams, a self design loop may find attack forms a fixed flow would never try.
arxiv-2601-12418:
A. K. Behera and a large team study sound waves that skim the surface of a layered chip. The layers pair a piezo thin film with silicon carbide. Such films trap sound in a thin zone, well below a wavelength in depth. That tight trap suits compact devices that mix and shift sound signals.

The team probe a nonlinear effect called four wave mixing in these guided waves. They work at gigahertz rates, where four waves trade energy in set ways. Effects like this can convert frequencies or process signals on a chip. The title flags a twist: cold helps. Running the device at low heat boosts the mixing, a fact of use for future phononic tools.
arxiv-2601-12818:
Minjia Shi, Jing Wang, and Patrick Sole prove nonexistence results for perfect codes in several metrics. Perfect codes are rare gems of coding theory, packing spheres with no waste. The team combine the Lloyd theorem of Sole from 1989 with the Schwartz Zippel lemma from computer science. Their proofs rest on asymptotic enumeration of integer partitions.

The results cover the Lee metric, the NRT metric, and the mixed Hamming metric. The sum rank distance is covered as well. Ruling out perfect codes saves searches for objects that cannot exist. It also steers code design toward near perfect families that can exist. Cross field proofs like this show how algebra and combinatorics reinforce each other.
arxiv-2601-13718:
Dinh-Long Vu, Hitomi Mori, and Patrick Rebentrost bring a classic sampling trick to quantum machines in 2026. The Box-Muller transform turns uniform random samples into Gaussian ones. Gaussian, or normal, spreads show up all over science and finance. Quantum methods can store a whole spread in the amplitudes of a quantum state.

Their Quantum Box-Muller transform builds a superposition of grid points. Those points stand for the multi-variate normal spread, with many variables at once. Fast Gaussian sampling helps Monte Carlo work and risk models. A quantum form could speed tasks that now take long runs.
arxiv-2601-13818:
Luigi Romano extends a rolling contact friction model to handle springy materials in 2026. The base frame is FrBD, Friction with Bristle Dynamics, in distributed form. Bristles stand for the small elements that bend as a tire or wheel rolls. Romano adds linear viscoelasticity, using classic Maxwell and Kelvin-Voigt models of the bristle.

The full system becomes a set of hyperbolic partial differential equations. It tracks bristle dynamics, friction forces, and inner deformation states at once. Such a model can capture relaxation effects, where grip fades or grows over time. Tire and rail engineers need that detail.
arxiv-2601-14118:
Trevor Incerti, Jonathan Elkobi, and Daniel Mattingly study foreign influencer operations on TikTok in 2026. Roughly half of TikTok users report getting news from social media influencers. Authoritarian regimes have increasingly outsourced content creation to these influencers. The team asks how such regimes strengthen global support for nondemocratic systems.

Their focus is how TikTok shapes American perceptions of China. Influencers can present a polished view in a friendly, personal style. That style may bypass the skepticism that state media faces. The work links platform design to foreign influence in daily feeds.
arxiv-2601-14518:
Jinhui Liu, Ximeng Zhang, Yanbo Ai, and Zhou Yu work on testing database agents in this 2026 paper. Evaluating Text-to-SQL agents in private business intelligence settings is hard. Realistic, domain-specific data are scarce, and private data cannot be shared. Synthetic evaluation data offer a scalable solution. Past generation methods, though, fail to capture business realism.

The missing piece is business logic: whether questions reflect real workflows and rules. The team's method is business logic-driven Text-to-SQL data synthesis. It builds test data that mirror how firms actually query their data. Readers get a way to grade business intelligence agents on tasks that look like real work.
arxiv-2601-15518:
Wenxin Zhou, Ritesh Mehta, and Anthony Miyaguchi build a search system for half-remembered things in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue task. In it, a user recalls a thing vaguely and asks for help finding it. The query is fuzzy by nature. Plain keyword search often fails on such requests.

Their system works in two stages. First, hybrid retrieval merges three methods: LLM-based retrieval, sparse BM25 search, and dense BGE-M3 search. Then learned reranking and LLM-based reranking sort the results. The team's name, DS@GT, marks it as a TREC entry. Anyone who has hunted for a song or film from a faint memory knows the task. The work brings modern retrieval tools to that everyday frustration.
arxiv-2601-15818:
Siyuan Chen, Mingchen Sun, and Jian Tang review muon beams for precision physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Accelerator advances have raised muon beam quality over past decades. Better beams enable sharper experiments. Studies of the muon and of muonium, its bound state with an electron, benefit most. These systems allow precise measurements of fundamental constants. They also support searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

The title promises progress and prospects. A review takes stock of where beam quality stands. It also maps what future beams could unlock. Muonium is a clean, purely leptonic atom, ideal for precision tests. Any deviation from theory there would be a loud signal. The paper serves physicists planning the next round of such experiments.
arxiv-2601-16018:
Özgür Uğur and a large team build language models for Turkish law in a 2026 arXiv paper. The models are the Mecellem family. Legal language is a specialized domain in any tongue. Turkish legal text adds its own terms and forms. The team trains models both from scratch and by continued pretraining. One contribution is an encoder model built from zero. It follows the ModernBERT design and trains on a Turkish-dominant corpus.

That corpus holds 112.7 billion tokens, per the abstract. The authors stress joint evaluation: pretraining choices and downstream task scores together. Domain adaptation often looks good on one axis and poor on the other. Legal tools for Turkish speakers need models that truly read their law. This work supplies candidates and a frank way to judge them.
arxiv-2601-14818:
Christian Fiedler writes on a branch of machine learning where the inputs are not single values. In his 2026 arXiv paper, each input is a full probability distribution. The work sits in statistical learning theory, the math of how models learn from data.

The catch is that the true distributions are never seen in full. The learner gets only samples drawn from them, in a two-stage setup. Fiedler links this setup to real tasks such as medical screening and causal learning. The paper builds theory for sorting such inputs into classes.
arxiv-2601-14918:
Kai Hendriks, Lorenz Zwick, Pankaj Saini, János Takátsy, and Johan Samsing study pairs of black holes that do not orbit alone. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gravitational waves from binary black holes. A third body nearby can pull the pair off a plain two-body path.

That pull speeds the pair up or slows it down along our line of sight. The shift leaves marks in the wave signal, an effect called dephasing. The team builds a full model of that dephasing. Their model adds curve and projection effects that simpler local treatments miss.
arxiv-2601-15218:
Luigi De Pascale and Igor Pinheiro revisit an inequality in the theory of optimal transport. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Wasserstein distances, which gauge the cost of moving one distribution into another. They ask how the largest such distance can be controlled by the smaller ones.

That control matters for both theory and numeric work. A first paper on the problem came years ago. Later work framed the same inequality for more general costs that grow with distance. The authors give a reverse form of the inequality and place it in that wider line of work.
arxiv-2601-15418:
T. J. Martz-Oberlander, B. Bulgaru, and a team of co-authors report a transistor with record-breaking electron mobility. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a three-terminal field-effect device, with source, drain, and gate. Mobility gauges how freely electrons move, and high values promise faster, cleaner electronics.

Several devices were built for the study. The best one used a symmetrically doped gallium arsenide quantum well. It hosts a two-dimensional electron gas, a flat sheet of electrons. Its mobility passes forty million in the standard units, a mark the authors report with great care.
arxiv-2601-16118:
Marco Ronzani and Cristina Silvano use web like graphs to place spike nets on brain like chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with nets that send brief spikes. Brain like chips hold many cores tied by a chip net. Each core runs a set of nerve cells. A poor place map wastes time and power as spikes cross the chip.

The pair model the net as a graph with hubs and links. Rich graphs with hubs, called hyper graphs, hold group links at once. That rich form helps find place maps with less cross talk. Good maps make spike nets run fast on small gear. The work links graph maths to chip design.
arxiv-2601-16218:
Aleix Torres-Camps and coauthors build a wide test of maths thought in pics and many tongues. Their 2026 preprint, named M3Kang, deals with vision and language models. Top models show strong thought on maths in one tongue. Their skill in many tongues at once is far less known. That gap counts for schools and tools used world wide.

M3Kang is the first test of its kind at this scale. It checks maths thought that joins pics with text in many tongues. Scores set next to human marks show the true gap. A shared test lets teams track gains tongue by tongue. The work aids fair maths tools for all users.
arxiv-2601-16618:
Jing Xu and three coauthors grow speech to speech skills in large models step by step. Their 2026 preprint, named PROST-LLM, deals with direct speech swaps. Speech to speech keeps tone and feel that text paths lose. Large models shine on text tasks but lag on speech swaps. Scant speech swap data is a main cause of that lag.

Step growth adds skills in a set order to beat scant data. Each step builds on the last with tasks of more depth. Gains would open speech swaps to more tongue pairs. They would also cut need for rare paired speech sets. The work gives a staged path for that growth.
arxiv-2601-16818:
Siyuan Hou and a team of nine co-authors use bent quasar light to test dark matter. Gravity from a galaxy can split a quasar's light into shots. In cusp sets, three shots sit close in a line. Their glow rates should match a set pattern. When they don't, small clumps of stuff may be at fault. Their 2026 preprint checks such off marks in the largest clean set yet.

That set holds seventeen cusp lens sets. The team pits the marks against three dark tales. Cold, self-touching, and fuzzy dark stuff each face the test. Fake lens sims show which tale fits the marks. Such tests can rule out whole dark tales at once.
arxiv-2601-17118:
Zixiang Jia, Fangzhou Jiang, Shubo Li, Ran Li, Jing Wang, and Ling Zhu bound how strong dark bits bump each next. Dark bits that bump can form soft cores in galaxies. Galaxy spin curves tell how those cores spread. Their 2026 preprint builds a sharp Jeans-type tool for the gauge. The tool starts from a heat-set halo form. Three upgrades make it more true to real halos.

Bump strength can shift with the bits' speed. Core fall-in, a late dense phase, gets a rule too. Firm fits sort true halo forms from false ones. SPARC spin curves give the test data. Bounds here curb whole dark tale classes.
arxiv-2601-17618:
Latent variable models study traits that cannot be seen at once, like mood or skill. Psychologists use them to link such constructs. Full one-stage fits can be hard to compute. Two-stage factor score regression is a common fallback. Stage one fits the measurement model and gets factor scores. Stage two uses those scores in regression. The record names no author for this entry.

The authors give a general two-stage solution. It is root-N consistent, a key large-sample trait. A sound shortcut matters when full fits fail. Many applied teams rely on the two-stage path daily. Proof that it can be consistent raises trust in its results. The work serves survey and test research.
arxiv-2601-17718:
Bo Zhan and three co-authors present a tree tensor network solver for quantum impurity dynamics. Impurity models place one interacting site in a broad bath. Real-time simulation of them is a classic hard problem. Their solver decomposes the bath Hamiltonian into a Cayley tree. That gives a tensor network shaped like the problem's own scales.

The tree captures multiscale entanglement in impurity-bath systems. Accuracy and speed both matter for real-time runs. Better solvers aid study of quantum dots and magnetic impurities. They also test methods for correlated materials. The work gives a solver built for the structure at hand. Generic networks waste effort that the tree saves.
arxiv-2601-18218:
Meziah Ruby Cristobal and co-authors explore AI help for turning papers into short videos. Their 2026 preprint deals with research communication. Sharing results matters, yet researchers often lack the time and skills to make engaging short-form video. Such videos are now a main way the public meets science. The team studies how generative AI can help scholars turn their papers into clear, watchable clips.

The study looks at the process, not just the output. Where does AI help, and where does it flatten the message? Answers guide tool builders and university media teams. Done well, AI help could bring more research to public view without fake polish.
arxiv-2601-18918:
Bram Lentjes and three co-authors build tools to study sudden shifts in delayed systems. Delay equations, where the present rate leans on past states, show up in control, biology, and climate work. When a slow forcing repeats in time, steady states can split or flip as knobs change.

The team first proves a smooth, low dimensional surface exists near a steady state that is on the edge of change. On that surface, the full system shrinks to a small normal form that is far easier to study. Their frame uses sun-star calculus to keep the proof strict.
arxiv-2601-19018:
Sahana Kumar and a large team study a rare, fast fading supernova named SN 2025coe. Its class, calcium strong transients, shines faintly, fades fast, and shows strong calcium lines with oddly weak oxygen. Some traits match exploding white dwarfs, while others match the collapse of huge stars, so the class's origin stays in doubt.

The team watched this event in X-rays, near infrared light, and radio waves. Each band adds a clue about the blast's energy, speed, and setting. More well watched cases like this one should settle what kind of star dies in this calcium rich way.
arxiv-2601-19518:
Andreas Angelou, Pourya Behmandpoor, and Marc Moonen study a design for future wireless networks. In a cell-free massive MIMO network, many access points are spread across an area. They serve all users together, rather than tying each user to one tower. When users send data up to the network, the work can be run in one central place or shared out among the access points.

Central control can give strong results but needs heavy data traffic between points. Sharing the work out cuts that traffic but can lose coordination. The authors propose a master-assisted design, where a lead unit helps the distributed points work together. Their aim is to keep most of the gains of central control while spreading the load. The work matters for building dense, fast networks that stay practical to run.
arxiv-2601-19618:
Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh and colleagues study a trade-off in medical AI: privacy versus accuracy. Differential privacy limits how much any single training image can sway a model. That protection usually costs diagnostic accuracy. Starting from pretrained weights softens the loss. The open question is which matters more: what the model was pretrained to do, or what data it was pretrained on.

The team trains chest X-ray classifiers under differential privacy from five different starting points. Their data covers close to six hundred thousand radiographs from five datasets. Comparing the runs separates the effect of the pretraining objective from the effect of the domain. The answer guides hospitals that must train on private scans. It shows where to invest effort before privacy is even applied.
arxiv-2601-19718:
Kaifeng Zhang, Kai Ming Ting, Tianrun Liang, and Qiuran Zhao rethink a classic data analysis method. Hierarchical clustering groups data into a tree of nested clusters. Divisive methods start with everything in one group and split it step by step. The authors show that current objective-based divisive methods produce trees missing three properties users would expect.

A good tree should not split groups without warrant. It should keep similar clusters together in the same branch. And its groups should correspond to the true groups in the data. The authors trace the failures to how splitting is judged, one set at a time. Their distributional viewpoint suggests a different criterion. The work aims at cluster trees that analysts can actually trust.
arxiv-2601-20118:
David Kin Wai Ho and three colleagues work on polar codes, a family of error-correcting codes planned for future 6G networks. A polar code needs a fixed order that says which positions in the code carry data. Finding a good order for each channel and decoder is a hard design task. The authors use reinforcement learning to build that order.

Their method is meant to be universal, so it can adapt to many channel conditions and decoding styles. It also scales to code lengths up to about two thousand, which suits real standards work. A single learned design tool could cut the effort of tuning codes by hand for each new setting.
arxiv-2601-20318:
Jiyuan Xu and five colleagues present CPiRi, a method for forecasting many related time series at once. Existing methods split into two camps. Channel-dependent models learn links between series but can overfit their order, so they adapt poorly when channels are added or shuffled. Channel-independent models treat each series alone, which is flexible but misses cross-links.

CPiRi is built to be invariant to channel permutation while still modeling relational interaction between channels. That pairing aims at both flexibility and accuracy. It matters for sensor networks and finance feeds, where the set and order of series change often.
arxiv-2601-20418:
Coralia Cartis and Wenqi Zhu study when nonnegative quartic polynomials can be written as sums of squares. Hilbert's seventeenth problem showed that not all nonnegative polynomials have such a representation, though he found classes where the two notions agree. The authors extend that equivalence to new subclasses of multivariate polynomials with quartic regularization.

They also characterize where these structured problems sit relative to the NP-hardness boundary. Sum-of-squares methods power a large family of optimization tools. Knowing exactly which polynomial classes are tractable tells users when those tools are guaranteed to work.
arxiv-2601-18418:
Ji Zeng and many colleagues train language models for a new kind of work: acting as agents that fix code on their own. The field has moved past one-shot code writing. A strong model must now roam a whole code base, change files, and run tests to check its own work. That kind of skill takes more than plain pre-training on text and code.

Their work adds a mid-stage of training built for agent work. In that stage the model learns from tasks that look like real software jobs. It learns to plan steps, to use tools, and to fix its own slips. The aim is a model that can take a bug report and work it through to a tested fix. Such skill would cut the hand work in large software teams.
arxiv-2601-18518:
Parvendra Kumar studies a light source built to send keys in a quantum safe way. Such keys are shared by a stream of lone bits of light. The share fails if a pulse holds two bits when it should hold one. The source here is a tiny dot with one spare charge, set in a small post of glass-like stuff that traps light.

Kumar tests two ways to wake the dot so it gives off one bit of light at a time. One way shines light that hums in tune with the dot. The next way sweeps the tune in a smooth path. He weighs which way gives a bright stream with the least double hits. A bright, clean source could make quantum key links work at a real scale.
arxiv-2601-21318:
Zirui Zhu and Xiangyang Li build a quantum learning system that keeps spotting network attacks as attack styles change. A detector must learn new attack stages without forgetting old ones. It also faces tight limits on computing power and rules that bar storing raw traffic for long.

Their framework pairs stability tricks with rehearsal that respects privacy. A fidelity anchor keeps old skills from drifting away. Synthetic replay refreshes old attack types without keeping the real data. The design is aimed at near-term quantum hardware, where qubits are few and noisy.
arxiv-2601-21518:
Xinyi Zhang and eight co-authors study how parents and teens think adults should respond to online grooming attempts. This form of abuse harms teens' mental health and physical safety. Most past work focused on spotting the offender's behavior, not on how a teen can answer.

The authors gather views from both parents and teens on unwanted advances. Their angle fills a gap: the targets' own perspective on what helps. Knowing which responses teens would actually use shapes better safety tools and guidance. The work aims at support that families can act on before harm is done.
arxiv-2601-21618:
Martiño Ríos-García, Nawaf Alampara, and Kevin Maik Jablonka test a basic sanity property of algorithms: the answer should not depend on what is being counted. Counting items is counting items, whatever the items are. More broadly, a method's behavior should stay fixed when only the meaning of its inputs changes.

Their test, WhatCounts, isolates that property cleanly. It asks for counts of clear lists with no traps, duplicates, or reasoning steps, across different semantic types. Earlier tests mixed this property with hard reasoning and prompt quirks. A clean failure here shows a model reacting to meaning where meaning should not matter.
arxiv-2601-22718:
Shiye Lei, Zhihao Cheng, and Dacheng Tao steady policy training for reasoning models by weighing the prefix of each try. RL post-training coaxes reasoning from models, but rollouts come from an older policy than the one being updated. Their 2026 preprint notes that this off-policy gap can shake training.

Their prefix importance ratio reweights each rollout by its early tokens. A steadier update should keep gains and cut collapses. The work targets the costly heart of modern model training. Small stability wins there pay off at scale. It is a focused fix, well placed.
arxiv-2601-21918:
Alessandro Nicola Nardi and Morgane Vacher simulate a molecule that rearranges itself when it absorbs light. In 3-hydroxychromone, excitation can trigger a proton to jump within the molecule, a process used by many fluorescent probes and sunscreens. The title frames the study around proton transfer between molecules and the paths that compete with it.

The authors use non-adiabatic dynamics, a simulation method that follows molecules as they hop between energy states after excitation. Tracking the competing pathways shows which motions win and which fade. Their 2026 study helps chemists design molecules whose light-driven behavior is predictable, a need in sensors, imaging dyes, and materials that must survive sunlight.
arxiv-2601-22018:
Jinhao Zhang and co-authors shrink the networks that turn three-dimensional vision into robot action. Diffusion policies based on 3D vision learn complex manipulation skills well. But they share an odd mismatch: a tiny, efficient point-cloud encoder feeds a massive decoder that produces the actions.

Given such a compact scene summary, the authors argue, the huge decoder wastes parameters. Their 2026 preprint presents PocketDP3, a pocket-scale 3D visuomotor policy sized to match its input. Lean policies matter on real robots, where compute is limited, batteries drain, and slow reactions can mean failed grasps. A policy that does the same work with far fewer parameters is easier to deploy outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-22118:
Johann Christensen and co-authors face a blind spot in the safe use of AI. A system that works in a plant, a ward, or a plane must first be cleared for use. The clear form must state the world the system will face: the places, loads, and edge cases. For real plants and wards, that form is too short.

Rich logs of past work exist, but the terms of safe use still must be drawn from them. The team shows how to draw those terms from the logs. Watchdogs in flight, health, and road use ask for such terms more and more. A system cleared for the wrong world is a risk with a stamp on it. Ground terms in real logs, and the stamp means more.
arxiv-2601-20818:
Quantum memory that looks after itself is the goal of Gesa Dünnweber, Georgios Styliaris, and Rahul Trivedi. Their 2026 paper presents a method for autonomous quantum error correction in two spatial dimensions. Standard correction needs active upkeep: constant measurements plus classical processing. Passive correction would avoid that burden. Until now it was only known to work in an unphysical number of dimensions.

The team's method is framed as a quantum cellular automaton. Each cell updates by a fixed, local rule that never changes across the grid. No outside controller steps in to measure or decide. The paper shows this simple setup can protect quantum memory on a flat grid. That is a notable step for quantum hardware. Self-correcting memory would cut the cost of keeping quantum data alive.
arxiv-2601-20718:
Julia Chuzhoy and Merav Parter keep sparse network stand-ins up to date while the network itself keeps changing. Their 2026 paper studies fully dynamic algorithms for graph spanners. A spanner is a sparse subgraph that preserves distances between all vertex pairs. The distances may stretch by a factor called t, the stretch. Sparsity is the point: far fewer edges than the full graph. Roads, networks, and data all use such stand-ins.

Fully dynamic means edges arrive and vanish over time. The algorithm must repair the spanner after each change, fast. Their route uses low-diameter router decomposition. The graph is broken into clusters that act as routers. A preliminary version appeared at SODA 2025. The work serves any system whose map changes while it is being used.
arxiv-2601-21118:
Jason Block measures how complex the models of a simple arithmetic can be. His 2026 paper classifies countable models of Presburger arithmetic. Presburger arithmetic is arithmetic with addition but no multiplication. It is weak enough to be fully decidable. Yet its models can still vary in rich ways. Block takes two approaches to that variety. They are Scott analysis and degree spectra, two tools from logic.

Scott analysis assigns each model a complexity rank. Degree spectra record which computers could rebuild the model. Block investigates which ranks and spectra actually occur. Many results come from one construction trick. Given a linear order, he builds a Presburger group that keeps much of its structure. That bridge imports hard questions from order theory. The paper maps the landscape of models for a tame arithmetic.
arxiv-2512-01518:
Abdo Abouelrous and co-authors learn routes for delivery vans under doubt. Their task mixes random travel times with more than one goal. Goals can clash, like cost versus late drops. Real dispatch must weigh those clashes daily.

Their method learns end to end with deep reinforcement learning. It faces travel time doubt head on. The policy adapts routes as conditions shift. It gives dispatchers a front of trade-off choices, not one fixed plan. Learned routing could cut cost and late rates for fleets in busy cities. Multiple goals are kept visible in the output, so a human dispatcher still makes the final call on cost, time, and fairness trade-offs.
arxiv-2512-01618:
Tetsuji Kato, Hideo Sugama, and Mitsuru Honda study turbulent energy swaps in plasma. Small-scale churn moves heat and particles. It also moves energy between electrons and ions. In weak-collision plasma, that swap can beat direct collision swaps.

Past local studies showed ion heating can be hindered by such churn. The team asks how the swap shapes global temperature profiles. Profiles set fusion reactor performance. If churn steals heat from ions, reactor plans must account for it. Their work links micro churn to macro reactor outcomes. Global profiles link to alpha heating in burning plasma, the very heat source a fusion reactor must keep inside its ion core.
arxiv-2512-00818:
Haozhen Gong and a large team introduce Med-CMR in a 2025 paper on medical AI. Large multimodal models are entering clinical work, where they must reason over images, text, and patient facts together. How well they handle complex medical reasoning is still unclear.

Med-CMR is a benchmark built to test that reasoning in fine detail. It joins visual evidence from medical images with clinical logic, the chain of thinking a doctor follows. A fine-grained test can show where a model reasons soundly and where it guesses. Hospitals and builders can use such results before trusting these systems near patients.
arxiv-2512-01118:
Jaimie Krankel, Guowei Wayne Tu, and Evgueni Filipov study woven columns in a 2025 engineering paper. Woven shell structures are attractive where light weight, damage resilience, and tunable design matter, such as wearables, soft robotics, and aerospace systems. The woven column is a basic building block of such structures.

Full finite element simulations can predict a woven column's stiffness and buckling, but they are computationally expensive. They also do not explain the mechanics behind the scaling relationships engineers need. The authors work toward understanding stiffness and buckling behavior directly. Clear scaling rules would let designers size woven columns without heavy simulation.
arxiv-2601-22818:
Charles Westphal, Keivan Navaie, and Fernando E. Rosas study how language models can hide secrets in plain text. A tuned model can encode a hidden message into its outputs, a trick called steganography. Earlier schemes hid data in ways that were easy to recover once spotted.

The authors define how recoverable a hidden payload is, then build a scheme that is much harder to undo. Their hiding method draws on the geometry of embedding space, where words sit as points. The work warns defenders what to watch for, and shows a stronger attack to test against.
arxiv-2601-22918:
Rubén Calvo and five co-authors study patterns in the microbes that live in and on us. New gene-reading tools have revealed steady statistical patterns across microbial communities. Simple models that treat species as loners, like gases, match many single-species patterns but miss how pairs of species move together.

The authors link the diversity of those pair links to how close a community sits to instability. Near that edge, small shocks can tip the whole system. The idea could help predict when a gut or soil community is about to change sharply.
arxiv-2601-23018:
Sandra Loop, Erik Bertram, Sebastian Juhl, and Martin Schrepp speed up the study of user feedback for software. Product teams pair survey scores with open-ended comments, which explain the scores. Reading thousands of comments by hand is slow, so many insights stay buried.

Their approach joins multi-label classification with generative AI to sort comments at scale. Each comment can carry several labels at once, matching how users mix praise, bugs, and wishes. Faster, faithful sorting helps teams fix what users actually complain about. Open-ended comments are the hard part at scale, because they mix topics freely and resist simple counting methods.
arxiv-2512-00018:
Arthur Ji Sung Baek and Geoffrey Martin present X-SYCON, a swarm design inspired by xylem, the water channels in plants. Their multi-agent system coordinates without planning or communication between agents. Instead, incidents and hazards write into scalar fields that spread and fade over time.

Agents simply climb a local utility built from those fields, with light rules against crowding. Coordination emerges from the passive field dynamics, aimed at dynamic disaster environments. Communication-free control is valuable exactly when networks fail during a crisis. Light anti-congestion and separation rules keep agents from piling onto the same spot once the fields draw them in.
arxiv-2512-00218:
Language models that show their chain of thought give safety monitors something to watch. Matt MacDermott, Qiyao Wei, Rada Djoneva, and Francis Rhys Ward study how training incentives affect that monitorability in 2025. Visible reasoning could reveal undesirable goals, such as pursuing harmful objectives.

How faithfully the written reasoning reflects the model's real process may depend on training choices. Incentives that reward certain outputs could teach models to hide or sanitize their reasoning. The study is AI safety research: it asks whether a promising oversight tool stays trustworthy once training pressure is applied. Monitorability is valuable only while the visible reasoning stays connected to the real process.
arxiv-2512-00518:
The Hydra I galaxy cluster, also called Abell 1060, is a nearby cluster that sits between types. Alpish Srivastava and co-authors present results from the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey in 2025, studying the cluster's hot gas. Hydra I shows properties between cool core and non-cool core clusters.

Little was known about its gas properties and large-scale structure beyond its inner region. All-sky X-ray survey data let the team trace the cluster's faint outskirts, where it merges with the cosmic web. Such outskirts record how clusters keep growing today, making Hydra I a useful nearby laboratory. eROSITA's all-sky coverage is what brings a nearby cluster's faint outskirts into view.
arxiv-2512-00618:
Graph indices compress a network's shape into a single number that predicts chemical or structural properties. Kinkar Chandra Das and Akbar Ali study the augmented Sombor index of graphs in 2025. The index is built from vertex degrees across the graph's edges.

For a connected graph with more than two vertices, each edge contributes a term involving the degrees of its endpoints. Bounding such an index tells chemists which molecular structures maximize or minimize it. Degree-based indices are cheap to compute, so sharp bounds guide screening of large compound libraries before costly experiments. Sombor-type indices weight edges by the degrees at both ends. Connected graphs are the natural domain, since isolated pieces would trivialize the index.
arxiv-2512-03118:
Tiny black holes from the early universe may still be out there. Paul Halpern and co-authors hunt for signs of them in this 2025 work. Such objects, called primordial black holes, could show up in data gathered for other aims.

The team sifted data from searches for planets outside our solar system. Those searches use two methods, radial velocity and gravitational microlensing. The authors looked for odd signs that a tiny black hole caused. Even a null result helps set limits on how many such objects exist. That feeds the wider quest to learn what dark matter is. Planet search archives are vast, so careful sifting can still yield fresh limits from old data.
arxiv-2512-03218:
Thin rubber capsules can be made with walls of even thickness. A. Eddi, S. Perrard, and J. Zhang show how in this 2025 work. Their capsules are about a centimeter wide, made from silicone, and bend very easily.

The team can tune wall thickness during making. Once filled and placed in water, the capsules can be inflated to set pressure and stress. Such soft drops serve as models for cells, bubbles, and soft materials. Controlled capsules help labs test how thin shells stretch, buckle, and flow. Uniform walls matter, since thin spots would burst or sag under pressure changes.
arxiv-2512-03318:
AI agents are entering social settings with humans and other agents. Chandler Smith and a large team test how well they generalize there in this 2025 work. They use Concordia, a framework for mixed-motive scenarios where interests partly align and partly clash.

Old evaluation methods fail to show if social skills transfer to new situations. The team measures that transfer for language model agents. Sound tests matter before agents negotiate, trade, or cooperate on our behalf. The work helps set standards for social AI. Novel social settings test whether agent skills are real or memorized from training scenes.
arxiv-2512-01918:
When two black holes spiral together, each one's gravity stretches the other, and the amount of stretch is summed up in numbers called tidal Love numbers. Classical general relativity says these numbers are exactly zero for black holes in vacuum. A 2025 paper uses the gravitational-wave event GW250114 to test that claim.

The event was recorded with an unmatched signal-to-noise ratio, giving an unusually clean test. If the numbers came out nonzero, the cause could be exotic matter nearby or a failure of general relativity itself. The authors derive the tightest constraints yet on black hole Love numbers, sharpening a precise probe of fundamental physics.
arxiv-2512-02118:
Faint dwarf galaxies are easy to miss and hard to find, yet they record how the smallest galaxies evolve. Catherine Fielder and a large team report in 2025 on four such galaxies found by SEAMLESS, a semi-automated machine learning search for semi-resolved galaxies in the nearby universe.

The four, named Hydrus A, LEDA 486718, Cetus B, and Sculptor 26, span a wide range of environments and evolutionary states, and one is reported here for the first time. Comparing dwarfs across settings shows how surroundings shape small galaxies. Each new nearby dwarf is a close-up laboratory for processes also at work, unseen, in the distant universe.
arxiv-2512-02418:
Stablecoins promise a digital dollar backed by reserves, but the proof is split: coin movements are public on the blockchain while reserve reports sit in unstructured documents. Yuexin Xiang and six co-authors work in 2025 on bridging that on-chain and off-chain transparency gap with large language models.

Coins like USDT and USDC couple issuance controls with reserve attestations, yet the two records are unconnected in practice. Language models can read the off-chain disclosures and line them up against the verifiable on-chain traces. Joining the halves would let auditors and users check a stablecoin's backing continuously instead of trusting periodic summaries.
arxiv-2512-02718:
Dražen Adamović and Veronika Pedić Tomić examine a family of algebraic modules built in recent work by others. The modules belong to an affine Lie algebra and are claimed to be smooth and irreducible, meaning they cannot be split into smaller pieces. Wakimoto modules are a classic explicit form of such objects.

The authors show the new modules admit a Wakimoto type realization at critical and noncritical levels. At the critical level, simple quotients match Wakimoto modules already known to be irreducible. Confirming these links strengthens the toolkit used to classify representations in conformal field theory. Firm ground here lets peers cite these modules with trust in proofs that build on them down the line.
arxiv-2512-03018:
Xiang Xu and five co-authors generate computer aided design solids directly, with exact geometry and closed surfaces. The boundary representation is the standard structure CAD uses to define solid models. Direct end to end generation with watertight topology has remained a challenge for learning models.

AutoBrep is a transformer that writes boundary representations autoregressively, one piece at a time. It aims for high quality and validity in the solids it produces. Reliable generated solids could speed product design, letting engineers start from an AI draft that CAD tools accept without repair. Drafts that open clean in CAD cut the fix up stage. That stage eats half the time in shops that turn AI draws into real parts for sale.
plos-pone-0010018:
Zhonghui Gai, Xiaoyu Wang, Xiaorui Liu, and co-workers studied pollutant-eating bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2010. Carbazole is a stubborn chemical with a dioxin-like shape, and it can damage genes and poison living things. Some bacteria survive it by gaining new genes that let them break it down for food.

In one Sphingomonas strain, the team found the genes that turn carbazole into catechol, a simpler compound. Mobile DNA chunks called IS6100 elements flank those genes on both sides. That layout suggests the clean-up trait can move between bacteria, a clue to how microbes adapt to toxic waste.
plos-pone-0010218:
Antonio Salas and Jorge Amigo asked how few markers can capture mitochondrial diversity in 2010. Mitochondrial DNA varies a great deal, because it mutates faster than nuclear DNA. Its patterns differ deeply between population groups and ethnic groups worldwide. Many studies wanted a small, standard set of markers to type that diversity without sequencing everything.

The pair showed that a reduced number of mitochondrial SNPs can saturate haplotype diversity. In plain terms, a modest marker set captures nearly all the group patterns. Their PLOS ONE finding can cut cost and effort in population genetics surveys.
plos-pone-0010318:
Hakryul Jo, Fabien Loison, Hidenori Hattori and colleagues published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They tested celastrol, a natural product, together with drugs that attack microtubules inside cells. Such drugs can halt cell division and then push cancer cells to die. Some tumors, though, resist them from the start or learn to resist over time.

When dividing cells stall but fail to die, treatment loses its punch. Celastrol, the team reports, weakens the tubulin pairs that microtubules are built from. That damage makes stalled cells more likely to die during division. Pairing a plant compound with standard drugs is the strategy on test here. If it holds up, resistant tumors might be beaten with a combined push.
plos-pone-0009918:
Judging how far away something is feels automatic, yet learning conditions can bend the judgment. Anna Oleksiak and colleagues tested how the way a scene is encoded changes distance estimates. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Encoding conditions are the circumstances under which a person first takes in a scene. Those conditions influenced how distances were later estimated. Distance cues include size, overlap, and perspective lines. The same real distance can thus be judged longer or shorter. The result matters for training drivers, pilots, and anyone who must judge space.
